en: Preface to the Direct Explanation of the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* was composed by the Great Master Aśvaghoṣa to refute the heterodox views of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhist schools.
It was written based upon the principles of one hundred Mahāyāna sūtras in order to give rise to correct faith. Therefore, the treatise establishes the Dharma-realm as its fundamental principle.

This treatise opens two gates—truth and delusion—and penetrates the root of birth and extinction; it exhausts the source of confusion and awakening, points out the correct path of cultivation, and reveals the wondrous gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Comprising more than eleven thousand words in total, there is no principle that it does not fully encompass.
It encompasses all matters and may truly be called the key to the Great Teaching and the compass for the Chan school.

Because its phrasing is concise yet its meaning is vast, and because it is profound and abstruse, it is difficult to interrogate. Xianshou’s old commentary provides the most precise and detailed structural analysis;

however, when combined with the vastness of the sub-commentary, students are like those gazing at the ocean, unable to fathom its depths. I have therefore made slight deletions from the original commentary.
Its detail is so vast that it was considered too sparse and brief for practical use. It has already been carved into woodblocks at Mount Shuangjing and is widely revered there.
Lately, I have reflected that the Dharma-gate is declining and lecture halls are falling into ruin. Novice practitioners have no masters to rely upon, and their own insight is not yet clear;
without depending on this treatise, there would be no way to enter the Mahāyāna or give rise to right faith. I fear that, over time, it may become unheard of. Thus, while dwelling in the mountains...
In the leisure between my delight in dhyāna, I have followed the ancient precedents of our patriarchs to provide a direct commentary on the original text according to my own understanding.

My aim is to ensure a single, coherent thread of meaning, avoiding the proliferation of extraneous citations and digressions. Thus, the principles of the true mind versus the deluded mind, and of delusion versus awakening, are made clearly visible as if looking at black and white.
This will surely be of great benefit to beginners; it is not something I presume to offer to the great masters. My disciple Chao-yi has long relied upon me...

We sat together and discussed the meaning deeply; it seemed we had grasped its essence. Now I am taking this draft back to Guangdong, with the intention of carving it into woodblocks as a Dharma-gift.

I say that even in lands where the Buddha-Dharma has not yet taken root, those among the later generations who are determined to investigate the Great Dharma should likewise take this as their "bet on the potsherd.
As for attaining the meaning and leaving behind the words, entering directly into the present-consciousness of Mind-Only—that lies in the hands of the individual.
Written by the Recluse from Kuangshan,
the Śramaṇa Deqing, on the first day of the second month of winter in the year Gengshen,
during the Taichang era, when he acted as the "Eye of Wisdom" for people.
The Essential Outline of the Dharmadhātu-Dependent Origination of the Huayan School:
Regarding the Seven Patriarchs of Huayan, with Aśvaghoṣa as the first, this treatise does not yet reach the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
Why, then, is he so designated? Previously, no one had understood this explanation, and subsequent students remained utterly bewildered, unable to discern it.
Therefore, I have not exerted further effort, for the ancients established their fundamental tenets yet ultimately could not fully elucidate them for the world.
Thus, I shall now briefly indicate their essentials so that you may know what they take as their foundation.
The Avataṃsaka’s Perfect Teaching unifies the four dharma-realms within the single true dharma-realm. Based upon these four dharma-realms, it establishes the ten mysteries (daśa-guhya-dvāra).

These four realms and ten mysteries are all established by means of the six characteristics (ṣaḷ-lakṣaṇa); thus, the six characteristics constitute the school of perfect interfusion and non-obstruction.
This treatise generally elucidates the six characteristics, thereby encompassing the principles and趣 (qū) of the four realms and ten mysteries.

Nothing is omitted. By taking the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) as the unifying principle of perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*), this treatise encompasses the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without end.
Therefore, it first designates the One Mind True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the essence of the Great General Characteristic Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, while this treatise takes the hundred sections of Mahāyāna scriptures as its primary authority, those hundred sections of Mahāyāna were established by the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha. That is to say:
The provisional [teachings] lead to the real. This treatise, in its entirety, subsumes the provisional vehicles and returns them to the single reality.
Its essential purpose is to reveal the reality that is inherent within the provisional, thereby leading [beings] back to the ultimate pinnacle of perfect interfusion—the ocean of fruition.

Although the principle of perfect interfusion is not explicitly stated in the treatise, the cultivation and realization of the three vehicles, the five natures, and the sudden and gradual approaches all ultimately converge in the source of the ocean of fruition, which is the one mind; thus, it is perfect.
Tanzhong’s possession of these virtues all constitutes the marvel of the One Mind; as this has already been established within the Huayan school, it will not be discussed here.

This treatise is intended solely to guide and gather beings back to the ocean of nature (xinghai). Therefore, that to which one first takes refuge in the treatise is the Reward Body Buddha (saṃbhogakāya), and that which is perceived upon the severing of delusions is likewise the Reward Body Buddha.
Furthermore, the meaning of the treatise fully clarifies that both the defiled and the pure are identical with the Truth, constituting the One Mind.
Regarding their characteristics and functions, taking a single thought-moment as the dependent origination of defilement and purity is entirely identical to the *Avataṃsaka*.

Taking the dependent origination of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as its primary tenet, it holds that the twelvefold dependent origination is none other than the Tathāgata’s universal radiance wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*).
Thus, one should know that to enter the dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, one must necessarily take this treatise as the gateway for entering the dharma-realm.
Regarding the "six characteristics," they are: totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration.
First is the characteristic of totality, which is the True Suchness of the One Mind; it serves as the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Totality of the Dharma-realm.

Second is the distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*): namely, the one mind with its two gates; the three subtleties and six coarsenesses; and the five mental consciousnesses and six defilements—the distinctions of cultivation and abandonment. Third is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):

namely, that the holy and the ordinary, the defiled and the pure, the cause and the fruit, and their essential natures and characteristics, are all identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*), just as [all] clay vessels [are identical in nature to the clay].
This is the analogy of fine dust.

Fourth is the characteristic of difference: that is, the various phenomena of defilement and purity are each distinct, neither identical nor intermingled, just as the dust in different vessels is not one and the same.
Fifth is the characteristic of formation (*sambhava-lakṣaṇa*): that is, all phenomena, whether defiled or pure, are formed through the dependent origination of a single thought-moment.

Sixth is the characteristic of disintegration (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*): that is, all phenomena, whether defiled or pure, each abide in their own position; each lacks intrinsic nature and cannot establish itself independently.

Regarding the four dharma-realms: they are the dharma-realm of principle, the dharma-realm of phenomena, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, and the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.
First is the dharma-realm of principle; this is the True Suchness of the one mind, with no other dharmas apart from it—entirely the single true principle.

Second is the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena (*shifa*). This refers to all the various differentiated phenomena of the mundane and the sacred, the defiled and the pure, the environment and its inhabitants, and cause and effect.

Third is the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai*). Because the aforementioned principle and phenomena mutually establish one another, there are ten gates [of this non-obstruction]. By means of these—

Since phenomena are established by grasping the principle, the principle in its entirety establishes phenomena. Because phenomena are established by means of the principle, phenomena in their entirety are the principle.
Since the principle can establish phenomena, phenomena do not obstruct the principle, but rather manifest it.

Since phenomena are established by grasping the principle, the principle does not obstruct phenomena, but rather integrates them. Because the principle can establish phenomena, phenomena in their entirety are the principle. Phenomena can...
It reveals the principle; thus, the principle is entirely the phenomenon. Because the principle and the phenomenon are mutually identical, the principle and the phenomenon are fused and unimpeded.
This is most clearly demonstrated in the tenfold analysis of the *Dharmadhātudarśana*. Here, I have briefly set forth its essentials.

The fourth is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*). Since the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai*) has already been established above, and now the principle is fully realized as phenomena, there is no need to speak further of that principle.
Because phenomena are fully identical with the principle, all phenomena interpenetrate one another without obstruction or hindrance.
By encompassing all phenomenal dharmas through the six characteristics (*liu xiang*), every dharma becomes perfectly interfused; thus, the ten [mysteries] are established.
The Gate of Profound Mystery (Chongxuanmen) is established to manifest the great function of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

Therefore, this treatise’s exposition of the six aspects (liu xiang) already encompasses the school of the perfect fusion and mutual interpenetration of phenomena and phenomena (shishi wuai yuanrong judé zong). The meaning of the ten mysteries (shi xuan men) is fully explained in the *Huayan Xuantan* (Profound Discourse on the Avataṃsaka); here, I shall merely list their names.
The ten gates of the profound mystery are:
first, the gate of simultaneous and perfect mutual correspondence; second, the gate of the sovereign non-obstruction between the vast and the narrow;
third, the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion; fourth, the gate of the sovereign interpenetration of all phenomena.
5. The Door of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of the Hidden and the Manifest through the Five Secrets; 6. The Door of the Mutual Containment and Stable Establishment of Subtleties;
7. The Door of the Realm of Indra’s Net; 8. The Door of Generating Understanding by Relying on Phenomena to Reveal the Dharma; 9.

The Door of the Accomplishment of the Distinctness of Dharmas Despite the Separation of Time; 10. The Door of the Perfect Fusion and Endowment of Virtues through the Interpenetration of Principal and Retinue.
The meaning of these ten gates of mystery is as explained in the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* and the *Profound Discourse*.
Regarding the title of this treatise, the *Direct Explanation of the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Volume One:
this title constitutes the fundamental framework of the entire treatise. As for the phrase "Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda" (Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna), it is for the purpose of...
In order to give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna, it is said that the "Mahāyāna" is the very essence of the dharma in which one has faith.
As for what is called "dharma," it refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
It possesses the three great meanings of essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*); therefore, it is called "Great" (*dà*).
As for "Vehicle" (*chéng*), it means that this one mind has the sense of conveying and transporting: the Buddhas ride upon it to realize *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*;

the Bodhisattvas ride upon it to extensively cultivate the myriad practices, transforming sentient beings below while seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above; and sentient beings ride upon it as they transmigrate through birth and death.

Death. Because this one mind is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all causes and effects pertaining to the delusion and enlightenment of both the holy and the ordinary, the subsequent text states:
"It is the very essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great General Characteristic of the One Dharma-realm.
Now, I wish to cause sentient beings to have firm faith that this mind is indeed the Mahāyāna, so that their correct understanding is unerring and they may truly give rise to the Mahāyāna.
Because it is based on right faith, it is called the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*. Here, "one who can believe" refers to the person, while "Mahāyāna" refers to the Dharma that is believed;
thus, the meaning encompasses both person and Dharma, as the treatise was established for the sake of those with the capacity [for this teaching].

This treatise was composed during the six hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at which time followers of the Hīnayāna did not believe in "mind-only," but instead grasped at phenomena as existing external to the mind, giving rise to many [erroneous views].
Regarding this treatise on debate: because non-Buddhists harbor false attachments and destroy the True Dharma, the Master of the Treatise gave rise to compassion and specifically composed this work.
Thus, the subsequent causal conditions state: "In order to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments.

Since doubt is the opposite of faith, if one now places faith in this mind, doubt will naturally be eliminated. This treatise is based upon the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Saṃcaya-gāthā*, and approximately one hundred other scriptures.
Composed as a Mahāyāna sūtra, it elucidates the principles of Mind-Only and Consciousness-Only, unifying all within the One Mind.

It serves as the essential framework for both the schools of Nature (Dharmatā) and Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa), profoundly investigating the roots of delusion and awakening, and pointing out the key essentials for spiritual practice.
As it comprehensively subsumes the profound and vast meanings taught by the Tathāgata, it is truly the fundamental tenet of the Great Teaching.
This is the essential purport of the Chan school. A "treatise" (*lun*) is that which definitively resolves right and wrong and elucidates correct principles;

because it distinguishes what is not from the *sūtras* and *vinaya*, it is clarified by means of a treatise. Xianshou’s original commentary is precise and detailed, yet its topical divisions are somewhat disjointed.

Previously, I had deleted redundancies to follow a concise style, calling it the "Abridged Commentary. However, there were still some passages within its prose and meaning that were not smooth; therefore, I have now [revised it].

I have followed the correct meaning of the original commentary and provided this straightforward explanation for the convenience of beginners. I do not dare to venture any arbitrary interpretations of my own.
May readers refrain from rejecting the words because of the person who spoke them; that they may take confidence in them within their own hearts—this is my hope.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa is the author of this treatise. As for "Aśvaghoṣa," it was given as his name because when this Bodhisattva was first born, a herd of horses neighed piteously;
furthermore, whenever he preached the Dharma, the horses would likewise all neigh piteously upon hearing him. (Commentary)
The *Mahāmāyā Sūtra* states: "Six hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, various heterodox teachers will compete to promote false views and destroy the Buddha-dharma.
There will be a bhikṣu named Aśvaghoṣa who is skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma and will subdue all the heterodox followers."
"Paramārtha Tripiṭaka" refers to the name of the translator.

There are two translations of this treatise. The first was by the śramaṇa Paramārtha (translated as "True Meaning") from the country of Ujjayinī in Western India, during the third year of the Chengsheng era of Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty, at Jiankang in Hengzhou.
It was translated [in one fascicle] at Xing Temple; it consists of twenty-four sheets.

Later, the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda from the Kingdom of Khotan—whose name means "Delight in Learning"—translated it into two fascicles, also consisting of twenty-four sheets, during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian of the Great Zhou dynasty at Foshouji Temple in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). The former translation is currently in circulation.
Commentary composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Taiyuan Monastery in the Western Capital of the Tang Dynasty;
Direct Explanation by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Fayun Monastery on Mount Mingkang.
Before composing this treatise, I first offer my respectful homage and request [the Buddhas] to bestow their grace. Hereafter, I shall formally expound the treatise itself. First:
Having taken refuge and paid homage throughout the ten directions, I am about to compose this treatise; first, it is necessary to take refuge in the Triple Gem and request their empowerment.

The reason for doing so is that this treatise is composed as an exposition of the sūtras, and since the sūtras were spoken by the Buddha, his wisdom is profoundly deep and cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings; therefore, I pray to the Three [Jewels].
Because it is empowered and sustained by the majestic power of the Jewels, this seal of the treatise accords with the Buddha-mind and demonstrates that the Dharma has a source of authority;
for the Three Jewels are the basis of reliance. Now, the expression "I take refuge" signifies the mind that performs the act of taking refuge.

To enter into the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one must first forget the mark of self (*ātman*). Since life governs and encompasses the six sense faculties, when one returns life [to its source], both body and mind perish;
this is the ultimate form of taking refuge. The ten directions constitute the boundary of that which is to be taken as refuge.
This means that the doctrinal principles of the treatise herein represent the essence of the ten dharma-realms; therefore, one must take refuge in them throughout the entirety of the ten directions.

Regarding the Three Jewels: because the mind has no boundaries, their objects are likewise immeasurable. The intent is to take refuge in the inexhaustible Three Jewels within the Indra’s Net of lands throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
"Omniscient in supreme activity, sovereign over form without obstruction—homage to this Buddha Jewel, the Greatly Compassionate Savior of the World.
The Buddha responds to sentient beings through the three wheels [of body, speech, and mind]. The three wheels to which we now take refuge are all most preeminent;
this indicates that he is neither a nirmāṇakāya nor a sāmbhogikakāya, but rather a saṃbhogakāya manifested from the Dharma. "Omniscient" refers to the mental wheel.

It is supreme. Ordinary beings do not know it; non-Buddhists have perverted knowledge of it; those of the Two Vehicles have partial knowledge of it; Bodhisattvas have fragmentary knowledge of it; only the Buddha knows it universally.

With his wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*), he realizes the principle, such that there is no aspect of the principle he does not penetrate. With his wisdom of expedient means (*upāya-jñāna*), he discerns the capacities of sentient beings, such that there is no capacity for which he is not appropriate.
Even down to the mental thoughts, inclinations, and desires of all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*, there is nothing he does not fully know; therefore, it is called "universal."

Furthermore, the unimpeded mastery over form is the most supreme of bodily actions (*kāyakarman*). In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said that the Buddha possesses immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and each mark possesses immeasurable secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).
Every faculty is perfectly interfused, pervasive and sovereign; the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) are distinct, neither corrupted nor intermingled—hence they are called "unimpeded.
The Great Compassion that saves the world is the most supreme of vocal actions (*vākkarman*); for the Buddha, by means of the wheel of sound...
He preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, such that each understands through a single sound; therefore, his speech is most supreme.

"World" (*loka*) refers to the world of sentient beings, the place to be saved. "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) is the mind capable of saving them. Because the Tathāgata employs only Great Compassion as his power, the term "he" (*sa*) points to this person.
And his physical form, the ocean of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*), and the treasury of immeasurable merit—this is the taking of refuge in the Dharma Jewel.
"And" means that one does not merely take refuge in the Buddha, but also takes refuge in the Dharma.
"His body" refers to the aforementioned body of the Buddha; because the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, it refers to the teachings that flow forth from *tathatā*.

The Dharma-body is eternally abiding, because the complete body of the Tathāgata already exists within it. This is intended to reveal that this Dharma is essentially non-dual from the Buddha’s own substance and characteristics.
Dharmatā-tathatā (the suchness of the nature of phenomena) specifically refers to the essence of the Dharma;

that is to say, the tathatā of dharmatā is the true substance of the Dharma-body. Because of this Dharma-body, it is called "Buddha-nature" when residing in sentient beings. When [residing in] non-...
Sentient nature (*citta*) is the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), because it constitutes the essential substance of all phenomena, whether defiled or pure.

Because it remains unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging, it is likened to the ocean: when encountering the wind, various waves arise, yet the moist nature remains non-dual;
thus, it is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). Within the Tathāgatagarbha, all virtues are contained and subsumed; therefore, it is called the "Treasury of Merits" (*guṇagañja*).

To practice according to reality as described above is what constitutes taking refuge in the Sangha Jewel. While the Sangha generally includes both ordinary and noble beings, as well as those of the Great and Small Vehicles, the phrase "practicing according to reality" here refers specifically to Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi).
According to a later translation, this refers to the "Sangha of the Treasury of Boundless Virtues who Diligently Seek Perfect Enlightenment. Thus, it is...
The first line praises his virtues; because he is able to gather all virtues within himself, he is called a "Treasury.
The subsequent lines describe the purpose for composing this treatise:
In order to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments, and to give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna.

Because the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed, this work is composed with the following intent. No teaching is established in vain; it must have a specific purpose. Herein there are four intentions:

first, because those of the two vehicles do not believe in "mind-only," this work reveals the correct meaning of the single mind to cause them to eliminate their doubts. Second, [the remaining three intentions follow].
First, because non-Buddhists harbor false attachments, this serves as an antidote to those false attachments, causing them to abandon their wrong views.

Third, because practitioners have not yet initiated correct practice, this distinguishes the characteristics of setting out upon the path, causing them to give rise to right faith as the foundation for practice.
Fourth, it is so that faith may be brought to fulfillment, enabling one to enter and abide in the path without regression and become capable of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood;
thus it is said that "the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed. It is for these many purposes that this treatise was composed.
The treatise says: There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it should be explained.

This is the general statement of the fundamental thesis of the treatise. "Dharma" refers to the fundamental thesis upon which the treatise relies, meaning that the single dharma of the One Mind possesses two gates and three great meanings;
thus, it correctly demonstrates the central doctrine. "Mahāyāna" is translated here as "Great Vehicle," meaning:
The mental factor that is our primary tenet is precisely the Mahāyāna; the ability to believe in this mind is the very root of the Mahāyāna.
Because it possesses such supreme benefits, it must be explained.
The exposition consists of five sections. What are these five? First, the section on causes and conditions; second, the section on establishing the thesis;
third, the section on explanation; fourth, the section on practicing faith; and fifth, the section on the benefits of encouraging practice.
This indicates the structural format of the treatise; it is the opening of the chapters. Now, as for the division into chapters, it is intended to make known that each meaning has its proper place.
Thus, the main text of this treatise is established with five sections in sequential order. Since phenomena do not arise in isolation, they must have causes and conditions;
therefore, the introductory causes and conditions are listed first. Once the causal basis is clarified, there must be a fundamental thesis; therefore—

Next is the establishment of the thesis (*pratijñā*). Since the fundamental tenets are profound and mysterious, they cannot be understood without explanation; therefore, this is followed by the explanation (*nirdeśa*). Once the meaning of the Dharma has been explained, it cannot be attained without practice;

therefore, this is followed by the cultivation of faith through practice (*caryā-pratipatti-śraddhā*). Although explanation and practice have been set forth, those of dull faculties may become indolent or regress;

therefore, this is followed by the exhortation to practice (*anuśamsā*). These constitute the major structural sections of this treatise. Generally, a sūtra consists of three parts; this [section on] causes and conditions is—
Preface. The middle three sections constitute the *zhengzong* (the orthodox teaching); the exhortation to practice constitutes the *liutong* (the dissemination).

Below is the commentary on the section on causes and conditions (*yinyuanyuan*). First, the section on causes and conditions is explained. Question: By what causes and conditions was this treatise composed? Answer: These are the causes and conditions.
There are eight. What are these eight? First is the general characteristic of the causal conditions:
namely, to cause sentient beings to leave all suffering behind and attain ultimate bliss, rather than seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Among these eight causes and conditions, the first is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which serves as the catalyst for this treatise.

Ordinary beings and non-Buddhists are deluded regarding this single mind, thereby incurring the sufferings of birth-and-death in discrete segments—the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Even the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas still possess the subtle suffering of the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarā-maraṇa*). Now, [this] is revealed and taught.
One should cultivate based on this mind, thereby realizing the joy of the Dharma of awakening and the bliss of the tranquility of nirvana;
yet one does so solely for the sake of causing sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness, not out of a desire for worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Second, it is for the purpose of explaining the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata, so that all sentient beings may attain correct understanding without error.
This serves as the basis for the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" and the "Section on Explanation," wherein the correct meaning is revealed and wrong attachments are countered.

This is the section on the causes and conditions for the arising [of this treatise]. Because sentient beings lack correct understanding and frequently give rise to false views—failing to penetrate the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata—I now establish within the "Section on the Establishment of the Meaning" the principles of the One Mind, the Two Gates, and the Three Greatnesses.
This is the very foundation of the Tathāgata; it is now explained in detail so that all sentient beings may attain correct understanding without error.
Thirdly, it is for the sake of enabling those sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured to become capable of non-retrogressive faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Therefore, this constitutes the causal conditions for the subsequent analysis of the characteristics of setting out upon the path. For that text states:
"It causes those of sharp faculties to develop resolute faith, to advance toward the Great Vehicle, and to become capable of abiding in non-retrogressive faith. This corresponds to...

Because they have fulfilled the mind of the ten stages of faith, it is called "matured. Because they enter the stage of the ten abidings within the assembly of those fixed in right determination, it is called "non-retrogressive.
Fourth, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings with meager roots of goodness to cultivate and practice the mind of faith.

This refers to the subsequent section on "Cultivating Faith. It means that for the sake of sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight, one causes them to give rise to the four kinds of mind and practice the five kinds of conduct, so that their roots of goodness may gradually reach maturity.
Because their faith is not yet full, it is called "slight"; because it causes them to advance toward fulfillment, it is called "cultivating faith."

Fifth: To demonstrate skillful means for the purpose of eliminating the obstacles of evil karma, properly guarding the mind, remaining far removed from delusion and pride, and escaping the net of heterodoxy.
Hereafter, for those of inferior faculties who are prone to regression, there are four [methods] because they rely upon many skillful means. Among these four, the first...
Third, there are the lower, middle, and superior [levels]. The last one encourages practice; here, it shall be the lower grade.

This means that for those whose karma is heavy and afflictions many, so that roots of goodness are difficult to arouse, the expedient means of prostration and repentance are taught to eliminate the obstructions of evil karma, to distance oneself from delusion and arrogance, and to escape the net of demonic influences.

Sixth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote to the mental faults of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

This corresponds to the middle grade. In the subsequent section on the gates of cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are clarified together to eliminate the dual attachments of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles; therefore, it is termed an "antidote."
Seventh: To demonstrate the expedient means of single-minded mindfulness so that one may be born before the Buddha and certainly never retreat from the faith;
this corresponds to the "Superior Grade. This refers to the exhortation to be born in the Pure Land at the end of the "Section on Cultivating Faith" below.

this is the summary conclusion regarding the reasons for composing the treatise. Indeed, the fundamental intention of the Bodhisattva is to deliver sentient beings; therefore, by means of...

Question: This teaching is already fully contained within the Sūtras; why is it necessary to state it again? Answer:

Although this teaching exists within the Sūtras, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal, and the conditions for their reception and understanding differ—namely, that while the Tathāgata was in the world, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties, and the speaker’s physical and mental karma was superior—so that when the perfect voice was uttered once, all diverse classes [of beings] understood equally.
If [the meaning] is already understood, then there is no need for further discussion.
This question clarifies the purpose for composing this treatise. Question: As shown above, each and every dharma-gate is fully contained within the sūtras spoken by the Buddha.
What leisure do you have to discuss them again? Answer: Because the faculties of sentient beings vary...
Regarding the sharpness or dullness of faculties: because the conditions for receiving the teaching are not equal, there are differences between the sūtras and the śāstras.

This refers to the explanation that the capacities of the root-faculties (indriya) differ, and thus their reception and understanding are each distinct; hence, there is a lack of uniformity in the extensiveness or brevity of the sūtras and śāstras.

Generally speaking, when the Tathāgata was in the world, the faculties of sentient beings were sharp because the causal conditions for their capacity were superior; they personally beheld the Buddha’s body and the excellence of his three karmas.

It is superior. To hear the perfect voice directly is itself a supreme condition. If this is so—that a single sound is proclaimed and beings of diverse categories understand it simultaneously—then this does not even depend upon the sūtras compiled by others; what need is there, then, for treatises?

If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings who are able to attain understanding through extensive hearing by means of their own power—this statement that "after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa" indicates that spiritual capacities (*indriya*) are not uniform and conditions (*pratyaya*) differ for each, such that their reception and understanding vary.
Consequently, regarding the sūtras and śāstras, there are differences in their breadth and brevity. Furthermore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the True Dharma...
At that time, not far from the Buddha, there were those with sharp faculties who possessed their own power of wisdom; thus, they were able to gain understanding by hearing many sūtras extensively.
There were also sentient beings who, through their own power, gained much understanding from hearing only a little.
These are also beings of sharp faculties who possess their own power of wisdom and do not depend on extensive learning;

at a single word, the ground of their minds opens up, and within a single scroll, the sky of meaning shines brightly. For such two types of individuals as these, there is no need for further discussion.
There may be sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding through extensive treatises;
these are of inferior capacity and dull faculties, lacking the intellectual power to understand the profound meaning within the sūtras themselves,
and must rely on the extensive learning of voluminous treatises to achieve comprehension.
Since sentient beings exist, and because extensive treatises are cumbersome due to their length, those who delight in *dhāraṇī*— which condenses many meanings into few words—
and are able to grasp the understanding [therein] [should listen].
Since there is a natural inclination toward wearying oneself with excessive detail, a concise exposition must be undertaken;
this is precisely the causal condition for this treatise.
Thus, this treatise should be explained in order to comprehensively encompass the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.
"This treatise"—this conclusion expresses the intent of composing the present work. This treatise, from beginning to end, consists of over eleven thousand words;
it thus comprehensively encompasses the vast and profound Dharma of the Tathāgata and its boundless, wondrous meanings, all of which are contained herein. It may truly be called a "text" (wen).
Though extremely concise, its meaning is most expansive; it encompasses the profound principles of the hundred Mahāyāna sections without exception.

It illuminates the single mind of the Dharma-realm as clearly as observing fruit in the palm of one's hand. Truly, this is the mysterious gateway for entering into principle and the sublime guide for spiritual practice.
May students not fail to devote their whole hearts to it.
The section on causes and conditions has already been explained. Next, the section on establishing the meaning (*arthavyavasthāna*) will be explained.

Regarding the Mahāyāna, there are generally two kinds. What are these two? First, the phenomena (*dharma*); second, the meaning (*artha*). As for what is called "phenomena," it refers to the mind of sentient beings.
This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena. Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed. Why is this so?

For this reason, the aspect of the suchness of this mind reveals the essence of Mahāyāna; the aspect of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind can reveal the essence, characteristics, and function of Mahāyāna itself.
This section on the Establishment of the Thesis first sets forth the fundamental essence of the One Mind to clarify the name and meaning of the Mahāyāna.
That which is called "Dharma" refers to the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single True Dharma-realm; it is the pure true mind of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Now, this mind is, in its essence, beyond both the holy and the ordinary; fundamentally, it is neither deluded nor awakened, for its self-nature is intrinsically pure.
It is utterly devoid of delusive defilement; it is free from names and free from marks; it transcends all dualistic oppositions;
it is the sole true source, wherein no second dharma exists. How, then, could there even be the name "Mahāyāna"? As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says, "The Mahāyāna is not a vehicle.

That we now speak of the "Mahāyāna" is merely because this name is established in reliance upon the minds of sentient beings. What is meant by "comprehensively encompassing the mundane and the supramundane" is as follows:
Regarding the Dharma, a sutra states that the Tathāgatagarbha transforms into the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings.
This is the mind of sentient beings, which is the Ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness) formed by the delusion of the Tathāgatagarbha into the Ālaya-vijñāna.
This mind is composed of the union of the unborn and undying [nature] with the arising and ceasing [phenomena]. As for this consciousness:
Its essence is fundamentally True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is also called Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). Originally, it is devoid of arising and ceasing;
however, now, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), that pure mind is stirred, giving rise to arising and ceasing, and thus it becomes the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).

Because this mind is fundamentally True Suchness, it encompasses the four supramundane dharmas of the noble ones (*ārya*). Because it relies upon karmic consciousness, there is birth and death (*saṃsāra*); therefore, it encompasses the six classes of ordinary beings.
Therefore, it is said that this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Now, in order to reveal the meaning of the Mahāyāna based on this mind, we do so because the single mind of the dharma-realm possesses the three great meanings of essence, attribute, and function.
Based now on this single mind, we open the two gates of True Suchness and Arising-and-Ceasing. If we consider them in relation to the gate of True Suchness, then...
It is free from all marks; both name and phrase are transcended. It merely reveals its essence, without revealing its marks or functions;

therefore, it is said that this directly demonstrates the essence of Mahāyāna. If one considers it according to the gate of arising and ceasing, then the false arises in dependence upon the true, thereby manifesting its marks and functions.

Therefore, within the gate of arising and ceasing, it fully reveals the three great meanings of essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*); for this reason, it is called "Great" (*Mahā*).
Based on these two dharmas—truth and falsehood—there are two forms of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); for this reason, it is called a "Vehicle" (*yāna*). Thus it is said:
"Based on the minds of sentient beings, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed. This generally sets forth the reasons for the name "Mahāyāna. First, it is shown:
The dharmas of true and false mind universally constitute the essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma-body.
Below, the meaning of the three greatnesses (trisvabhāva) is shown.
As for what is called "meaning," there are three kinds. What are these three? First is the greatness of essence (svabhāva-mahattva), which refers to all dharmas.

First is the greatness of essence (*tathatā*), because it is equal and neither increases nor decreases. Second is the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with immeasurable innate virtues (*guṇa*).
Third is the greatness of function (*vṛtti*), because it can produce all mundane and supramundane causes and fruits of goodness;
it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted, and all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the state of a Tathāgata.

This is the section on the headings that enumerates the categories of meaning, intended to reveal how the Mahāyāna obtains its name; it serves as the foundation for the correct exposition that follows.
As for what is meant by "meaning" (artha): names are established based upon meanings. For what reason, then, is the name "Mahāyāna" established?
Indeed. Because it possesses the three great meanings, it receives the name "Great" (Mahā); because it possesses the two meanings of "transportation," it receives the name "Vehicle" (Yāna).

These names and meanings exist due to the conjunction of the two dharmas of reality and delusion; therefore, it is said that "the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed based on the minds of sentient beings.
If one speaks of its essence, however, it is solely the single True Suchness (Tathatā), which is impartial.

They are equal and non-dual; neither increasing nor decreasing, they are therefore referred to simply as "essence" (*tattva*). Now, based on the *tathāgatagarbha*, it follows the conditions of defilement and purity.
When it follows the conditions of purity, it possesses immeasurable qualities of its own nature (*svabhāva-guṇa*), thereby constituting supramundane cause and effect.
When it follows the conditions of defilement, it transforms its own natural qualities into afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, thereby constituting [mundane cause and effect].
The causes and effects of the world thus manifest through their characteristics and functions.

Because these three greatnesses (*mahat*) are never deficient in either the defiled or the pure, and remain unchanging throughout birth and extinction, they are called "great. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas ride upon this mind;
therefore, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*). The primary purport of this treatise is solely to explain this meaning; therefore, it serves as its fundamental tenet.
The section on the establishment of the doctrine has already been explained. Next, the section on the explanation will be discussed.
This serves to conclude the preceding and introduce the subsequent.
There are three kinds of explanation. What are the three? First, the manifestation of the correct meaning; second, the counteracting of errors.
[The commentary] says: Third is the section on the characteristics of the differentiation of the path of practice (*pratipatti*).
This is the heading, enumeration, and explanation of the names. "Manifesting" (*saṃdarśana*) refers to the correct explanation of the doctrines and meanings upon which the Mahāyāna is based.

"Counteracting" (*pratipakṣa*) means that once the primary essence has been clarified, one must eliminate erroneous views. The above explains the meaning of "Great" (*mahā*). "Practice" (*pratipatti*) refers to the progressive advancement toward [the goal].
Next, the meaning of the Vehicle is correctly elucidated. This is one section of the main body of the teaching and consists of three parts.
To explain according to the meaning and reveal the correct principle: based on the dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates.
What are these two? First, the gate of the Suchness of Mind; second, the gate of the Arising and Ceasing of Mind. These two gates each comprehensively encompass all dharmas.
What is the meaning of this? It is because these two gates are not separate from one another.
This marks the fundamental thesis and the correct principle; by explaining the established doctrine based on the minds of sentient beings, it reveals the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
This serves as the essential framework for the entire treatise. This treatise was composed based on the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other sūtras. Now, first—
The two gates of mind are established based on the sūtras. The sūtra states: "That which is quiescent extinction is called the one mind; the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
This single dharma of the mind does not establish anything; both existence and non-existence are discarded, and both sentient beings and Buddhas are empty.
Therefore, it is said that it is far removed from the awakened and the awakened-to; both of these are entirely abandoned. Thus, neither the real nor the false is established.
It is quiescent and profoundly still. Therefore, in the sutra, Mahāmati asks about the names, marks, and delusive thoughts of the hundred-and-eight phrases based on the ten dharma-realms.

Thus, the Buddha replies that "all are not. Now, it is said that this mind is *tathatā* (suchness), serving as the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the single dharma-realm; this is precisely the "quiescent one-mind" indicated in the sutra. Because of this—
The quiescence of the mind is ineffable and cannot be demonstrated. Therefore, Mahāmati asks how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses;
this is because within the gate of arising and ceasing, verbal expression is possible. Thus, the five dharmas and the three natures all exist based upon the gate of arising and ceasing.
For the Sūtra states that the various consciousnesses briefly have three kinds of characteristics, namely: true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
Regarding the "manifesting consciousness" (*khyāti-vijñāna*) and the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*):

thus, when this treatise establishes two gates based on the one mind, it establishes the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) based on the true consciousness, and establishes the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) based on the manifesting consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena.
Therefore, the "True Suchness" discussed here is the True Suchness of the one mind; hence, all characteristics, names, and deluded thoughts are entirely non-existent, and not a single dharma exists.

Established. All four propositions are discarded because they rely upon the two consciousnesses; thus, the three subtleties, the six coarsenesses, the five mental faculties, and the six defilements all belong to the delusions of names and marks (*nāma-nimitta-vikalpa*) and are subsumed within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*). This is the fundamental tenet of this treatise’s established doctrine.
As for the previous statement in the established doctrine that "the mind of sentient beings encompasses mundane and supramundane phenomena," this refers generally to the True [Suchness].
The single mind of the fusion of the false and the real comprehensively contains all phenomena, both defiled and pure;

it is to manifest this that the Mahāyāna is named after its basis. Now, to say that these two gates each collectively encompass all phenomena is to reveal that the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna—being the fusion of the true and the false—each possess their own functional power and mutually contain one another.
This reveals the wondrous nature of inconceivable perfuming and transformation.

Since the Tathāgatagarbha possesses all pure merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is now deluded into becoming the ālayavijñāna, whereby those sands of pure merits are transformed into defiled conditions.
Now, regarding the statement that each [aspect] is "comprehensively subsumed": when the *tathāgatagarbha* is perfumed by pure dharmas, the True is empowered while the false is rendered powerless;

thus, the conditions of defilement are immediately transformed into pure dharmas, and these conditions of defilement are comprehensively subsumed within the *tathāgatagarbha*, universally functioning as inconceivable pure activity. Conversely, if it is perfumed by the defiled conditions of ignorance, then the false...
That which possesses power is, in truth, powerless; thus, pure qualities (*śubha-dharma*) immediately transform into defiled conditions.

Consequently, these pure qualities are subsumed within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), functioning collectively as inconceivable karmic activity. This, then, is in its entirety the Tathāgatagarbha.

It is simply through following the perfuming and transformation of defilement and purity that the real and the false become distinct from one another, yet they mutually contain and encompass each other;
thus it is said, "Because these two gates are not separate. This clarifies the wondrous inconceivable perfuming and transformation of the Tathāgatagarbha;

therefore, these [distinctions] are used as headings to comprehensively indicate and manifest this principle. Below, in the main body of the treatise, [the section on] the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing addresses defilement...
The pure perfuming merely unfolds these three characters.

That which is the suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā*) is precisely the substance of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm; it is what is called the nature of the mind, neither arising nor ceasing.
All dharmas exist only through the distinctions created by deluded thought. If one is separated from deluded thought, then...

There are no marks of any objective realm. Therefore, all phenomena have from the very beginning been free from the mark of verbal expression, free from the mark of names, and free from the mark of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change, and indestructible.
It is solely this one mind; therefore, it is named *tathatā* (Suchness).
This refers to the "Mind-as-Suchness" within the section on the Establishment of the Thesis. Why is it called *tathatā*?
It is because it is the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-Gate of the Single Dharma-Domain (*dharmadhātu*). As for the "Single Dharma-Domain," it is the non-dual reality.

The mind is that upon which all phenomena rely as their cause. "Dhātu" (realm) means cause. As for the essence of the general characteristic dharma-gate, it is the general characteristic of the causes and effects of the environment and inhabitants of all noble ones and ordinary beings; all of these take this mind as their essence upon which they rely.
However, the substance of this mind is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; it is what is called the eternally abiding true mind.
Since it is said to be the single reality, it originally possesses no marks of differentiation. That there is now differentiation is merely a manifestation revealed in contrast to deluded thought.
If there were no deluded thought, then the single mind would be profoundly still and tranquil, entirely devoid of any marks of differentiated realms.
Although the myriad phenomena (*dharma*) are differentiated, each and every phenomenon is true. Therefore, from the very beginning, all phenomena are beyond the reach of words and thought;
the sphere of mental activity has ceased. Consequently, all verbal expressions, names, and conceptual discriminations are unattainable;
thus, they are all said to be "detached" (*viveka*). Because of this, defilement and purity cannot be distinguished as different; hence it is said that they are ultimately level (*sama*).
It is not transmuted by the four characteristics; therefore, it is without change. It does not belong to the conditioned; therefore, it cannot be destroyed.
It is solely this one mind, with no other dharmas. Because it is non-delusive and unchanging, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness).

Because all verbal expressions are merely provisional names without reality, existing only in accordance with deluded thoughts and being ultimately unattainable, even that which is called "true suchness" (tathatā) has no characteristics. It is the ultimate limit of verbal expression; one uses words to dispel words.
This essence of true suchness cannot be dispelled, for all phenomena are entirely true suchness. Nor can anything be established, for all phenomena are identical.
It remains as it was. One should know that all phenomena are ineffable and inconceivable; therefore, they are called *tathatā* (suchness).
This explains the aforementioned "separation from conditions" (*ālambana-viveka*) to demonstrate that *tathatā* is beyond all relational dependence.

Question: Why is *tathatā* free from the characteristics of names and speech? Answer: Because all verbal expressions are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and lack substantial reality. Question: Why is it free from the mind?
"Is it an object of conditions? Answer: "Because it cannot be apprehended by following after deluded thoughts. Question:
"If it is said that the mind’s objects are all transcended, how can this be the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness)? Answer: "Suchness itself has no characteristic.

Because the essence of suchness is free from characteristics and is quiescent, it cannot be grasped by means of characteristics. Question: "Since it is free from names and transcends characteristics,"
Why is there the name "Tathatā" (Suchness)? Answer: The name "Tathatā" is the ultimate limit of verbal expression;
beyond this name, there is nothing further that can be added. Therefore, the name "Tathatā" is used merely to dispel attachment to names and words;
it is not that Tathatā possesses any characteristic that can be named. Question: If names and words have already been dispelled, [what remains?]
"Can the essence of this *tathatā* (suchness) also be negated? Answer: "The essence of this *tathatā* is real and without delusion;
therefore, it cannot be negated. For that which can be negated is delusion, while that which cannot be negated is reality.
Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely true, there is nothing that can be negated. Question: "If all delusions are negated together, does one then establish only the True [Reality]?"
Is there even a single dharma? Answer: There is likewise nothing that can be established. This is because if there were a dharma existing separately from suchness, then speech could be established;
however, since all dharmas are of the same essence as suchness—neither two nor distinct—how could anything be established?
Because this is the case, one should know that all dharmas are ineffable and inconceivable. Therefore.
It is named True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is the ground that is ultimately free from all characteristics. Question:
If this is the meaning, how can sentient beings accord with it and thereby attain entry? Answer:
If one knows that although all phenomena are spoken of, there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken; and although they are contemplated, there is likewise no one who contemplates.
It can be recollected; this is called "conformity" (*anuloma*). If one is free from recollection, it is called "attaining entry.
This question clarifies conformity and entry, thereby elucidating the sphere of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). A question is asked:

Since the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is said to transcend the paths of thought and language, such that raising the mind is an error and stirring a thought is a deviation, how then can all sentient beings...
How does one accord with and attain entry? The answer is: if one knows that although all phenomena are spoken of, there is nothing that can be spoken;
and although they are contemplated, there is nothing that can be contemplated—this is the skillful means of accord. To be free from such contemplation is called "attaining entry.
Because the realm of freedom from thought can only be realized through direct correspondence [with reality], it is called "attaining entry."
The preceding section clarifies the object of contemplative wisdom by means of transcending words;
the following section clarifies the object for generating faith by means of explaining virtues through words.
Furthermore, regarding *tathatā* (suchness), there are two kinds of meanings distinguished according to verbal expression: first, emptiness as it truly is (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*). By means of...
Because it can ultimately manifest reality; second, it is not empty in accordance with reality, because it possesses its own essence and is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature.

This explains the characteristics of the true suchness of this mind from the section on "Establishing the Meaning" by means of analyzing its qualities through words. The former [section] has already manifested [this].
To depart from words is merely to indicate its essence; therefore, it is said that "it is the single dharma-realm, an essence that is equal and non-dual.
Now, however, relying on words to differentiate its characteristics, it is said that "there are two kinds of meanings. "Meaning" (*artha*) is equivalent to "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).

Because these are characteristics that are identical to the essence, only *tathatā* (suchness) is designated; this is to reveal that the essence possesses two meanings: emptiness and non-emptiness. Regarding "emptiness as it truly is":

This means that within the substantial reality of *tathatā* (suchness), there is no false defilement. Because the false is empty, the substantial reality manifests of itself; hence it is said that "the reality is ultimately manifested.

Regarding the statement that it is "not empty according to reality" and possesses its own essence: this is because it differs from the false, which has no essence; thus, its own essence is not empty, meaning it is not a state of annihilation.
As for the statement that it "is fully endowed with the nature of untainted virtues": [it refers to the fact that these virtues are inherently present].
Because it differs from the *āsrava*-afflictions, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is said to be "fully endowed" and so forth.

This means that although the substantial reality is empty and devoid of false defilements, it is nonetheless capable of being fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-guṇa*). The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states:
"Because adventitious dust is empty, it is separated from the *dharmadhātu*; the unsurpassed Dharma is not empty, and thus it accords with the *dharmadhātu*."
Thus, although delusive defilements are empty, their virtuous characteristics are not empty.
That which is called "emptiness" means that from the very beginning, all defiled dharmas have been non-corresponding;
that is to say, they are free from the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena because there is no false mental ideation.

This is a brief explanation of the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It refers to the true substance of *tathatā* (suchness). Because it is fundamentally non-existent in dependence upon deluded defilements, its essence is said to be empty.
However, if one were to be separated from deluded defilements, there would be no "emptiness" that could be predicated;

for this true essence has, from the beginning, never been associated with any defiled phenomena. That is to say, once one is free from all the differentiated characteristics of deluded phenomena, [all conceptualization] is cut off.
Regarding the objective realm: because there is no mind of false conceptualization, the mind is severed; when both mind and object are severed, it is therefore called "emptiness as it truly is.

One should know that the self-nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is neither characterized by existence, nor characterized by non-existence, nor characterized by the absence of existence, nor characterized by the absence of non-existence.

It is not the characteristic of both existence and non-existence; it is not the characteristic of identity; it is not the characteristic of difference; it is not the characteristic of neither identity nor difference;
it is not the characteristic of both identity and difference.

This is an extensive explanation of the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), intended to reveal the true substance of *tathatā* (suchness), which is fundamentally free from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*) and transcends the hundred negations.
However, the four extremes of existence and non-existence are the conceptualizations of those within the Buddhist tradition who have not grasped the essential meaning;
the four extremes of identity and difference are the erroneous calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Thus, the essence of *tathatā* is none other than the true *prajñā*.
Emptiness. If the meaning of Prajñā is not realized, one falsely gives rise to four reckonings; these constitute the four types of slander.

Now, it is revealed that since the four positions are already transcended, the hundred negations are naturally dispelled. The true substance of Prajñā manifests impartially before one; therefore, it is collectively described as "not."
The one hundred and eight negations (*lakṣaṇa-aṣṭottaraśata*) of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* do not, in total, transcend these two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
To speak of them collectively: because all sentient beings possess a deluded mind that discriminates from moment to moment, [all things] are fundamentally non-corresponding;
therefore, they are said to be empty. If one is free from the deluded mind, there is truly nothing that can be called empty.
This passage clarifies the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It refers to the true substance of *tathatā* (suchness), which is not an object of conceptualization or discrimination.
Therefore, the various deluded thoughts and discriminations of sentient beings are entirely inconsistent with this substance.

To eliminate those deluded notions, it is said that the substance is empty. If one were separated from the deluded mind, even "emptiness" would not be established; how much less so [any other attribute]?
The single word "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) can be spoken. This means that once deluded thoughts have departed, even "reality" (*tattva*) is not established;
this is what is called the ultimate manifestation of the real.

As for what is called "non-emptiness," it is because the essence of phenomena has already been revealed as empty and devoid of delusion; this is precisely the true mind (*bhūtamanas*), which is eternal and constant.

When the pure dharmas are fulfilled through transformation, it is called "not empty. Furthermore, there is no characteristic to be grasped, because this is a realm free from conceptual thought, accessible only through realization and correspondence.
This clarifies the meaning of "not empty. It means that this "not empty" is not a separate dharma;
rather, it is precisely the previously revealed emptiness of the dharma-body, which is free from false defilements. This is the true mind, the substantial reality that is eternal and unchanging.

This commentary establishes the section on the "Characteristics of the Causes and Conditions for the Arising and Ceasing of the Mind. It first clarifies the mind subject to arising and ceasing in order to reveal the source of the one mind.
The phrase "relying upon the Tathāgatagarbha" refers precisely to the True Suchness (Tathatā) of the one mind that has been established.

Its nature is inherently complete; therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Because this *garbha*-nature is fundamentally devoid of delusion or enlightenment and lacks any distinction between the holy and the ordinary, it serves as the basis for all causes and effects of the holy and the ordinary within the ten realms of existence.

Thus, it is described as "the essence of the great universal characteristic dharma-gate of the single dharma-realm. Therefore, the treatise establishes this as the true source of the one mind. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of birth and death; whether arising or ceasing, it currently exists within the gate of birth and death.

It is necessary to reveal that this mind is the basis for both delusion and enlightenment; therefore, it is said that the mind of birth and death arises in dependence upon the Tathāgatagarbha, just as waves depend upon the ocean water.
If one relies on this single mind of True Suchness (tathatā), then one realizes the ultimate transcendence of the sage.
Therefore, it is said that "the three realms are mind-only," meaning that not a single dharma can be found outside of the mind.

Now, it is revealed that the distinctions between sage and ordinary person, delusion and awakening, and cause and effect, are all subsumed within the gate of arising and ceasing. This is because one fails to understand the principle of the single dharma-realm;

thus, through the movement of non-awakened thought, ignorance arises. Being deluded regarding this true mind, it transforms into the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). As the Sūtra says: "Consciousness..."

The Tathāgatagarbha is concealed within it; therefore, it is said that the unarisen and undying [nature] is in conjunction with the arising and ceasing [phenomena], being neither identical nor different, and is termed the Ālayavijñāna.
The sutra uses the metaphor of waves depending upon water to precisely demonstrate that all phenomena are consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra).

Therefore, the treatise establishes this consciousness as the root of the arising of dharmas. Thus, the subsequent three subtle and six coarse states, along with the five mental functions, [proceed from it].
The six defilements all arise based on the transformations of consciousness; thus, returning from delusion to the truth likewise relies on this consciousness for severance and realization.
Therefore, according to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, from the perspective of the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), everything is non-existent and no discourse can be admitted.

That which can be spoken of is merely from the perspective of the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha*). This is the fundamental basis of this treatise, and students must first recognize its source.
Therefore, I shall provide a general indication here.
This consciousness has two meanings: it can encompass all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena. What are these two?
First is the meaning of awakening; second is the meaning of non-awakening.
This is based on the synthesis of the true and the delusive. The explanation of this consciousness involves two aspects, which reveal the causal basis for both delusion and enlightenment.

These two aspects are the meanings of "awakening" (*jue*) and "non-awakening" (*bujue*). As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting the thirty-two marks, enters into the bodies of all sentient beings.
Because this consciousness is designated as mind, thought, and mental consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*), it is so named.
Regarding "sentient beings": this consciousness is fundamentally constituted by the Tathāgatagarbha and is the innate Buddha-nature of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the meaning of "awakening" (*jue*). Now, being obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*), they do not know it; therefore, it is called the meaning of "non-awakening" (*bujue*).

Regarding "that which can encompass and give rise to": this refers to the causes and effects of both the noble and the ordinary, as well as their environments and inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), all of which are established based upon this single mind and are encompassed therein without exception;
hence it is said that "it encompasses all phenomena. Now, following the flow of ignorance, there arise the three subtle and six coarse states—all the defiled phenomena of the mundane world.
By relying on initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) to reverse that flow, one gives rise to the four [supramundane] [states].

The pure dharmas of the sages—thus, both the causes and effects of defilement and purity all arise from the transformative influence of the true and the false; they are all the functional power of this consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that [this consciousness] is "capable of encompassing" and "capable of generating."

What is called the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) refers to the essence of mind being free from thought. This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception.
It is the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharmakāya. Based on this Dharmakāya, it is termed "original awakening" (mūla-bodhi).
This reveals that sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha-nature of non-delusion.
What is called the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the Tathāgatagarbha; it is truly the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.

Although it now transmigrates through the five realms as sentient beings, its fundamental essence remains serene, eternally abiding, immovable, and all-pervading, never lacking anything. It is only due to [sentient beings]...
A single thought of ignorance and deluded mind arises, obscuring and veiling it so that it does not manifest;
therefore, one acts throughout the day without realizing it, for sentient beings have never been apart from discursive thought.

If one can become free from such thoughts, then the fundamental substance is vast and open, like the great void, pervading everywhere without exception, whereby all differentiated states of deluded thought melt away.
It becomes the single-flavor true mind, wherein there is only the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and no further opposition.

This alone is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which is the original possession of all sentient beings; therefore, based upon this Dharma-body, it is termed "original enlightenment" (mūla-bodhi).
As the Great Sūtra says: "I realize equal and perfect enlightenment within the bodies of all sentient beings. This is precisely because of this [Dharma-body].
Because the *dharmakāya* is equal [to all], it is said that sentient beings have been enlightened from the very beginning; this is based on this meaning. Why is this so?

Regarding the meaning of "original enlightenment" (*mūlajñāna*), it is spoken in contrast to "initial enlightenment" (*ādikṣāntijñāna*). This is because initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment.
Regarding the meaning of "initial enlightenment," it exists because of original enlightenment, and it is called "initial enlightenment" because of non-enlightenment (*ajñāna*). Furthermore...
Because one awakens to the source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*); because one does not awaken to the source of the mind, it is not ultimate awakening.

This is a designation derived from investigating the fundamental awakening, intended to reveal that initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is the wisdom of returning to purity by reversing the flow [of consciousness].

Since the preceding section clarified that delusion arises dependent upon the True, it is said that both awakening and non-awakening exist based on the *ālayavijñāna*. This refers to the delusion of ignorance—

This is the general characteristic. Now, within a single awakening, we distinguish between the two meanings of the fundamental and the initial. This is intended to specifically reveal the return from delusion to enlightenment;

it is essential that one rely upon the wisdom of initial awakening (śikṣābodhi) as the foundation for this manifestation. Nevertheless, regarding this nature of awakening, if we consider it in terms of non-delusion:

It is simply named "Awakening" (jue). Now, because one remains within delusion, there is a total lack of awakening; it is specifically through initial awakening (shijue) that [original awakening] is manifested.

Yet, this is not something newly produced; rather, it is the fundamental possession of sentient beings, and is therefore called "Original Awakening" (benjue). It is only today that one is finally awakened to it.
Therefore, it is said that this is explained in contrast to initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). Furthermore, this initial awakening does not come from without;
it arises specifically through the power of internal permeation by original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). There are no two distinct entities; thus, it is said to be identical to original awakening.
This means that initial and original awakening are non-dual, being originally one single awakening. Moreover, what is now called the meaning of initial awakening is also not something newly created.
It arises, indeed, from within the mind of ignorance that is deluded regarding fundamental awakening (mūlābodha). Having been perpetually non-awakened, it now begins to awaken;
this is primarily to reveal that it is truly due to the power of internal permeation by fundamental awakening. Therefore, it is said, "relying on fundamental awakening," and so forth.
It is like a person who is awake yet experiences a dream; one who awakens from that dream is simply the original waking person, not someone else.
Examining this nature of awakening, it fundamentally possesses no duality. Now, as we consider the three subtleties and six coarsenesses, the source of delusion has already receded far.
If one returns the flow and reverts to purity, it is essential that initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) exerts its efficacy for fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) to become manifest.

However, based on the four phases, the phase of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) of initial awakening gradually awakens until it reaches the phase of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). Once the phase of arising is shattered, one returns to the source of the single mind;

the Dharma-body is fully manifested, which is termed ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*). On the path between these stages, as long as one has not yet reached the source of the mind, none are ultimate.
Therefore, the following section explains the gradual nature of initial awakening (ādikṣaya-bodha) by means of the four phases.

What is the meaning of this? For example, when an ordinary person perceives that a preceding thought has given rise to evil, they are able to restrain the subsequent thought so that it does not arise;

This clarifies the characteristic of abiding in enlightened awareness; it refers to the Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the term "Dharmakāya":

Attachment. Because one analyzes and realizes [reality] in parts, it is called "partial awakening. These three aforementioned stages are all not ultimate, as they have not yet reached the source of the mind.
