Since there is no longer any characteristic of arising or transformation, it is solely the source of the One Mind; therefore, it is said that the mind is eternally abiding.
Reaching this point, the beginning and the fundamental merge as one, which is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are heading toward Buddha-wisdom.
This serves as proof that non-thought is the swift and essential path to attaining Buddhahood. The meaning is that it is not only Bodhisattvas who practice [this].
Severing [delusions] until one reaches the state of non-thought is called the ultimate.
Thus, if all sentient beings can, during the twelve periods of the day and night, observe this state of non-thought, then every thought-moment will be directed toward Buddha-wisdom.
There is no essential method for attaining Buddhahood that surpasses this; therefore, it is specifically revealed here.
Furthermore, as for the arising of the mind, there is no initial characteristic that can be known. To speak of knowing an initial characteristic is itself called non-thought.

For this reason, all sentient beings are not said to be awakened; because from the very beginning their thoughts have continued in succession, never having been separated from thought, it is called "beginningless ignorance."
This reiterates the absence of mental activity (*amanasikāra*) in order to resolve doubts regarding the initial characteristics of the mind.

Fearing that those who are deluded might hear the teaching on the first arising of the awakened mind and conclude that there exists an initial characteristic that can be known, this commentary explains: "Furthermore, as for the arising of the mind, no initial characteristic can be known.
What is now called 'knowing the initial characteristic' refers, in fact, to knowing that from the very beginning it was fundamentally non-existent."

It is *nian* (thought). Taking this non-thought (*wunian*) as ultimate awakening, one knows that all sentient beings cannot be called awakened because they have never been free from thought since time immemorial.
Because they possess this thought, it is called beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyā*).
Viewed in this light, the boundless cycle of birth and death for all sentient beings is tied solely to a single thought.
If one attains non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*), then one knows that the characteristics of the mind—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—are equal through non-conceptualization;

thus, in reality, there is no distinction of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). This is because these four characteristics exist simultaneously, none of which possess independent self-existence, being fundamentally equal and identical with awakening.
This clarifies the ultimate true source of the one mind. For the true source is profoundly still and tranquil, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing.

Yet this arising and ceasing exists only because of deluded thoughts. Now, if one attains non-thought, one will know that the four characteristics are simultaneous, quiescent, and equal—a single true mind without any sequence of before or after. This is the perfection of true awakening.
It is clear that, being fundamentally non-deluded from the beginning, how could there be any awakening? Within the mind of quiescent extinction, the four marks arise simultaneously;

since their essence is fundamentally empty, none possess independent existence. Because they are, in their very substance, unarisen, it is said that they are equal and identical to true awakening (*tathatā*).
Since there are no four marks to be awakened to, how could there be any distinction of "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*)? This...
This is the ultimate principle of the single mind.

Therefore, it is called "arising. Since function is not separate from essence, it is said that they do not abandon one another.

As for the "characteristic of the purity of wisdom," this refers to the fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening) emerging from its entanglements, as the wisdom of initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) removes defilement and returns to purity. As for the "characteristic of inconceivable activity,"...
This refers to the fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening) transforming defilement back into purity, whereby there spontaneously arises inconceivable function. This is the statement of the name;
below follows the explanation of its characteristics.

Regarding the characteristic of the purity of wisdom: it means that by relying on the power of the Dharma and through the cultivation of habitual perfuming, one practices according to reality and fulfills the skillful means, thereby destroying [defilements].

Thus, when the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* refutes the seven consciousnesses, it states that the Tathāgata manifests the "other-enjoyment" body for the sake of those bodhisattvas on the ten stages who serve as the responsive capacity.
Since it is so for all Buddhas, if sentient beings are able to cultivate and attain fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), their wondrous function will likewise be so.
This reveals the perfection of initial awakening (*ādikṣaṇika-bodhi*).
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the intrinsically pure original enlightenment (prakṛti-viśuddha-ādi-bodhi) as it accords with defilement.

Hereafter, the intrinsically pure original enlightenment is explained. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the essence of awakening, there are four kinds of great meanings that are equal to space, like a pure mirror.

This indicates the essence of the intrinsically pure awakening (*prakṛti-viśuddha-bodhi*). It is intended to reveal the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) that is free from delusion. That is to say, it refers directly to the aforementioned essence of awakening;

hence, it says "furthermore. The preceding section, concerning the characteristic of the purity of wisdom manifested by initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), was intended to show that it belongs to what is produced through cultivation.
The following four points clarify that these belong to the original existence; thus, they are called the "characteristics of the essence of awakening.

Space is used as a metaphor for its vastness and capacity for inclusion, while the pure mirror is used as a metaphor for its perfect luminosity and ability to manifest. These two metaphors complement one another, which is why they are presented together.
If one relies on the single mind of the *dharmadhātu* and refers to the *sāgaramudrā-samādhi*, then space itself is the mirror, because [within it] all phenomena...

The myriad phenomena are all manifested within the mirror of emptiness. If the ocean is tranquil and empty space is clear, then the reflections in the mirror of emptiness are imprinted upon the seabed;
this is called the "Ocean Seal" (Sāgaramudrā). Because the Buddha-mind universally seals the entire Dharma-realm, it is named the Ocean Seal Samādhi.
This principle is even more evident here.
What are the four? First is the mirror of emptiness as it truly is. It is far removed from all marks of the objective realm of the mind;
no phenomena can appear therein, for it does not possess the nature of cognitive illumination.

This clarifies the meaning of the true substance of the intrinsically pure original enlightenment being empty in essence. That is to say, the primordially existing true mind is the true substance of *tathatā*;
it is inherently pure from the beginning, does not belong to either delusion or awakening, requires no artificial cultivation, and is vast and all-encompassing.
Being quiescent and extinguished, it is free from characteristics; thus it is said that one is far removed from all mental objects and their marks.

Transcending all oppositions, there is only the single true mind; thus it is said that no dharma can be manifested. Being quiescent and extinguished, profoundly still, it is said not to have the meaning of cognitive illumination.
This is the dharmakāya inherently possessed by sentient beings, which does not depend upon initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*) to exist.
Second is the mirror of causal perfuming (*hetu-vāsanā-ādarśa*), which is "as-it-is" and non-empty;
all worldly objects appear within it, neither emerging nor entering, neither being lost nor destroyed, eternally abiding within the one mind, because all phenomena are themselves reality.

Because it is the nature [of reality], and because it cannot be defiled by any defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*). The essence of wisdom is immovable, for it is fully endowed with untainted (*anāsrava*) influence that permeates sentient beings.
This clarifies the meaning of the "non-emptiness" of the intrinsically pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*) as it truly is. This has two aspects: first, the clarification of non-emptiness; next...
This clarifies the permeation of cultivation. To say it is "not empty" means that the essence of this true awakening is like a great, perfect mirror, within which all worldly objects appear.

Because the causes and effects of the defiled and pure aspects of the ten dharma-realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are all clearly manifested within this single mind, and because this mind is fundamentally without internal or external, it is said to be "non-emergent."
It does not enter; it manifests immediately when conditions arise, and thus it is said to be "unfailing. What manifests is itself the Real, and thus it is said to be "indestructible.

Because it is free from arising and ceasing, it is said to be "permanently abiding within the one mind. This mind is also called the Permanently Abiding Dharmakāya; it is the true nature of all phenomena.
Therefore, when present in insentient things, it is called "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena); when present in sentient beings, [it is called the Buddha-nature].

This is called Buddha-nature. Because it is inherently possessed by sentient beings, it serves as the cause for internal permeation. Furthermore, from the phrase "Moreover, all" below, the meaning of permeation is clarified.
This means that although this awakened nature exists within the defilements of the ignorance of sentient beings, [it nevertheless functions as the cause for awakening].

Its essence is pure; therefore, it cannot be defiled by any defiled dharmas. Because the essence of wisdom is immovable, and because its nature inherently possesses the countless pure virtues of the *asaṃkhyeya* sands of the Ganges, it can act as the cause for internal permeation (*antara-vāsanā*) for sentient beings.
Therefore, it causes sentient beings to awaken to impermanence, to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death, to resolve to practice, and to seek the path of liberation.
In truth, this very essence serves as the internal permeating cause; thus, it is called "causal permeation."

Third is the mirror of the transcendence of dharmas. This refers to non-empty dharmas that transcend the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to knowledge, being free from the characteristics of composite phenomena due to their pure and luminous nature.
This luminosity indicates that the originally existing awakened nature transcends by relying upon dharmas; that is to say, the awakened nature of sentient beings is inherently complete.
There exists the characteristic of wisdom and virtue; yet, due to deluded thoughts and inversions, it is not realized.

Now, through the power of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*), one treats the hindrances and leaves defilement behind, severing the two kinds of obstructions and shattering the synthetic consciousness (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*). Thus, that which is originally present is manifested, for it is inherently pure and luminous.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is cleared away, the brightness appears. Although it is said to have been soiled, its radiance was originally there.
It exists. It is not newly produced; it has merely been obscured all along and now begins to emerge.

Fourth is the mirror of the perfuming of conditions. This means that because it emerges based on the Dharma, it universally illumines the minds of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate roots of goodness and manifesting according to their thoughts.

This clarifies that the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) which has emerged from the entanglements can serve as an external condition (*bāhya-pratyaya*) for the熏習 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) of sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma’s transcendence," this refers to the aforementioned fundamental awakening that has transcended obstacles and emerged from the entanglements. It means that this essence of awakening is identical in both ordinary beings and Buddhas;
it serves as the internal cause of perfuming (*antara-vāsanā-hetu*) for the originally existing Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) within sentient beings. Now, the practitioner...

Having departed from hindrances and emerged from the entanglements, one realizes the *dharmakāya*. Thereby, one is able to universally illumine the minds of sentient beings and give rise to great compassion based on the identity of essence (*samatā-kāruṇya*).
Manifesting various bodily forms, one subdues sentient beings and acts as an external condition for their cultivation.
Through the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, all things are impartially revealed; this radiance mutually illuminates the luminosity of the minds of sentient beings. Because sentient beings are deluded...
Non-awakening. Because awakening-wisdom is perfectly luminous, it is able to shine universally.
The above explains the meaning of awakening; the following explains the meaning of non-awakening.
As for what is called the meaning of non-awakening: it refers to not knowing, as it truly is, that the dharma of True Suchness is one; thus, the mind arises through non-awakening.

Yet there is this thought. Thought has no intrinsic characteristic of its own; it does not depart from original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*). It is like a person who becomes lost by relying on the directions:

if one were to leave the directions behind, there would be no such thing as being lost. Sentient beings are likewise: they become deluded by relying on enlightenment. If they were to leave the nature of enlightenment behind, [there would be no delusion].

Thus, there is nothing that is not non-enlightenment. Because of the existence of the deluded mind of non-enlightenment, one is able to understand names and meanings, and for its sake, true enlightenment is explained.
If one were to depart from the mind of non-enlightenment, then there would be no self-characteristic of true enlightenment that could be explained.
This clarifies that non-enlightenment exists in dependence upon enlightenment; it is intended to reveal that non-enlightenment is itself enlightenment. Question:
The nature of enlightenment is profound stillness, perfectly luminous, quiescent, and illuminating. How is it that non-enlightenment arises? Answer:

It is because one does not accord with reality and fails to know that the *dharmatā* of True Suchness is one. Suddenly, the mind arises and possesses thought; this very [thought] is [non-enlightenment].
This "thought" (smṛti) is called the ignorance of the characteristic of arising. Because of this ignorance, one immediately loses fundamental clarity; hence it is called "non-awakening.
This single thought originally has no self-characteristic of its own and does not depart from the substance of fundamental awakening.
Thus, the entire substance of true awakening becomes non-awakening. It is like a person who becomes lost because they rely on directions; so too do sentient beings rely on awakening.
Therefore, there is delusion. If one were apart from the nature of awakening, then the characteristic of non-awakening would not exist. Question:
How do we know that non-awakening is itself true awakening? Answer: Indeed, non-awakening is the mind of delusive conceptualization belonging to sentient beings.
Although sentient beings are entirely non-awake due to this delusive conceptualization, if one now points out that "this very mind is Buddha," [then non-awakening is seen as true awakening].
One is thus able to know names and meanings. Because one can know names and cognize meanings, this is precisely the nature of original, true awakening (*tathatā*).
It serves as the norm and sustainer that gives rise to understanding; for this reason, it is taught that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is itself true awakening.
Since this very non-awakening is constituted by the entire substance of true awakening, if one were to depart from the mind of non-awakening, then [true awakening] would not exist.

The self-characteristic of true awakening can be described, for this non-awakening is itself awakening. If sentient beings turn their light back even for a single thought-moment, they are identical to what is originally possessed.
Being able to know the state of no-thought, they immediately realize the Dharma-body.
The first part clarifies fundamental non-awakening; the second part clarifies derivative non-awakening.
First, ignorance and non-awakening give rise to the three subtle states; second, with objective realms as conditions, the six coarse states develop.
Furthermore, first:
next, based on non-awakening (*abodha*), three kinds of marks arise; they correspond to and are not separate from that non-awakening.

This indicates that ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the cause for the arising of the three subtle states. Since the derivative does not depart from the fundamental, it is said they "correspond" (*xiāngyìng*).
Separation. What are the three? First is the karmic characteristic of ignorance. Because it relies on non-awakening, the mind moves;
this is termed "karma. Awakening is immobility; movement is suffering. For the fruit does not exist apart from its cause.
This indicates the "karmic aspect of ignorance" (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*). It is so designated to distinguish it from the inconceivable activity of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Thus, it is called the "karmic aspect of ignorance. Because it arises based on the movement of the mind in that initial moment of non-enlightenment, this very moving mind is termed the "karmic aspect.

By contrast, this reveals that enlightenment is immovability; that is, when one is awakened to True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is no movement of thought. From this, one can fully understand non-enlightenment.
Therefore, the mind moves. That movement gives rise to suffering because the boundless fruits of suffering within birth and death all arise from this movement of thought;
thus it is said that "the fruit does not depart from the cause. If one departs from the movement of thought, then the two types of death will forever cease;
thus it is said that "if one contemplates non-thought, one is heading toward Buddha-wisdom."

Second is the characteristic of the capacity to see: because it relies on movement, there is the capacity to see; without movement, there is no seeing. Third is the characteristic of the objective realm:
because it relies on the capacity to see, the objective realm falsely appears; apart from seeing, there is no objective realm.
This indicates and explains the two aspects of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and manifestation (*pratibhāsa*). As for designating "that which can see" as the aspect of transformation:

this refers to the wisdom that illuminates True Suchness (*tathatā*). Originally, there is neither subject nor object; however, having now become deluded regarding the essence of wisdom, it transforms into false seeing.
Because there are falsely existing objects that can be seen, it is called "transformation. This seeing arises based on the movement of thought; it exists because a single thought-moment stirs.
When the mind loses its essential clarity, it becomes false vision; conversely, this reveals that if there is no movement, there is no seeing.

As for the "characteristic of the objective realm," it refers to the manifested aspect. Because the true mind, which is devoid of characteristics, undergoes a single moment of deluded movement, it takes on the form of an object and becomes the objective realm perceived by false vision. Therefore, it is said: "Because one relies upon the perceiving subject, there is the objective realm."

It manifests falsely. However, this realm is precisely the false appearance of space and the four great elements. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*’s "Three Subtleties" states: "Based on clarity, the objective is established;
once the objective is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. In that case, the manifestation comes first and the transformation follows;

here, however, the transformation comes first and the manifestation follows. Yet, while that [text] concerns the phase of the arising of mountains, rivers, and the great earth, emphasizing the objective realm, this...
To speak briefly in terms of the characteristics of the arising of mental dharmas, the emphasis is placed on the mind;
yet in reality, these three subtleties arise simultaneously, and fundamentally there is no sequence of before and after. These three subtleties all depend upon ignorance for their establishment.

As stated previously, "If ignorance is extinguished, then the continuous mind is extinguished," because the continuous mind is established in dependence upon these three subtleties; they are inseparable.
Therefore, when they cease, they cease together.
The preceding section clarifies how ignorance and non-awakening give rise to the three subtle states;
the following section clarifies how objective conditions give rise to the six coarse states.
Because there are objective conditions (*ālambana*), six further characteristics arise. What are these six? First is the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*):
based upon an object, the mind gives rise to discrimination between the pleasant and the unpleasant.
This indicates the six coarse [delusions]. First, it clarifies the characteristics of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Cognition is precisely the discriminating mind.

This means that regarding the objects previously manifested, one fails to realize they are merely the mind’s own false projections; thus, one first gives rise to the mental factor of discernment (*mati*) to differentiate between the favorable and unfavorable, the agreeable and disagreeable.

The second is the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*). Because it relies upon cognition, it gives rise to suffering and pleasure; as the mind perceives and thoughts arise, they correspond and continue without interruption.

This explains the characteristic of continuity. That is to say, based on the two types of objects—favorable and unfavorable—that are conceptually discriminated, if they are desirable, [pleasure] arises.
Pleasant feeling, when not craved, gives rise to painful feeling. These arise repeatedly, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.

They give rise to delusion which moistens karma, drawing forth and sustaining the cycle of birth and death in an uninterrupted succession; therefore, it is called the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*).

Third is the characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-nimitta*). It depends upon the continuity [of consciousness] and takes objects as its condition; because the mind gives rise to attachment while maintaining pleasure and pain, this explains the characteristic of grasping.
That is to say, one first takes objects as conditions and fails to realize that suffering, pleasure, and so forth are empty.

Delusion. Because they give rise to deep attachment and grasping, the subsequent text states: "This very continuous consciousness, based on the increasingly deep grasping of ordinary beings, conceives of a self and what belongs to a self."

The fourth is the characteristic of calculating names (*nāma-kalpanā-lakṣaṇa*). This is explained as follows: based on false attachment, one discriminates the characteristics of provisional names and words;

this is the interpretation of the characteristic of calculating names. That is to say, based on the prior grasping of a falsely imagined mental object, one discriminates the characteristics of provisional names and words;

thus it is called the characteristic of calculating names. Regarding the four characteristics mentioned above, if they are correlated with the two types of attachment—to self (*ātman*) and to phenomena (*dharma*)—the preceding...

Second, the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). The latter two are the attachment to self (*ātma-grāha*). Furthermore, there are the three of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*): the former four are all afflictions, while the latter two are karma and suffering.
Fifth is the characteristic of the arising of karma: based on names and designations (*nāmadheya*), one seeks out names and grasps at them, thereby creating various kinds of karma.

This explains the characteristic of initiating karma. That is to say, based on the previously analyzed provisional characteristics of names and speech, one seeks out names and grasps at them with attachment, thereby activating body and mouth to create various kinds of karma; this is called the characteristic of initiating karma.
Sixth is the characteristic of suffering bound by karma (*karmabandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*). This refers to the characteristic of suffering bound by karma as explained here:

because one receives retribution based on karma and lacks autonomy, it is called the suffering bound by karma. That is to say, due to the wholesome and unwholesome karma previously created, one experiences the retribution of suffering and pleasure, transmigrating through the three realms and being long fettered within birth and death; because of this lack of autonomy, it is termed "suffering bound by karma."
One should know that ignorance (*avidyā*) is able to give rise to all defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭa-dharma*), because all defiled phenomena possess the characteristic of non-awakening (*abodha*).
This conclusion ultimately returns to the root in order to demonstrate that ignorance is the cause of the defiled phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). However, one...
All defiled dharmas arise based upon fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Fundamental ignorance is the very first movement of thought.
Because sentient beings have never been free from thought since time immemorial, it is said that all defiled dharmas are the manifestations of non-enlightenment (*a-prabodha*).
This implies that if one realizes the state of no-thought, then all afflictions (*kleśa*) will be suddenly severed. Therefore...
The binding of the fingers takes the very first thought as the root of the suffering of birth and death. This is intended to cause the practitioner to perceive suffering and understand its cause;
it is essential to know that the departure from discursive thought is the core of spiritual cultivation.

The preceding section provides a general explanation of ignorance (*avidyā*) as the cause of defiled phenomena. The following section distinguishes between the true and the deluded in terms of their similarities and differences.

Furthermore, regarding awakening (*bodhi*) and non-awakening (*abodhi*), there are two kinds of characteristics. What are these two? First, the characteristic of sameness; second, the characteristic of difference.

This explains the characteristics of the identity and difference between the real and the false. Previously, it was stated that based on the *tathāgatagarbha* there arises the mind of birth-and-death (*utpādanirodha-citta*), which is a union of the unborn-and-unceasing and the birth-and-ceasing; it is neither identical nor different, and is named the *ālayavijñāna*.

Now, having clarified the mind of birth-and-death, it is necessary to clarify that birth-and-death is itself the unborn-and-unceasing; therefore, this section distinguishes their identity and difference.
Regarding their identical characteristics: for example, various earthenware vessels all share the same nature and characteristics of fine dust;
likewise, the various illusory manifestations of karma—whether untainted or characterized by ignorance—all share the same nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

This analogy illustrates that arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing. Just as a ceramic vessel exists in dependence upon fine dust, the analogy illustrates that both defilement and purity, as well as arising and ceasing, all depend upon true suchness (*tathatā*).
"Outflow-free" refers to the pure dharmas of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); "ignorance" (*avidyā*) refers to the cause of defilement.
These two are the causal conditions for the manifestation of True Suchness (tathatā) according to conditions; therefore, they share the same nature of True Suchness.
Regarding "the various illusions of karma," this means that original enlightenment possesses inconceivable activity capable of producing all supreme and wondrous realms.
The power of ignorance and karma can give rise to the three subtle and six coarse states, producing all matters of birth and death, suffering and pleasure, and so forth.
Both these true and deluded dharmas are illusory existences; that which is called birth and death and nirvana are both like illusions and dreams.

Therefore, it is said that all are identical in their nature and characteristics as True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, both defiled and pure dharmas are the characteristics and functions of True Suchness.
For this reason, based on this meaning, the *Sūtras* state that all sentient beings are primordially and eternally abiding in entry into *nirvāṇa*.
The dharma of Bodhi is not a characteristic that can be cultivated, nor is it a characteristic that can be produced; ultimately, there is nothing to be attained. Furthermore—
There are no form-characteristics that can be seen; yet those who perceive form-characteristics do so only through the illusory workings of karma following defilement.
This is not the nature of the non-empty wisdom-form, for the characteristics of wisdom cannot be seen.

This citation from the sutra establishes the meaning of "common characteristics" (*sādharmya*). That is to say, both awakening (*bodhi*) and non-awakening (*abodhi*) are identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, sentient beings have been abiding in nirvāṇa from the very beginning. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess the characteristic of nirvāṇa; they do not undergo further extinction.
This means that both original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) are identical to True Suchness. Therefore, all Buddhas...
Awakening (*bodhi*) is not a characteristic that can be cultivated; ultimately, there is nothing to be attained. The preceding [passage] refers to non-awakening as being suchness (*tathatā*);
therefore, sentient beings have been in *nirvāṇa* from the beginning. The subsequent [passage] refers to awakening-wisdom as being the truth;

therefore, the *bodhi* of all Buddhas has nothing newly acquired. Question: Since sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, why do they not perceive the physical forms of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*?

The answer is: This is spoken solely in reference to the inherent virtues of *tathatā* (suchness), because the essence of the *dharmatā* of *tathatā* is fundamentally devoid of any visible form or characteristic (*rūpa-nimitta*).

Again, it was asked: "If the *dharmatā* of *tathatā* is not a form or characteristic, for what reason do the Buddhas, upon realizing it, manifest various forms and characteristics as *saṃbhoga-kāya* and *nirmāṇa-kāya*? The answer is: Those forms and characteristics of the Buddhas are merely...
It manifests through the transformation of the delusory mind according to the defilements of sentient beings; it does not exist within the non-empty nature of original enlightenment (prakṛti).
This is because the wisdom of original enlightenment is not an object that can be perceived as a phenomenal mark.

As for their distinct characteristics: just as various earthenware vessels are each different from one another, so too are these untainted [dharmas] differentiated by the delusive transformations of defilement, and the nature [of the mind] differentiated by the delusive transformations of defilement.

This analogy clarifies that they are identical yet distinct. It is said that although various earthen vessels are the same as mere dust particles, they differ individually according to the conditions of their manufacture.

Likewise, although the two dharmas of fundamental enlightenment (mūla-jñāna) and ignorance—truth and delusion—are both the same single *dharmatā* of true suchness (*tathatā*) and are fundamentally without distinction, they now appear in various forms due to the influence of defiled, illusory conditions.

Regarding the distinction: when it is said that both the true and the false are differentiated according to defilement, it is because all pure merits are established by reversing the state of defilement.
Therefore, this refers solely to the illusory nature of defilement; that is to say, if the mind-nature moves, there arises the principle of false defilements exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
if the mind-nature does not move, there arise the characteristics of pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
This is a manifestation of meaning. It refers solely to the transformations within the minds of sentient beings; therefore, it is called "illusory according to defilement.
The intent is that these distinctions are merely the distinctions of defiled illusion, and not that there are distinctions within the true nature of *tathatā*.
This concludes that these knots ultimately resolve into the meaning of non-differentiation.
The above explains the mind of arising and ceasing; below, the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing are explained.

Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing: it refers to sentient beings revolving according to the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is the meaning.
How so? Because based upon the ālayavijñāna, it is said that there is ignorance which arises through non-awakening;
it is able to see, able to manifest, and able to grasp objects, giving rise to a continuous stream of conceptualization; therefore, it is called the manas.
This clarifies that the arising and ceasing of the one mind constitutes the mutual causality between the real and the false, thereby manifesting how the ālayavijñāna gives rise to all phenomena.
That sentient beings continue through birth and death in uninterrupted succession for long kalpas is due solely to the gravity of the single factor of *manas*;
this is because sentient beings revolve according to the mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Based on...

Regarding the "mind" (*citta*): a sutra states that the *tathāgatagarbha* is subject to arising and ceasing. Since the consciousness-store (*vijñānagarbha*) is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is said to be based on the mind.
However, this store-consciousness is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; rather, it is the mental faculty (*manas*) that manifests as a continuous succession of arising and ceasing.
That which gives rise to delusion and constructs karma is the consciousness of the *manas*. This phrase establishes the definition.
The subsequent interrogation and explanation asks: "What is the meaning of this? How is it that that which undergoes the continuity of arising and ceasing is the *manas*? The answer states:
It is because, based upon the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it is said that ignorance arises through non-awakening; this is the source of arising and ceasing. It depends on the mind (*citta*).

"Et cetera" means that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the One Mind, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing. However, through the deluded movement of a single thought-moment, it perfumes the essence of the mind;
by losing sight of its original perfect luminosity, it is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

This ignorance arises based upon the Truth and perfumes the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), transforming it into the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Thus, with True Suchness as the cause and ignorance as the condition, the *ālaya* is brought into being.

This is the phase of karmic activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, the mind encompasses both the true and the false. However, this phase of karmic activity of ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet differentiated between subject and object;
it is entirely devoid of opposition. Therefore, although it is "arising," it is non-arising; it merely functions as ignorance retroactively perfuming the *ālayavijñāna*.
Thus, the originally existing light of wisdom transforms into the deluded vision that is capable of seeing, and the signless true essence transforms into the deluded objects manifested as the seen.
Because this division of seer and seen establishes the duality of subject and object, the deluded vision grasps at its objects;
the mind and its objects then coalesce, giving rise to further attachment and conceptualization in an uninterrupted succession. Therefore, this characteristic is so described.
The "continuum" (samtati) refers to the *manas*, not the *citta*. This arises with ignorance as its cause and objective conditions as its support;
thus, it further gives rise to the six coarse characteristics. That the cycle of birth and death continues uninterrupted for long kalpas is due to the fault of the *manas*.
The treatise reveals that the *manas* is the master of arising and ceasing, as the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are collectively termed [the *manas*].
Therefore, the subsequent explanation lists five types.

This "mind" (*manas*) further has five names. What are these five? First, it is called the *karma-vijñāna* (action-consciousness). This refers to the movement of the mind due to the power of ignorance;
this reveals the initial phase of arising, which is precisely what is termed "mind. Second, it is called the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness), which depends upon that movement.

Because the mind is able to perceive appearances (this also implies that it is the true wisdom which undergoes transformation and becomes deluded perception). Third is what is called the "manifesting consciousness" (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*).
This refers to its ability to manifest all objective realms, just as a clear mirror manifests forms and images. The manifesting consciousness is likewise:

in accordance with the five sense-objects, as they encounter it, they are immediately manifested without any sequence of before or after, arising spontaneously at all times and remaining ever-present.

First, the so-called *manas* (the mind-consciousness): this reveals the essence of the *vijñāna* (consciousness) as being bright and penetrating; it manifests the objects of the five sensory realms in their entirety, such that it arises spontaneously and constantly, maintaining them without loss. That which is always present before one is also the power of the *manas*, which takes these as its objects.

These are the three subtle [evolutions]. Fourth, what is called *jñāna-vijñāna* (the wisdom-consciousness): this refers to the discrimination between defiled and pure phenomena. This reveals that although the eight consciousnesses can manifest the five sensory realms in their entirety, they do so without discrimination.

As for the discrimination of defilement and purity, and the grasping or rejecting thereof, the *manas* acts as the primary agent. This is the aspect of wisdom among the six coarse [evolutions]. Fifth, what is called the *anuvartaka-vijñāna* (the continuous consciousness). Because...

Because it is associated with mindfulness and is uninterrupted (this precisely reveals that what continues uninterruptedly from moment to moment refers back to the *manas*; for although the initial ignorance of a single thought-moment gives rise to the three subtle states, mind and object have not yet coalesced and thus are not associated.

Due to the discrimination of the *vijñāna*, these are grasped as objects, and as one clings to them in every thought-moment, this arising without cessation is called the "characteristic of continuity. Since all of this is the transformation of the *manas*, these three subtle and two coarse states are all termed the *manas*).
It maintains and upholds the good and evil karma of immeasurable past lives, ensuring they are not lost (the previous mention of "moment to moment" [refers to...])

"Continuity" refers to the continuity of its own essence. Now, it is said that past karma and so forth are maintained without being lost; this causes the continuity of birth and death for others. With this intention, one grasps at dharmas such as good and evil, defilement and purity, taking the locus where the *ālayavijñāna* stores them as the seeds;

this is called "the storehouse of self-love and attachment. Therefore, they are not lost or destroyed, serving as the cause for birth and death throughout long future kalpas—this is also due to the power of the mind (*manas*).

Furthermore, it can bring to fruition the retributions of suffering and pleasure in the present and future without error (this clarifies that the previously stored seeds of good and evil act as the cause capable of inducing future birth and death).

That the fruits of suffering and pleasure do not deviate [from their causes] is also due to the power of the mind (*manas*). It can cause one to suddenly recall events already past in the present, and to unconsciously harbor false anxieties regarding future matters.

(This clarifies that the daily life of sentient beings, in which every thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) clings to objects, arises because the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) internally perfume and incite active manifestations (*samudācāra*), which arise uninterruptedly from moment to moment;

that these manifest activities are also due to the power of the mind. Below, the source of delusion is concluded. Therefore, the three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind. Apart from the mind, [they do not exist].

Then there would be no realm of the six sense-objects (this concludes the refutation and returns to the intended meaning. It means that within the Tathāgatagarbha, there are fundamentally no provisional signs of birth-and-death within the triple world; therefore, it is called "mind-only.

The one mind becomes perfectly luminous.
If this is so, from where could the realms of the six sense-objects possibly arise? This serves to reveal that birth-and-death is indeed the activity of the *manas* based upon the mind).

This clarifies that regarding the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, it initially takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the cause and the ignorance (*avidyā*) of a single moment of deluded movement as the condition;
thus, that true mind is transformed into the karmic aspect of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Subsequently, deluded thought retroactively perfumes the karmic consciousness, whereby it is transformed into the capacity to perceive and the capacity to manifest. This is the arising of the non-enlightenment of ignorance.
These are the three subtleties. When the perceived object and the perceiving subject arise as one, the mind and its objects stand in opposition;

deluded thought grasps them as "mine," discriminating between the pure and the defiled, clinging to them without relinquishing. Through these various discriminations, which continue in succession from moment to moment, one takes up birth and death for long kalpas.
This arises with ignorance as the cause and objective realms as the condition, giving rise to the six gross characteristics.

In short, all of these take the continuous succession of moment-to-moment thoughts as their fundamental basis. Therefore, these three subtle and two coarse states are collectively termed "mind" (*manas*).

Consequently, the *Eight Consciousnesses Treatise* (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*) generally designates them as "cognition and deliberation" (*manana*). Thus, it is known that the mind is the root of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, this treatise states: "Sentient beings evolve in dependence upon mind (*manas*), thought (*citta*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Specifically, that which undergoes the continuity of arising and ceasing is the evolution of the *manas*.
As for the arousal of afflictions and the creation of karma, this refers to the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*); it is simply the consciousness produced by this *manas*.
Consequently, the mental consciousness is explained separately below to demonstrate that this *manas* serves as its root. As previously stated in this treatise...

The seven consciousnesses are not established [as separate entities]. Now, this aspect of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) that continues in succession constitutes the mind (*manas*), which is precisely the seventh consciousness.

Therefore, it is said: "One kind is deliberation; the seventh consciousness is specifically named *manas*. When the three subtle and two coarse [consciousnesses] are collectively termed *manas*, this refers to the mental application (*manasikāra*) of true yoga.
For it is that which arises and ceases moment by moment which constitutes mental application; thus, by means of this *manas*...
It is the source of arising and ceasing.

What is the meaning of this? (The question: since it is said that arising and ceasing belong to the mind, how can one say that arising and ceasing depend on the mind? It is because all phenomena arise from the mind.

Arising from deluded thought (meaning that the mind is the essence of the universal characteristic of the Dharma-realm; it is fundamentally unarisen and devoid of even a single dharma. That all dharmas now manifest arise from the mental activity of deluded thought, not from the arising of the mind).
All discrimination is the discrimination of one’s own mind (all dharmas are manifested solely by the mind; because of ignorance and lack of realization, one falsely gives rise to discrimination.

In reality, that which is discriminated is nothing but one’s own mind, for there are no dharmas outside the mind). The mind does not see the mind; no characteristics can be apprehended (for that which is discriminated is merely a false appearance. The True [Mind]...)

The mind is without marks; how could it be subject to discrimination? One should know that all worldly objects of experience exist and are sustained solely by the deluded mind of ignorance in sentient beings (if one realizes that the true mind is without marks, then the three realms are suddenly empty; one should know that the appearance of the three realms currently existing is merely sustained by the deluded mind).

Therefore, all phenomena are like images in a mirror; they have no substantial essence that can be apprehended. They are merely the false manifestations of the mind—the delusive appearances of the triple world produced by the illusions of karma.

Fundamentally unreal, they are like images appearing in a mirror, existing only through the discriminative activity of the deluded minds of sentient beings. This is because when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
From the phrase "How is it from this meaning? onwards, the text interrogates and clarifies that all phenomena arise and perish through the mind;
this effectively emphasizes that a single thought-moment is the root of the arising of dharmas. This is because the true mind is fundamentally without arising or perishing;
it is only due to the initial movement of ignorance (*avidyā*) that the vast, signless true mind is transformed into the delusion of the three realms.

Dharma. Thus, all phenomena arise from the mind; they are produced by deluded thought. If one investigates a single thought and finds it originally lacks self-substance, existing only in dependence upon the True, then delusion is fundamentally the True.
Therefore, all phenomena are mind-only, and those who engage in deluded discrimination do so entirely within their own minds.
As it is said: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; that which is not illusion creates illusory phenomena."
However, because sentient beings do not understand that the mind is fundamentally without marks, delusory objects are not empty.
Thus, one knows that the delusive phenomena of sentient beings all abide and are sustained by the deluded mind, yet they cannot be found at all within the true mind.
Because of a single moment of delusion, the myriad dharmas manifest simultaneously; hence it is said: "When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise. If one understands this single moment...
When there is no arising, the triple world is suddenly empty; hence it is said that when the mind ceases, all manifold phenomena cease.
This treatise points directly to the one mind: if one simply realizes that a single thought-moment is without arising, one immediately awakens to the stage of Buddhahood.
As it is said: "If one can contemplate non-thought, one is then heading toward Buddha-wisdom. How tragic! Sentient beings, from the very beginning, have been in every thought-moment...
Because it continues in succession without ever being free from thought, birth and death are not severed.
The above clarifies the meaning of continuity; below, it clarifies the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding what is called "mental consciousness," it is precisely this continuous consciousness which, based on the deepening grasping and attachment of ordinary people, is reckoned as...

The various false attachments to "self" and "what belongs to self," which involve clinging to objects and discriminating among the six sense-fields, is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

It is also termed the "separating consciousness" (*prativijñaptivijñāna*) and further designated as the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastuvikalpavijñāna*). This consciousness is so named because it grows and increases based upon the afflictions of views and craving (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā-kleśa*).
This clarifies that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is precisely the aforementioned continuous consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).

It is called "the consciousness of the mind" because it relies solely on ordinary beings' grasping at external objects, clinging to them as "self" and "mine," and apprehending the six sense-objects for its own enjoyment.
Since it takes this continuity as its root, it is the mental consciousness alone that deeply clings to self-love, gives rise to delusions, and creates karma. This...

The grasping at the six coarse [objects] and the reckoning of names constitute the two coarse aspects. Because this consciousness relies on the five sense organs externally to discern and grasp objects, it is called the "discriminating consciousness" (*prativijñapti-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, because it universally conditions various internal and external phenomena—the faculties and their objects—it is also called the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastu-prativikalpa-vijñāna*).
Regarding the statement that this consciousness relies on "viewing and craving" (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā*), this refers to the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).
Ignorance (avidyā) reveals the preceding five types of mental states; they all rely upon the ground of ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi).
These afflictions of the four grounds of dwelling—namely, views, craving, and so forth—within this mental consciousness are about to give rise to delusion and create karma.

The preceding section clarifies how, through the causes and conditions of the arising and ceasing of the one mind, one follows the flow of ignorance to give rise to the defiled dharmas of birth and death;

the following section clarifies how, by relying on the causes and conditions of the arising and ceasing of the one mind, one returns from defilement to purity, thereby elucidating the differences between the sudden and gradual approaches.
Regarding the consciousnesses arising from the perfuming of ignorance: these cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can they be realized through the wisdom of the two vehicles.

It is said that based on Bodhisattvas who, from their initial stage of right faith, give rise to the resolve for enlightenment and engage in contemplation, if they realize the Dharma-body, they attain a partial knowledge;
yet even up to the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva, they cannot know them exhaustively. Only a Buddha fully understands them.
This brief explanation of returning to purity serves to manifest the profound depth of dependent origination.

That is to say, this fundamental ignorance and the karmic consciousness are profoundly deep and extremely subtle. Now, wishing to turn back from delusion and return to truth, one must directly shatter this fundamental ignorance—the karmic consciousness—before one can realize the source of the One Mind; only then is it ultimate. This is truly because this consciousness is so...

Profound. Its cultivation requires effort that is not easily accomplished. It is a realm unknown to ordinary beings and is not something realized by the wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), because the two vehicles do not know that this consciousness exists.

Thus, when Bodhisattvas practice, beginning from the initial arousal of the mind through right faith, they progress through the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*). Yet, because they rely on inferential observation (*anumāna*), they know it only partially, and so forth.
The Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) and attained the Dharma-body perceive only the abiding marks [of this consciousness];
even when reaching the ultimate perfection of the tenth stage, they cannot know it exhaustively, for all such knowledge remains partial. Only a Buddha can fully comprehend it;

thus one knows that this consciousness is profoundly deep—how could it be easily shattered? This speaks to the difficulty of sudden enlightenment. Alas! As for those practitioners of Chan today, this consciousness is active...
Even the Buddhas do not fully know it; yet you take pride in having awakened to the Way yourself—could this not be the mark of one with *adhimāna* (arrogance)?
The following explains why it is difficult to know.
Why is this? Because from the very beginning, this mind is pure by its own nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), yet it possesses ignorance (*avidyā*). It is because of this ignorance that...

That which is defiled possesses a defiled mind (this clarifies that although originally undefiled, it becomes defiled; thus it is difficult to comprehend). Although there is a defiled mind, it is eternally constant and unchanging (this is being defiled yet undefiled;
it is difficult to comprehend). Therefore, this principle can be known only by a Buddha; namely, because the nature of the mind is eternally free from thought, it is called "unchanging.
Because one does not realize the single Dharma-realm, the mind is dissociated [from its true nature], and suddenly thoughts arise.
Its arising is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
This inquiry clarifies why it is so profound and difficult to know. Question: For what reason is consciousness (*vijñāna*) known only by a Buddha?
Answer: Because within the pure mind there is originally no defilement; yet, due to ignorance, it comes to exist.
The defiled mind: that this is undefiled yet appears defiled is difficult to comprehend. Although there is a defiled mind, the essence of the mind is pure, eternal, and unchanging.
Because it is defiled yet remains unchanging, it is difficult to comprehend.
Because it is so profound and subtle, it is beyond the reach of those on the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood; only a Buddha can fully understand it. Question:
Since it is said that there is defilement, why is it described as permanent, eternal, and unchanging? The answer is:

because sentient beings’ deluded thoughts攀緣 (pān-yuán, objectify and cling to) from moment to moment, while the essence of this mind is eternally constant and fundamentally free from thought; thus, within the station of mindfulness, there is no thought.
Therefore, it is said to be unchanging; this is why it is difficult to comprehend. Question:
Since it is said that this mind has been pure by its very nature from the beginningless past, for what reason does ignorance exist? Answer:
Because one does not penetrate the single Dharma-realm, the essence of the mind and [ignorance] are inherently incompatible. When a thought suddenly arises, it is called ignorance. That is to say:
This place where it suddenly arises is most extremely subtle and inconceivable.

That is to say, because it is perfumed by the inconceivable, it is difficult to comprehend; because it arises from within that [inconceivable], only a Buddha can know it, and thus it is not something known by bodhisattvas.
The preceding section briefly clarifies the causes and conditions for returning to purity;
the following section provides a detailed exposition on the severing of delusions according to the stages, extensively elucidating the causes and conditions for returning to purity.

There are six kinds of defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*). What are these six? First is the defilement associated with attachment (*saṃprayukta-kliṣṭa*); this refers to the six coarse [delusions] that involve grasping and calculating names and designations.

2. The defilement associated with detachment (*asaṃprayukta-kleśa*). Because of the distancing from the liberation of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) and the stage corresponding to faith (*adhimukti-saṃprayukta-bhūmi*), this [should be understood as the sixth consciousness’s delusions of views and thoughts;

thus, the two vehicles and those in the ten stages of faith are able to abandon them]. Second, the defilement associated with non-interruption (*anuccheda-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is the characteristic of continuity.

By relying on the skillful means of cultivation in the stage corresponding to faith (from the ten stages of faith up to the ten stages of dedication), one is gradually able to relinquish it, attaining ultimate separation upon reaching the ground of pure mind (from the three levels of worthiness up to the first bhūmi). Third...
First is the defilement associated with the wisdom of discrimination (the characteristic of this wisdom);

it is gradually abandoned based on the stage of possessing precepts (the second stage), until it is ultimately abandoned at the stage of the skillful means of signlessness (it can be abandoned from the second stage through the seventh stage). Fourth is the defilement dissociated from the manifestation of form (the manifestation of the three subtleties);
it can be abandoned based on the stage of mastery over form (the eighth stage). Fifth is the defilement dissociated from the mind that is capable of seeing (the characteristic of seeing).

Because one can become free from it by relying on the Stage of Mastery over the Mind (the ninth stage). Sixth is the defilement of non-conformity with the fundamental karma (the aspect of karma of ignorance).

Because one can enter the Tathāgata stage by relying on the Bodhisattva Stage of Exhaustion, one becomes free from it. This refers to those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm.

From the stage of association with faith, one observes and trains in abandonment; upon entering the stage of the pure mind, one attains detachment according to one's capacity, until finally, at the stage of the Tathāgata, one is able to achieve ultimate detachment.
This provides a detailed analysis of the stages to distinguish the gradual depth of the separation from delusions, and extensively clarifies the causes and conditions for returning to purity.

Since the previous brief demonstration of returning to purity—namely, the sudden shattering of the initial fundamental ignorance—is something that cannot be achieved by those of the three stages of worthiness or the ten stages of sagehood, but can only be realized by a Buddha, this section provides a detailed demonstration of the sequence of gradually departing from delusions according to the stages. It says:

Regarding the Stage of Correspondence with Faith (*śraddhā-saṃprayukta-bhūmi*): one enters the dwelling from faith and enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

One exclusively breaks through the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which are the afflictions of view and craving (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*). Although at this stage one resolves to sever ignorance (*avidyā*), its power is not yet sufficient;

thus, while the coarse defilements fall away first, it is only able to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts. As for the "defilement corresponding to attachment" (*abhiniveśa-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), it refers to the grasping and calculating of names within the six coarse [delusions].
The characteristic of letters (*akṣara-lakṣaṇa*) constitutes the afflictions of view and craving; it belongs to the sixth consciousness and is precisely what is severed by the Two Vehicles.

It does not sever the "defilement associated with continuity" (*sambandha-saṃkleśa*), which is the characteristic of continuity itself. Tiantai designates this as the "dust-like delusions within and without the realms" (*dhātu-antaḥ-bāhya-reṇu-saṃmoha*).

The Three Sages sever these and thereby ascend to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*); thus, from the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*) up to the First Ground, one is able to depart from them by abandoning conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Due to the two obstructions, the defilement associated with discriminative cognition is a subtle division of the six gross [defilements]; it is the "characteristic of cognition" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and belongs to innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).

Although those on the stages (*bhūmi*) are intent on destroying ignorance (*avidyā*), because they rely primarily on contemplation with signs (*nimitta-bhāvanā*) from the first stage through the seventh, they are only able to destroy innate self-clinging.
The defilement dissociated from manifest form is the manifest consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).
This occurs at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Having already realized the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*) and attained mastery over form, one is able to abandon it;

the defilement dissociated from seeing is the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which constitutes the aspect of seeing. At the ninth stage, one attains mastery over the mind and is thus able to abandon it;
the fundamental karmic defilement dissociated from seeing is the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), which is the aspect of karma. This [abandonment] relies upon the tenth stage.

The "fulfilled mind" (pūrṇa-citta): Upon reaching the stage of the Vajra Path of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi-vajra-mārga), one severs this [mind] and immediately enters the ocean-like fruition of the Tathāgata.
This is the gradual process of becoming free from defilement and returning to purity. As stated above, being defiled by ignorance, there exists a defiled mind.
Thus, all six types of defilement take ignorance as their root; the six defilements are merely the differentiated manifestations of ignorance.
Now that the defiled mind has ceased, ignorance likewise ceases accordingly.

When it is said here that "one does not penetrate the meaning of the single Dharma-realm" and so forth, this specifically refers to the ignorance that suddenly gives rise to thoughts, which is also observed from the stage of "correspondence with faith."
Examine these words at length, up until the point where it says that even the stage of the Tathāgata is ultimately free [from ignorance].

In the True Teaching (*śuddha-dharma*), the severance of ignorance is categorized into forty-two divisions. The meaning of "initially giving rise to the mind of faith with the resolve to sever ignorance" is seen herein.

However, the principle of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing encompasses both the defiled and the pure aspects of arising and ceasing; this refers specifically to the causes and conditions for returning to purity.

Regarding the meaning of "conformity" (saṃprayoga): it refers to the fact that while the mind, mental factors, and dharmas are distinct, they are known to be identical in their characteristics of cognition and their objects of perception, based on the differentiation between defilement and purity.

Regarding the meaning of "non-conformity" (viprayoga): it refers to the state where the mind is not awakened; it is eternally without distinction and does not share the same characteristics of cognition or objects of perception.
This explains the aforementioned six points regarding the correspondence and non-correspondence of defilements, as well as the similarities and differences among their objects.

Regarding the first three defilements, they are said to be "associated" because the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are distinct; thus it is said that "the mind and mental phenomena are different.

While the objects of their perception differ in being either defiled or pure, if the mind-king perceives an object that is defiled or pure, the mental factors likewise follow along with it. Therefore...

It is said that because the characteristics of cognition and the characteristics of the object are identical, they are termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*). As for "non-associated" (*viprayukta*), this refers to the mind’s lack of awakening;

it has not yet differentiated between the sovereign [mind] and its objects, and thus does not associate with external phenomena. Therefore, it is eternally without distinction, and is thus called "non-associated.
Herein, it is explained how ignorance perfumes the true mind to form the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), giving rise to the three subtle states.
It is simply that the mind is not yet awakened; because it has not yet distinguished between the sovereign (the mind) and its objects, it is said to be "non-concordant.
Furthermore, the meaning of the defiled mind is termed the "hindrance of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), for it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā*.
The meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed the "hindrance of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), for it can obstruct the spontaneous wisdom of worldly activity.
This clarifies that the defiled mind exists in dependence upon ignorance (*avidyā*). Although their essence is identical, the nature of their obstruction differs.
Because the defiled mind is agitated and restless, it constitutes the "obstruction of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*); therefore, it obstructs fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Because the characteristics of defilement are differentiated, they obstruct the equality of *tathatā*. Ignorance is characterized by delusion and confusion; therefore, it obstructs the spontaneous activity-wisdom (*anābhoga-karma-jñāna*) of the mundane world. This is as follows:
[This refers to] the wisdom of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*). This [section] establishes its essential nature; the following investigates its characteristics.

What is the meaning of this? The intent of the question is as follows: Ignorance (*avidyā*) is subtle and should therefore obstruct the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*); the defiled mind is coarse and should therefore obstruct the wisdom of valid cognition. Why is this so?
Not so. The following explains the reason why:
because by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to see and manifest [objects], falsely grasping at objective realms, which contradicts the nature of equality.
This explains the reason why the afflictive hindrances obstruct the principle. "Able to see and able to manifest" refers to the three types of non-associated defilements.

Furthermore, the deluded grasping at objects is the defilement associated with the three marks. This means that while true suchness is the fundamental wisdom of equality, which is devoid of the marks of subject and object, the defiled mind now deludedly grasps at objects.
Thus, subject and object stand in opposition; their very natures are mutually contradictory, thereby obstructing the wisdom of principle and phenomena.
Because all dharmas are eternally quiescent and lack the characteristic of arising, ignorance fails to realize this;
thus, it falsely opposes the Dharma and is unable to attain the various kinds of knowledge that accord with all worldly objects.
This explains that ignorance obstructs the wisdom of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).

Because all worldly phenomena possess the characteristic of eternal quiescence and lack any arising or movement, this can be known only by the wisdom of valid cognition. Now, because ignorance is deluded and confused, it falsely gives rise to birth and cessation;
failing to realize the tranquility of all phenomena, it falsely opposes them. Therefore, it directly obstructs the wisdom of valid cognition, preventing it from functioning accordingly.
This is the knowledge of the various aspects of worldly convention.
The preceding section explained the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing; the following section explains the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of characteristics of arising and ceasing. What are these two? The first is the coarse, which is associated with the mind.

Therefore, there are two types of subtle [phenomena]. Because they are dissociated from the mind, they are subtle. Furthermore, that which is coarse among the coarse is the domain of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
That which is subtle among the coarse and coarse among the subtle is the domain of Bodhisattvas. That which is subtle among the subtle is the domain of Buddhas.
These two kinds of arising and ceasing exist based upon the permeation of ignorance; that is to say, they depend upon causes and conditions.
Dependence on cause refers to the meaning of non-awakening; dependence on condition refers to the meaning of falsely constructing objective realms.
If the cause ceases, then the condition ceases. Because the cause ceases, the dissociated mind ceases; because the condition ceases, the associated mind ceases.
This explains the "Characteristics of the Arising and Ceasing of Mind" from the section on Establishing the Thesis. It means that the mind is originally without characteristics;
it manifests its characteristics due to the defilement of ignorance and delusion, which involve arising and ceasing, and are coarse or subtle. Regarding the term "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*):

when there is the conceptualization and grasping of the three kinds of coarseness, external objects correspond with the mind. Furthermore, there is correspondence between the sovereign [mind] and its attributes (*caitta*), as well as non-correspondence.

This is because the mind and its objects have not yet been differentiated; thus, there is nothing with which they can correspond. This explains the characteristics of the coarse and the subtle. Below, this is clarified by way of persons:
that is to say, the two types of defilement involving grasping and calculation are the coarsest among the coarse, and are what is awakened to by those in the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śukla*).

The continuous succession of conceptual differentiation is the subtle among the coarse. Furthermore, the two types of defilement involving the transformation and manifestation [of consciousness] are the coarse among the subtle. This is...
This is what is realized by Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*). If it were the karmic aspect of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*), it would be the subtlest among the subtle;

only a Buddha can fully comprehend it. This concludes the major section on the departure from defilement (*vimala*). As for the statement that the two kinds of arising and ceasing depend upon ignorance:
This demonstrates that this defiled mind arises based on causes and conditions, and likewise ceases based on causes and conditions.
Initially, due to ignorance as the cause, non-awakening gives rise to the three subtle states; with objective realms as the condition, the six coarse states are extended.

Now, when the cause ceases, the condition also ceases. Therefore, when the cause ceases, the three subtle states cease; when the condition ceases, the six coarse states cease. These depend upon one another.

A question is asked: "If the mind is extinguished, how can it be continuous? If it is continuous, how can you say it is ultimately extinguished?"

the fire within the wood is a metaphor for the "direct cause" (*zheng-yin*); the human effort of drilling to extract it is a metaphor for the "conditional cause" (*yuan-yin*); and the fire emerging and consuming the wood is a metaphor for the revealing cause of severance and realization.

Sentient beings are likewise. Although they possess the power of the permeation of the true cause, if they do not encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends, and others as conditions, it is impossible for them to spontaneously sever their afflictions and enter nirvana.
Even if there is the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharmas have not yet acquired the power of perfuming,
one will still be unable to ultimately weary of the suffering of birth and death and joyfully seek nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature, which serves as the primary cause (*nidāna-hetu*).

The True Suchness (*tathatā*) taught by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), along with the Dharma teachings that flow from it, serve as external conditions. Because these internal and external factors mutually permeate one another, it is easy to sever delusions and realize the truth.
If even one of these is lacking, one will be unable to cultivate revulsion for the suffering of birth and death and seek the joy of Nirvana.
If the causes and conditions are complete— namely, possessing the power of one's own habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*),

and being protected by the compassionate vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— one is able to give rise to a mind that loathes suffering, believe in the existence of *nirvāṇa*, and cultivate roots of goodness.
Because the roots of goodness have been cultivated to maturity, one encounters Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who provide instruction, benefit, and joy;
thus, one is able to advance toward the path to Nirvana.
This clarifies that because the causes and conditions are complete, it is easy to achieve the fruit of the Path. That is to say, for the practitioner, internally—

By relying on the power of the superior cause of the permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and through the external power of the superior conditions provided by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to assist and inspire, one is enabled to swiftly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*. "Showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening" refers to obtaining instruction and admonition, as well as benefit and joy;
this represents the excellence of these auxiliary conditions.
The preceding clarifies the function of intrinsic nature; the following clarifies the function of *tathatā*.
As for "functioning as perfuming," this refers to the power of external conditions for sentient beings. Such external conditions possess immeasurable meanings.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds. What are these two? First, the differentiated condition; second, the equal condition.
These two conditions constitute the inconceivable karmic activity that arises spontaneously for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have already realized the Dharma-body.
Responding to the perceptions of sentient beings' minds, they manifest through the power of their compassionate vows, assuming various forms.
The activity of form manifests objects and conditions to serve as external auxiliary causes for sentient beings who have resolved their minds to seek the Way.

This is the function of the Dharma-body; therefore, it is the function of True Suchness. Since the essence of the originally enlightened mind possessed by sentient beings is identical to the equal Dharma-body of all Buddhas, their substance is the same and their function is likewise the same. Thus, sentient beings possess...

Because the function of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) evokes the function of the Buddhas’ accomplishment [of that aspiration], it is said that there is both differentiation and equality.

This is because the capacities of those who evoke [the response] vary; since their generation of the aspiration is not uniform, there must accordingly be a non-identity of differentiation and equality.

This means that for those who give rise to the mind from the *karmic consciousness* (*ye-shi*), various transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifest according to their respective types to serve as differentiated conditions.
For those who give rise to the mind from the *consciousness of karma* (*ye-shi*), the reward body (*sambhogakāya*) manifests to serve as an equalizing condition,
appearing in response to what each being perceives.

Regarding the specific condition (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*): this person relies upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others from the initial generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Throughout this interval, they are either seen or recollected [by those beings], appearing as a member of their retinue, a parent, a relative, a servant, a friend, or even an enemy;
or they manifest the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*).
This briefly demonstrates the characteristics of the various conditions. Although these distinctions are many, they are not beyond being subsumed within compassion and love:

serving those who are inferior, benefiting those who are one's equals, and subduing those who are enemies; these are the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), which comprise the five categories.
Therefore, whether one beholds their physical form or contemplates their virtues, it is by means of these five types that [one should act].
Thus, even regarding all the immeasurable conditions of their activities, through the power of the habitual perfuming of great compassion they have aroused,
they are able to cause sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness, for those who see or hear them obtain benefit.

This reveals that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas bring sentient beings to maturity by acting as external conditions, it is none other than arising from the power of the habitual perfuming of non-conceptual great compassion (*nirnimitta-mahākaruṇā*);
it is certainly not an act performed with a deliberate mind. This speaks to the distinctions in the functioning of transformation.
These conditions are of two kinds: first, proximate conditions, because one attains liberation quickly; second, remote conditions, because one attains liberation after a long duration.
These two types of conditions, both proximate and remote, are further distinguished into two kinds. What are these two? First, the condition for increasing practice;
