second, the condition for receiving the Path.

This clarifies the distinction between the long and short durations of the transformative capacity [of the Buddha]. These two kinds of conditions pertain to both the beginning and the end, as well as cause and effect;
hence they are called "long and short. For example, when the Buddha was a disciple under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he planted the seeds of the conditions for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

These have now reached maturity, such that each has received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); this is a case of long-term conditions. Another example is when the Buddha dwells in the world at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Regarding the capacities of those to be converted: for those who see the Buddha as one newly resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, this serves as a proximate condition and also as a causal condition for their future liberation.

This is explained generally in terms of time. Furthermore, a sutra states: The Buddha said, "I have now appeared in the world to reveal and instruct all sentient beings, so that those who have not yet gained faith may gain it, and those who already possess faith may cause it to increase. This refers to the condition for such increase. It further says:

Each attains growth; this is the condition for receiving the Way. If categorized by the proximity or distance of their stages: if it concerns the growth of the Two Vehicles or the Three Grades of Sages, it is near;

if it concerns the accomplishment of the Ten Stages or the fruit of Buddhahood, it is distant. Generally speaking in terms of the capacities of sentient beings, this can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the impartial condition: all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally vow to deliver all sentient beings;

through natural perfuming and habitual cultivation, they never abandon them. By virtue of their power of the wisdom of identical substance, they manifest karmic activities in accordance with what is seen and heard by others.
This means that sentient beings rely upon samādhi to attain the equal vision of all Buddhas;

this clarifies the equality of conditions. It means that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by virtue of their original vows to deliver all sentient beings, constantly permeate them with non-abandoning compassion and wisdom of identical essence (*sahaja-karuṇā-prajñā*), because sentient beings reside within the hearts of the Buddhas.
Therefore, they perfuse and habituate sentient beings moment by moment, never for a single thought-instant abandoning them.

Thus, whenever there are sentient beings capable of entering samādhi, [the Buddhas] manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma within that samādhi according to those beings' prior habits of seeing and hearing, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
This is like the manifestation of Samantabhadra and the responsive appearances of Avalokiteśvara; all are equal.
This is the condition.
This cultivation of essence and function is further divided into two types. What are these two?

First is that which is not yet in correspondence, referring to ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds; they cultivate through the mental consciousness, relying on the power of faith.
Therefore, one is able to practice. Because it accords with the essence, one has not yet attained non-conceptual mind;
because it accords with its function, one has not yet attained the practice of mastery over karma.
This passage clarifies that while the essence and function of the perfuming True Suchness (*tathatā*) are equal, there are distinctions among the capacities of those who are perfumed.

This is because ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved to attain enlightenment rely solely on the perfuming of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Their resolve is shallow; they practice based only on the power of faith and have not yet been able to enter deeply into the samādhi of True Suchness, nor have they attained [the state of] non-... [omitted].

The mind of conceptual discrimination corresponds with the essence (*svabhāva*); it has not yet attained mastery over the activity of wisdom (*jñāna-karman*), which corresponds with its function (*vṛtti*). This distinction depends upon the capacity of the practitioner.

The second case is that of those who have already attained correspondence, namely the *dharmakāya* Bodhisattvas, who have attained non-conceptual mind and correspond with the wisdom-activity of all Buddhas.
It is in accord. Relying solely on the power of the Dharma, one practices spontaneously, perfuming True Suchness (*tathatā*) and thereby extinguishing ignorance.

This illustrates the equality of the essence and function of the body [of reality]. That is to say, because Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) have already realized True Suchness and attained non-conceptual cognition, they are able to be in accord with the essence and function of True Suchness; this is because they rely solely on the power of the Dharma and act according to it.
One advances in cultivation; therefore, one attains correspondence with the essence and function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Because one illuminates the principle through true wisdom, it is called the "power of the Dharma" (*dharmabala*); because it proceeds spontaneously and without effort, it is called "natural" (*svayambhū*).

By means of this wisdom-activity, one perfumes True Suchness, thereby extinguishing the delusions of ignorance and attaining correspondence with the essence and function of all Buddhas. This is by means of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Upon reaching the seventh stage, one accords with the essence; from the eighth stage onward, one accords with the function.
Because those of the two vehicles and the three stages of the ordinary person rely on the six consciousnesses for inferential contemplation, they have not yet attained such accord.
The preceding section on the mutual support of defilement and purity regarding the perfuming of defilement and purity is concluded.
The following section clarifies the meaning of whether the perfuming of defilement and purity is exhausted or not.
Furthermore, the defiled dharmas have been perfuming uninterruptedly since beginningless time; even after attaining Buddhahood, they continue to exist.
There is cessation. However, the perfuming of pure dharmas never ceases; it continues until the end of the future. What is the meaning of this?

Because the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) constantly perfumes, the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) manifests. Since it gives rise to the perfuming of its functional activity (vṛtti), there is no cessation.
This summarizes the meaning of the cultivation of defilement and purity, and their severance or non-severance.

That is to say, defiled dharmas have no beginning but have an end, whereas the pure dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) has neither beginning nor end. This is because the defiling cause of ignorance arises in dependence upon *tathatā*;
thus, *tathatā* is the "beginningless beginning. Furthermore, when the cultivation of *tathatā* exhausts and severs ignorance, [the cycle of birth and death comes to an end].
One attains Buddhahood. This means that at the moment ignorance is extinguished, the Dharmakāya manifests, possessing inconceivable and great functions that are inexhaustible and boundless.
Thus, while defiled phenomena come to an end, pure phenomena are inexhaustible.
The preceding explanation of the characteristics of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind within the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing" is now complete.

What follows explains the three great aspects—essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*). This is because the initial heading states: "The characteristics of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind."
This is because it is able to demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna; thus, at this point, the explanation is concluded.
Furthermore, regarding the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā): all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas [are included herein].
It is without increase or decrease; it is not born in the past limit, nor does it perish in the future limit. It is ultimately eternal and constant.
From the very beginning, its self-nature has been fully endowed with all meritorious qualities.

This statement means that the ten dharma realms universally take true thusness (*tathatā*) as their essential nature and characteristic. This is precisely what is called the essence of the "Great Universal Characteristic Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma Realm.
Because both the holy and the ordinary equally receive this endowment, it does not belong to either delusion or enlightenment; therefore, it is without increase or decrease.
Since it is fundamentally and inherently true and constant, without arising or ceasing, it is vast and all-encompassing, with the defiled and the pure being mutually integrated. Therefore...
It is said that all merits are fulfilled;
this refers to the meaning of the great light of wisdom.
From here below, it speaks of the merits inherent in the nature. The constant radiance shines brightly, such that the darkness of ignorance and afflictive defilements cannot prevail.
Therefore, it is said that its own essence possesses the great light of wisdom; this is precisely the true body of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana,
because its meaning is that of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.
True wisdom illuminates principle; there is no principle it does not penetrate. Expedient wisdom mirrors phenomena; there is no phenomenon it does not exhaust.

Because it is the authentic cognition of meaning, it employs perfect illumination to forget conditions and transcend the measures of the sensory faculties; therefore, it is called "authentic cognition."
This is because of the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind;
that is to say, the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is eternally free from the defilement of afflictions, and is therefore called "intrinsically pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
This is because it possesses the meanings of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
To remain unchanging throughout the three periods of time is called "Permanence" (nitya). To be amidst manifold sufferings without being disturbed is called "Bliss" (sukha).
To dwell within birth and death without being constrained is called "Self" (ātman). To pass through the nine stages of decay without being defiled is called "Purity" (śubha).
Because it signifies purity, coolness, immutability, and sovereignty:
it is called "pure and cool" because it is forever free from the affliction of feverish distress; it is called "immutable" because it cannot be altered by the four marks of existence;
and it is called "sovereign" because karma cannot bind it.
Because it is fully endowed with such inconceivable Buddha-dharmas— more numerous than the sands of the Ganges— which are inseparable, uninterrupted, and non-different,
and because its meaning is fulfilled without any deficiency, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and is also called the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*.
The merit-attributes as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are not different from the true essence; therefore, it is said they are "not separate. They have been continuous since beginningless time;

therefore, it is said they are "uninterrupted. They are equal and of one flavor; therefore, it is said they are "not distinct. Because nature and attributes are mutually penetrating, and the one and the many are without obstruction;

because principle and phenomena interpenetrate, and defilement and purity are non-dual; therefore, it is called "inconceivable. This is inherently possessed by the Dharma-body, which only a Buddha realizes.
It is ultimate; therefore, it is called the Buddha-dharma. Because there is no dharma that it does not encompass and nothing lacking therein, it is called "fulfillment.
Because it can contain and integrate immeasurable inherent virtues, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, also named the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*.
Since the initial passage describes the essence of the Great Dharma-gate of universal characteristics, it concludes by returning to the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*.

Question: It was stated above that the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is equal and free from all marks (lakṣaṇa). Why, then, is it further said that its essence possesses such various kinds of virtuous qualities (guṇa)?
This is a difficulty regarding the nature of the doubt concerning this adherence.
The answer is: although these various meanings of meritorious qualities truly exist, they lack any distinguishing characteristics; they are equal and of a single flavor.
The single true suchness (*tathatā*). What is the meaning of this? Because it is non-conceptual and free from the marks of conceptualization, it is non-dual.
This answer is given by means of the mark that is identical to the essence; since the mark does not differ from the essence, there is no conceptualization.
It is like the water of the great ocean, which has a single taste. Because it is the single true reality, that which is differentiated is merely the conceptualizing mind. True.
Just as they are eternally free from the discrimination of subject and object, they are indeed non-dual.
Furthermore, by what principle can their distinctions be explained? They are indicated by means of the marks of arising and ceasing based upon the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
Since the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*) are non-dual, for what reason is it said that there are such distinctions?

It is because, based upon the evolving consciousness of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-karmavijñāna*), there exist defiled dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; therefore, one knows that by transforming the defiled and returning to the pure, there arise the distinct characteristics of pure virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
How is this demonstrated? Because all phenomena are fundamentally mind-only, there is in reality no such thing as thought;

yet, because there is a deluded mind that does not realize the arising of thought and perceives various objective realms, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When the nature of the mind does not give rise to [deluded] views, this is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom.
If the mind gives rise to views, then there is the characteristic of non-seeing; when the nature of the mind is free from views, then—

This is because it has the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm (for when defiled dharmas arising from the deluded mind of ignorance are reversed and purified, one knows that True Suchness possesses the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom).

If the mind is stirred, it is not the true cognition; it lacks intrinsic nature (because movement is itself delusive thought, and what is delusive is not true; delusion lacks intrinsic nature, and movement follows defiled conditions;

therefore, one knows that non-movement is the truly real cognition, which is free from defilement and truly pure). It is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure. It is characterized by feverish affliction and decay; thus, it is not...

Mastery (which is the opposite of these defiled dharmas) means that one knows True Suchness possesses the meanings of true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity. Furthermore, it possesses the meanings of the delusory defilements that exceed the sands of the Ganges;

because of these [defiled] meanings, when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there manifest the characteristics and meanings of the various pure meritorious virtues that likewise exceed the sands of the Ganges.
The passage beginning with "What is this? extensively elucidates the meaning. It means that True Suchness (tathatā) is fundamentally unmoving and devoid of differentiated characteristics;
how then can it be known? It is only in contrast to the movement of the mind that there arise such sands-of-the-Ganges-like marks of false defilement.
If one does not move away from this, then one knows that it possesses all the pure merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If the mind arises and perceives further dharmas as objects of recollection, then there is something lacking.
Such pure dharmas and immeasurable merits are themselves the One Mind; there is nothing further to be recollected. Therefore, being complete and fulfilled, it is called the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.
"Coming to the treasury":

this clarifies the meaning of the fulfillment of the pure dharma. If there is any arising of the mind, then the defiled dharmas of ignorance have not been exhausted and the pure mind has not yet reached perfection;
thus, there would still be something to be contemplated outside of the mind, which constitutes a deficiency. Now, by means of...
When the single mind is perfected and all delusions are purified, then immeasurable pure virtues are precisely this single mind.
With nothing external to be contemplated, its nature is spontaneously complete; this is called the Tathāgata-garbha of the Dharma-body. When it encompasses immeasurable pure virtues, it is so named;
yet when, through delusion, it becomes the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it then encompasses immeasurable defiled dharmas. Now, by returning from delusion to the source, therefore—
Thus, one accomplishes immeasurable pure virtues.
The above concludes the explanation of the two greatnesses regarding the characteristic [of the Dharma-body]. Below follows the explanation of the greatness of its function.

Furthermore, as for the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it refers to the fact that when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were originally on the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), they gave rise to great compassion.
They cultivate the various *pāramitās*, gather and transform sentient beings, and establish great vows, desiring to deliver and liberate all realms of sentient beings without exception.
They do not limit themselves to a fixed number of eons, but continue until the end of the future, because they regard all sentient beings as their own selves.

Furthermore, one does not grasp at the mark of sentient beings (this cites the original great vow; it is the vast mind and the long-term mind, citing the great skillful means of compassion and wisdom. "As with one's own body" refers to the depth of compassion).

Not grasping at signs is the profundity of wisdom (and it also implies the absence of a perverted mind). For what reason? It means that one knows all sentient beings and oneself as being equal in true suchness (*tathatā*), because there is no distinction between them.

This passage cites the cause in relation to the fruit to clarify the fundamental basis of the Great Function. That is to say, while in the stage of the causal path, the Buddhas perceive that all sentient beings and themselves share the same True Suchness Dharmakāya;

out of compassion for their delusion and immersion, they give rise to great compassion of identical substance (*sahaja-karuṇā*), vowing to deliver all beings and pledging to exhaust the realm of sentient beings without limit to the number of kalpas. It is by virtue of this that they practice.
To practice the six perfections as one's primary conduct and to teach and transform sentient beings without weariness or fatigue—this is the vast mind and the long-term mind.
The reason for not retreating is that one regards all sentient beings as identical to oneself.
This is because one does not perceive the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). Sentient beings are like one’s own body;
thus, compassion is profound and one does not grasp at marks, while wisdom is profound—these two constitute the non-perverted mind. Why does one not grasp at the mark of a sentient being?
Because one knows, as it truly is, that sentient beings and oneself are equal in *tathatā*. This is the first mind. Therefore, the Treatise says:
Vast, foremost, and supreme, his mind is free from inversion; this is the causal mind of all Buddhas.
Possessing such great wisdom of skillful means, he eliminates ignorance and beholds the original Dharma-body.
Spontaneously, there arise inconceivable activities and various functions that are coextensive with True Suchness (Tathatā) and pervade all places. Furthermore, they are also non-existent...
There is a functional aspect that can be apprehended.
This clarifies that through the wisdom of the cause, delusions are extinguished and the Dharma-body is manifested; thus, inconceivable functions arise spontaneously.
That is to say, this great function is inherently possessed by the Dharma-body, yet it was previously obscured and unmanifested by ignorance. Now, because of...
Wisdom is manifested by destroying delusions; it is equal to *tathatā* (suchness) and pervades all places.
Because *tathatā* is free from characteristics, its function likewise has no characteristics that can be apprehended.
Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the body of the Dharma-body characterized by wisdom, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

They have no sphere of experience belonging to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and are free from all conditioned activity. Nevertheless, they are said to possess "function" because sentient beings obtain benefit according to their respective seeing and hearing.
Question: Why is it said that there is no aspect of activity? If there is no aspect of activity, how can one benefit sentient beings? Answer:
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the body of the Dharma-body and the aspect of wisdom, they are free from deliberate action; therefore, there is no aspect of activity.
However, in accordance with the capacities and inspirations of sentient beings, they derive benefit according to what they see and hear; for this reason, it is spoken of as "activity."
This is what is called the pure *dharmakāya*. It is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.
When the water of sentient beings' minds is clear, the reflection of *bodhi* appears within it. Therefore, it is said that its function is "non-functioning" in nature.

Conversely, this reveals that if there were no responsive resonance with capacities, it would be nothing more than the fundamental wisdom of wondrous principle, devoid of any further characteristics of worldly conventionality, such as arising and ceasing.

This function is of two kinds. What are these two? First, that which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects), is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Because they do not know that it is manifested by the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses), they see it as coming from the outside;
they grasp at its physical dimensions and cannot know it exhaustively.

The following section addresses the cause in order to clarify that the characteristics of its function differ [from those of ordinary perception]. Ordinary beings and followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand that all is consciousness-only;
they instead postulate external objects. Consequently, their six consciousnesses engage in discrimination, and thus they perceive the Buddha-body as coming from the outside.

Because they do not know that the subtle marks are manifested by the seven consciousnesses, they see only the coarse marks of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which is the Buddha of the thirty-two marks.
This refers to the three classes of transformation-bodies and emanation-bodies seen through the contemplation of emptiness.

The reason they cannot see the subtle marks is that they do not understand that these are manifested by the evolving consciousnesses. [This concludes] the section on the retribution of the lower realms.
The body is that which is manifested by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). As for the statement that one sees the Buddha by relying on consciousness:

because the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is none other than the *tathatā* buddha-nature of the original enlightenment inherent in sentient beings, now, through the power of the internal cause of perfuming, sentient beings give rise to the aspiration to loathe suffering and seek the Buddha.
Since the six consciousnesses receive this perfuming, and these consciousnesses are coarse and their perfuming is shallow, the marks of the Buddha likewise [appear as such].
This is a coarse explanation; therefore, seeing the Buddha is described here in terms of fundamental perfuming (*mūla-vāsanā*), and it does not appear without a cause.

As for the statement that "the subtle [aspects] appear based on the evolving consciousnesses" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the intent is to clarify that although ignorance (*avidyā*) deludes True Suchness (*tathatā*) to form the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), it is merely a single moment of non-awakening and has not yet departed from True Suchness.
Because they have not yet merged, subject and object have not yet been differentiated. This remains so until the evolving...
Thus, arising and ceasing are conjoined with non-arising and non-ceasing.
This transforms the true wisdom of the *dharmakāya* into deluded vision and transforms ultimate truth into deluded appearances, serving as the beginning of sentient beings.

Now, returning from delusion to truth—from the coarse to the subtle—one severs [delusions] up to the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), whereupon fundamental wisdom manifests and the *dharmakāya* is revealed.
When one illuminates the principle with wisdom, the inherent merits within the Tathāgatagarbha manifest all at once.
One then perceives the subtle and wondrous marks of the Buddha-body and realizes that these are manifestations of the mind alone; thus, they do not come from without.
This is because they arise from the karmic consciousness perfumed since beginningless time; therefore, it is said that they are "manifestations of the evolving consciousness."

The second is based on the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). This refers to that which is perceived by Bodhisattvas from their initial generation of the resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*) up until the mind of the ultimate Bodhisattva stage;
this is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).

This clarifies that the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) manifests based on the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). From the initial stage of the ten levels of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), this bodhisattva takes the fundamentally perfumed *karmic consciousness* as the basis for the contemplation of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

Throughout the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), within the ultimate state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the Buddha-body perceived is the subtle aspect of the reward body.
It truly manifests from within the mind alone and does not come from without; yet it is spoken of in terms of its functional activity.
This is the function of the very essence of original enlightenment and true suchness (tathatā), not the function of an external Buddha manifesting his body.

As for the notion that a Buddha manifests according to the capacities of sentient beings through deliberate effort, this is not the meaning here. This is because the intended sense of this passage specifically concerns the function of perfuming and transformation (vāsanā-pariṇāma).
(While a thorough examination of the context of the preceding and following passages suggests that "a Buddha manifesting according to the capacities of sentient beings" is indeed correct.)
The body possesses immeasurable colors; these colors possess immeasurable marks; these marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
The fruits upon which they rely are likewise immeasurable. Their various adornments, according to what is manifested, are boundless and inexhaustible.
Free from the characteristics of limitation, they are able to constantly sustain themselves as appropriate, neither decaying nor being lost.

This passage cites both the primary and secondary retributions (*vipāka*) to collectively manifest the subtle characteristics of what is perceived. This is precisely the Buddha Vairocana of the *Avataṃsaka*;
his body and land, self and others, are without obstruction or hindrance, pervading the entire Dharma-realm equally. Thus, they transcend all boundaries.
This is the realm of the single true retribution, wherein even when the great fires burn, this land remains secure; hence it is said to be "neither destroyed nor lost."
Such merits as these are all accomplished through the permeation of the untainted practices of the various pāramitās and through inconceivable permeation;
because they are fully endowed with immeasurable marks of bliss, they are called "retribution."
This result arises from causes; this explains the naming of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Thus, both the retributions of the environment and the sentient beings are due to the power of the cultivation of the ten perfections and the inconceivable internal cultivation of original enlightenment (*prakṛtistha-gotra*). This concludes the clarification of the meaning of causal cultivation.
Furthermore, that which is perceived by ordinary beings is its coarse form; according to the six realms of existence, each perceives it differently as various distinct types.
Since these are not the marks of experiencing bliss, they are said to be "corresponding" (prātibhāsika).
This separate explanation indicates that the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not singular; it is simply that what is perceived differs according to the various types of beings.

Because the six classes of beings perceive the Buddha each according to their own karmic retributions, his manifestations appear differently. Since they perceive him as being of their own kind, it is said that he does not possess the marks of one who experiences pleasure.

Furthermore, that which is perceived by Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds upon enlightenment is seen only partially because they possess deep faith in the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena.

They know that such matters as the adornments of physical forms neither come nor go, are free from spatial limitations, and manifest solely in dependence upon the mind, never departing from *tathatā*.
Nevertheless, these Bodhisattvas still engage in conceptual discrimination, for they have not yet entered the stage of the *dharmakāya*.
Therefore, this separate explanation concerns what is seen by those on the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka-ārya*), which differs from that of those on the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*).

What was previously stated—that based on the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*), from the initial resolve until the ultimate ground, what is seen is generally described as the marks of the *saṃbhoga-kāya*—also applies within this context. However, therein...

There are degrees of depth; it is not that there is no distinction between partial and complete realization. Therefore, this is explained again. This clarifies the initial resolve of the three stages of worthiness (śaikṣa), which aims to sever ignorance and possesses deep faith in True Suchness (tathatā).
However, they rely solely on the conceptual analysis and inferential contemplation of the six consciousnesses; thus, their awakening is merely "semblance-awakening" (sādṛśa-bodhi).

Therefore, it is said that they see only a small portion. Because discrimination has not yet been abandoned and True Suchness (tathatā) has not yet been realized, they differ from those on the [bodhisattva] stages;
thus, it is said they have not yet entered the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).

If they attain the pure mind, what they perceive becomes subtle and wondrous, and its function becomes increasingly superior, continuing until the end of the bodhisattva stages, where they see it fully.
"Ultimate. This clarifies that the *saṃbhogakāya* perceived on the stages (*bhūmi*) also gradually becomes perfected until the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi.
Because true reality is exhausted and delusions are utterly eliminated, it is said that "one sees it ultimately."
If one were apart from the karma-consciousness, there would be no appearance of seeing; for the Dharma-body of all Buddhas has no such mutual perception of self and other through material forms.

What was stated above—that seeing occurs in dependence on the karma-consciousness—refers to the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), which still possesses something seen because it has not yet realized the Dharma.
Because of the body. Now it is clarified that if one is separated from the *karmic consciousness*, one then perceives the *dharmakāya*.

Since the true essence of the *dharmakāya* is solely the single true mind, which transcends all oppositions and is entirely devoid of form, characteristics, subject, or object, it is said that "there is no mutual seeing between self and other.
This means that although that which is visible is subtle and wondrous, it merely belongs to what is manifested through cultivation; it arises from within delusion.
Because one has not yet turned back to realize [this], one has not yet departed from the characteristics of subject and object. This true essence of the Dharmakāya is the true source of the one mind;
it does not belong to delusion or awakening, nor does it depend on conditions for its arising. This innate truth constitutes the "correct cause" (samyag-hetu) of Buddha-nature.
Therefore, pointing at one's finger is established as the ultimate and final principle.
Question: If the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is free from the marks of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), how can it manifest forms?
This question clarifies that while the Dharma-body is free from marks, it is not obstructed from manifesting them.
The answer is: Because this very *dharmakāya* is the substance of form (*rūpa*), it is able to manifest as form. That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual.
Since the nature of form is itself wisdom, the substance of form is formless and is called the "wisdom-body" (*jñānakāya*).
Since the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) which pervades all places. The forms thus manifested have no boundaries or limitations.

In accordance with the mind, one can manifest the worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable bodhisattvas, immeasurable reward bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), and immeasurable adornments, each distinct from the others, all without boundaries and yet not obstructing one another. This cannot be known through the discrimination of the mental consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).
This is because of the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The intent of the answer clarifies that the Dharma-body and Reward-body are darkly unified, and form and mind are non-dual;

it collectively reveals the single true, unobstructed Dharma-realm, thereby returning to the ultimate source of the one mind. The "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) is an alternative designation for the one mind.
Furthermore, because the mind is the source of all transformations, it is called the *dharmakāya*. Because it is the substance of form, it is able to manifest form.
For example, just as empty space is not form yet can give rise to the appearances of form, it is said that from the very beginning, form and mind are non-dual.
Since phenomena are formed by grasping the principle, and emptiness itself becomes form, it is said that the nature of form is [identical to emptiness].
Because it is the nature of wisdom, and because the substance of form is fundamentally empty, it is called the "wisdom-body" (jñānakāya);
this is what is meant by "form is itself emptiness. Because the principle is fully realized as phenomena, phenomena are themselves the principle;
it is like space, which pervades all places, whether of form or non-form; this is what is meant by "emptiness is itself form. Since principle and phenomena are non-dual, form conforms to emptiness.
It is all-pervasive and without boundaries. Because it is non-dual and undivided, there is no obstruction or hindrance between body and land, or self and other;
thus, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the reward bodies of immeasurable bodhisattvas and their lands adorned with the excellence of their collective retribution are present.

Each is distinct, yet all are without boundaries and do not obstruct one another. Thus, within the Flower Treasury Ocean, the various lands of the Indra-net interlace and entwine in successive layers.
Because principle and phenomena are non-obstructive, the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena is realized.
This is not something known by the ordinary mind or consciousness; it is entirely the great sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is truly because its essence is all-pervasive and...

This is because all functions are the functioning of the single-mind *tathatā*. Since the central tenet of this treatise is that the single mind constitutes the essence of the Great Universal Mark Dharma-gate of the One Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*), the correct meaning is explained and ultimately resolved herein. That is to say:

"There is nothing that does not flow forth from this dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this dharma-realm. Therefore, within the gate of arising and ceasing, [the nature of] phenomena is investigated...
This ultimately reveals the ultimate principle of the one mind.
In the preceding section on "Revealing the Correct Meaning," the major divisions were divided into two. First, it revealed that movement and stillness are not distinct;
this began from the passage "From the True Suchness of the One Mind" and concludes here with the completion of these two gates of analysis.
The second assembly below explains the mutual entry of phenomena and reality to reveal the non-duality of movement and stillness.
Furthermore, it demonstrates how one enters the gate of True Suchness directly from the gate of Arising and Ceasing.
This causes one to contemplate that arising is fundamentally non-arising; thus, by means of arising and ceasing, one enters the gate of True Suchness.
This refers to investigating the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), matter and mind, and the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*): ultimately, they are without thought.
Because the mind has no form or characteristics, one may search for it throughout the ten directions and never find it. It is like a person who, due to delusion, mistakes the east for the west;

yet the direction itself does not actually change. Sentient beings are likewise: because they are deluded by ignorance (*avidyā*), they mistake the mind for thought; yet the mind is truly unmoving. If...
By being able to observe and know that the mind is without thought, one immediately attains compliance with and entry into the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*);

this demonstrates correct contemplation for the sake of the sudden awakening to the wondrous nature of the One Mind. That is to say, within the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*), there is fundamentally neither form nor mind;
how, then, could there be sentient beings composed of the five aggregates? This is truly due to the initial single thought of non-awakening. This is...
This refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). By the power of ignorance, the single mind is transformed into the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*).

Based on this karmic consciousness, the two divisions of subject and object arise, which constitute the union of form and mind; thus, there are sentient beings composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Therefore, the five aggregates of sentient beings all exist because of a single thought-moment. Consequently, one need not now calculate the true nature of sentient beings.
This is false. However, observe the place where a single thought arises; fundamentally, there is no thought from the very beginning. Where there is no thought, there is no arising.

Where there is no arising, sentient beings fundamentally do not exist. How, then, could there be the various phenomena of form and mind? Therefore, the teaching instructs one to directly observe non-thought;
this allows for immediate and sudden entry into the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This single point of observing non-thought is the essential core of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

This is the essential instruction for the practice of cultivation. Therefore, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he instructed the Second Patriarch, saying, "Bring forth your mind so that I may settle it for you.
The Second Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is ultimately unattainable. The Sixth Patriarch said, "Originally there is nothing at all.
From these patriarchs downward, there have been none who did not point toward the state of being free from discursive thought. Thus, in practicing Chan today, one must understand this non-thought.
To give rise to various kinds of profound and subtle deliberations regarding this intent—how could that be the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Not only this treatise, but even the entire Great Canon and its seventeen hundred cases all ultimately converge upon the single phrase "no-thought" (wunian);
there is no teaching remaining beyond this. Let students recognize this.
The above concludes the demonstration of the correct principle (*samyak-artha*).

Below follows the counteractive treatment of erroneous attachments (*mithyā-abhiniveśa-pratipakṣa*). Regarding this counteractive treatment of erroneous attachments: all erroneous attachments depend upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). If one is free from the self, then there are no erroneous attachments.
This view of self is of two kinds. What are these two? First is the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*); second is the view of a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the "view of self" (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*): those who hold this view calculate that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) truly possess a sovereign master. This refers to beginners within the Buddha’s Dharma who are practicing the Mahāyāna;

they are deluded regarding the teachings and hold false attachments, clinging to the literal meaning of words rather than their intended sense. This is not something arising from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the like. [This is] the teaching on phenomena (*dharma*).

The view of selfhood (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the calculation that all phenomena, such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this is what arises in the followers of the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*).
As for the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it is said to be of five kinds according to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). What are these five?

This first clarifies the view of a personal self (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*). There are two types: first, ordinary beings grasp the five aggregates as a real self and, based upon them, falsely give rise to erroneous attachments.
Second, within the *tathāgatagarbha* there is the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*);

they grasp this as that which realizes [enlightenment], and thus it is said, "preserving the self and awakening to the self. This is what is grasped by Bodhisattvas; here, however, it is termed the "view of a personal self."

This refers to ordinary beings who are beginners in the Buddha-dharma; having heard the preceding two gates of differentiation, they do not understand that it transcends words and thus give rise to attachments following the literal expressions.
Therefore, all [the statements] are made in terms of the Buddha-dharma as it has been heard.
First, there are those who, upon hearing the Sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is ultimately quiescent and like empty space, fail to understand that this is taught to destroy attachment.
They consequently claim that empty space itself is the nature of the Tathāgata. How is this to be remedied?
It is clarified that the characteristic of empty space is a false phenomenon; its essence is unreal. It exists only in contrast to form; it is a visible characteristic that causes—
The mind gives rise to arising and ceasing. Because all phenomena of form are fundamentally the mind, there is in reality no external form.
If there were no form, then even the characteristic of empty space would not exist. That which is called all objective realms exists only because the mind falsely arises.
If the mind is free from false movement, then all objective realms cease, and there remains only the single true mind, which is omnipresent. This is what is meant by:
The meaning of the Tathāgata’s ultimate nature of vast wisdom is not like the characteristic of empty space;
this refutes the false attachment that takes the emptiness of phenomena as the essence-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddha.

Because sentient beings do not comprehend the principle that the *dharmakāya* is without marks, they cling to the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) as being a material substance subject to obstruction. Therefore, it is said that the *dharmakāya* is like...

[The teaching] uses space as an analogy to shatter that attachment; yet those who hear it do not understand and thus falsely claim that "insentient emptiness" (*mūḍha-śūnyatā*) is the nature of the Tathāgata.
This is a perverse attachment. How is it to be remedied? It is countered by declaring: "Space is a false phenomenon."
This is merely a pervasive conceptualization of deluded sentiments; its substance is unreal, for in principle it is fundamentally non-existent.
Why is this? Because this empty space is manifested in contrast to form; one conceptually fabricates it as being existent, causing the mind to undergo birth and extinction. It is not the Dharma-body.
Why is space a false phenomenon? Because all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are manifested solely by the mind;
matter is fundamentally non-existent. If there were no material phenomena, then space would also not exist. Why do both space and matter not exist?
It is because all objective realms exist only due to the deluded arising of the mind. If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all realms [cease to exist].
When the realms are suddenly extinguished, there remains only the single true mind, which is all-pervasive.
This is what is called the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, the nature of vast wisdom; it is not like the characteristic of empty space.

Second, having heard it stated in the sūtras that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence, and even the dharmas of nirvāṇa and *tathatā* (suchness) are ultimately empty, inherently empty from the beginning, and devoid of all marks, one fails to understand that this is for the purpose of destroying attachment.
Consequently, one claims that the nature of *tathatā* and nirvāṇa is merely emptiness itself. How is this to be remedied? By clarifying the truth.

Just as the essence of the Dharmakāya is not empty because it is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic qualities, this [view] refutes True Suchness and Nirvāṇa as being a void of annihilation. This is due to a failure to understand mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Provisional names are not real; for those who reckon them as truly existent, it is taught that their essence is ultimately empty in order to shatter that reckoning.

Those who hear this do not understand that these words are intended to destroy attachment, and they consequently grasp at the words to falsely reckon True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Nirvāṇa as a nihilistic emptiness.
How is this to be remedied? It is clarified that the self-essence of the Dharmakāya of True Suchness is not empty, being fully endowed with the nature of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because of their merit, those above hold empty space to be the Dharmakāya, while these hold the Dharmakāya to be a void of annihilation;
both fall into the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*).
Third, they have heard the Sūtras state that the Tathāgatagarbha neither increases nor decreases, its essence being fully endowed with all merits.
Regarding the Dharma of the Virtuous One: because it is not understood, it is claimed that the Tathāgatagarbha possesses the distinct characteristics of material and mental dharmas.

How is this countered? It is because it is taught solely with reference to the meaning of True Suchness (tathatā), and because the distinctions are manifested and taught by way of the defiled meaning of arising and ceasing.
This refutes the attachment that the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is identical to the differentiated phenomena of matter and mind.

For instance, there are those who, upon hearing it taught that the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* is inherently endowed with all virtues, fail to understand that these are fundamentally non-differentiated.

Consequently, they grasp at the *tathāgatagarbha* as being identical to the differentiated dharmas of matter and mind. This is an incorrect interpretation; it is to cling to the True as being identical to the deluded. How is this to be remedied? It is said: "One..."
All phenomena are fundamentally without differentiation; they exist solely by virtue of True Suchness (tathatā) following conditions.

Every phenomenon is true, for there is only one True Suchness. Matter and mind are non-dual, originally without distinction; it is only due to the meaning of arising, ceasing, and defilement that various differentiations are manifested.
Thus, differentiations are spoken of only in contrast to delusion and as a reversal of defilement. How could the self-nature of True Suchness be the same [as these]?
"Is it a distinction between matter and mind? This refutes the false attachment that the *tathāgatagarbha* is identical to matter and mind.

Fourth, having heard the *sūtra* state that all worldly phenomena of birth, death, and defilement exist in dependence upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, and that all dharmas do not depart from *tathatā*, because they do not understand this, they claim that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the self-substance (*svabhāva*).
All phenomena of birth and death in the world are possessed [by sentient beings]. How are they countered?

Because the *tathāgatagarbha* has, from the very beginning, possessed only pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, which are inseparable from, uninterrupted by, and non-different from the meaning of *tathatā*.
Because the defiled phenomena of afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges are merely falsely existent, their nature is inherently non-existent from the start. From...
Since beginningless time, they have never been in accord with the Tathāgatagarbha;
therefore, it is impossible that the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha should contain deluded dharmas such that, upon realization, those delusions could be forever stilled.
This refutes the attachment to the Tathāgatagarbha-nature as possessing the defiled dharmas of birth and death.

Because one hears it taught that the false arises in dependence upon the true, yet fails to understand the meaning of "following conditions" (*pratyaya*), one consequently clings to the notion that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha inherently contains the defiled dharmas of birth and death.
This is the attachment to the True as containing false defilement. How is this to be remedied? It is said that from the very beginning, the Tathāgatagarbha is solely...
It is endowed with the nature-qualities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and is not different from True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Because all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are merely falsely existent and have never possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they have from the beginning never been associated with the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-gotra*).

If the substance of the storehouse were to actually contain deluded phenomena, then it would be impossible for one who realizes the Truth to extinguish those delusions. These two [the pure and impure] grasp the nature of the storehouse as being identical to matter and mind.
There are defiled dharmas of birth and death. Because they do not understand that [the self] follows conditions, they falsely cling to it as being substantially existent.

Fifth, having heard the Sūtras state that birth and death exist because of the Tathāgatagarbha, and that Nirvāṇa is attained because of the Tathāgatagarbha, because they do not understand this, they claim that sentient beings have a beginning. Because they perceive a beginning, they further claim that the Tathāgata...
The nirvāṇa that has been attained has its end; one returns to becoming a sentient being. How is this countered?

Because the Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), the characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning. If it were said that there are sentient beings who first arise outside the triple world, that would be the teaching of the non-Buddhist scriptures.
Furthermore, because the Tathāgatagarbha has no posterior limit (*aparākoṭi*), all Buddhas...
The nirvāṇa that is attained is in correspondence with this, for there is no subsequent limit (*aparānta*).
This refutes the view that holds that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa have a beginning and an end.

Because they hear it taught that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa exist in dependence upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet fail to understand it, they consequently cling to the notion that sentient beings have a beginning and that nirvāṇa has an end.
They return to becoming sentient beings. This arises because, upon hearing [the teaching], they rely on the false and give rise to the notion that the True precedes and the False follows;

thus, they cling to the idea that sentient beings have a beginning and further cling to the idea that *nirvāṇa* has an end, whereby they return to becoming sentient beings and give rise to views of beginning and end.
How is this to be remedied? It is said that sentient beings exist because of ignorance, being deluded regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*. Furthermore, as for the *garbha*:
The nature has no prior limit; how much less so for ignorance which is beginningless? How could there be a first arising of sentient beings?
If one were to say that there is a first arising of sentient beings outside the three realms, that would be as stated in the non-Buddhist *Mahābhūta-sūtra*, and not the teaching of the Seven Buddhas.
Furthermore, while the Tathāgatagarbha has no posterior limit, the nirvāṇa attained by all Buddhas is merely...
It is merely to correspond with them; how could there be any end to it? These five views above belong to ordinary people who possess the view of a self.
Upon hearing the teachings of the Buddha-dharma, they employ the six consciousnesses to discriminate, unable to transcend words to grasp the meaning.
They perversely cling to verbal expressions and erroneously give rise to these calculations.
Regarding the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*): because the two vehicles possess dull faculties, the Tathāgata taught them only the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

Since that teaching was not ultimate, they perceived the five aggregates as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; thus, fearing birth and death, they falsely grasped at nirvāṇa. How is this to be remedied?
By means of the five aggregates, [one realizes] that since their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not arise, there is no cessation; they are originally in a state of nirvāṇa.
This refutes the false views of the two vehicles that there is a saṃsāra to be loathed and a nirvāṇa to be realized; it is because they hold the view of a self in phenomena (dharma-ātman).
They have heard that the Tathāgata has only taught that the five aggregates are impermanent, but have not yet heard that saṃsāra itself is truly eternal.
Because it is taught that [the self] is not ultimate, one falsely gives rise to this conception.
Since one regards saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as dharmas belonging to a self, it is called the "view of a self in phenomena" (dharmātman-dṛṣṭi).
The preceding clarifies detachment through antidotes; the following clarifies ultimate detachment.

Furthermore, regarding ultimate detachment from false attachments, one should know that defiled phenomena and pure phenomena are entirely mutually dependent and possess no self-characteristics that can be described.
Therefore, all phenomena, from the very beginning, are neither form nor mind, neither wisdom nor...
Consciousness is neither existent nor non-existent; its characteristics are ultimately ineffable.

That there are verbal expressions [regarding it] should be understood as the Tathāgata’s skillful means, employing provisional speech to guide sentient beings. Its ultimate intent is solely for them to transcend conceptual thought and return to True Suchness (tathatā).
This is because conceiving of all phenomena gives rise to the birth and death of the mind, preventing entry into true wisdom.

This clarifies that, ultimately, words are forgotten and all is returned to non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*), wondrously accords with *tathatā*, and thereby dispels the superficial characteristics of verbal expression.
The previous explanations—such as the mutual opposition of defilement and purity, or the refutation of emptiness and existence—were like prescribing medicine according to the illness;
these are all dualistic teachings that have not yet reached the ultimate transcendence of language. Now, both the medicine and the illness are discarded.
Subject and object are both forgotten; the path of language is cut off; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished; and the tracks of the intellect are severed.
All phenomena, mundane and supramundane, are entirely non-existent, for this realm free from conceptualization can only be realized through direct correspondence with realization.

Since its characteristics are ultimately inexpressible, it is only then that one is ultimately free from speech, thereby manifesting True Suchness (*tathatā*). Within that which is inexpressible, there is...
What has been explained above is, in fact, the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). He employs provisional verbal expressions to guide sentient beings;
the ultimate intent behind these is solely to cause them to abandon discursive thought (*vikalpa*) and return to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The reason one must necessarily abandon discursive thought is that contemplating all phenomena causes the mind to undergo arising and ceasing, thereby preventing entry into true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). For this reason...
The preceding section on the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) states: "All verbal expressions are provisional names without reality;
one should know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are ineffable and inconceivable, and are therefore called 'True Suchness. Furthermore, it says: 'If one is free from thought, this is called entering.'"

Thus, the explanation of these two gates is complete. This has collectively clarified the mutual dependence of defilement and purity, pointing toward the ultimate goal of non-conceptual *tathatā*, and universally dispelling the characteristics of conventional discourse. How subtle its purport is!
The preceding section on the counteraction of false attachments is concluded. Below follows the analysis of the characteristics of setting out upon the path (*pratipatti-lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*).

As for the analysis of the characteristics of setting out upon the path, it refers to the path realized by all Buddhas, in the sense that all Bodhisattvas set their minds [on enlightenment], practice, and proceed toward it.
This serves as the heading and etymological explanation for the section on "Establishing the Meaning," specifically clarifying the meaning of the Vehicle (*yāna*).
It refers to the two gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Arising-and-Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) previously elucidated, which are collectively subsumed within the One Mind.
All Buddhas realize this as the path and fruit of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa; this is what is meant by "Great" (*mahā-*)—the destination toward which all Bodhisattvas direct their resolve and practice.

The aforementioned [stage] also takes this mind as the ultimate ground, which is what is meant by "the vehicle. This means that although one has already attained intellectual understanding previously, it cannot be reached without practice;
therefore, one now advances toward the realm of understanding through practice in order to attain actual realization, rather than remaining in mere empty understanding.
Nevertheless, regarding the practice toward which one proceeds, although the initial aspiration is one, its degrees of depth and shallowness are not equal; thus, it must be distinguished.

Each possesses its own characteristic; therefore, it is called "the characteristics of the stages of progress on the path. Because one practices based on understanding, practice gives rise to the cessation of conceptual understanding;
therefore, it is called "the characteristics of the path."
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of generating the resolve for awakening. What are these three? First, the generation of the resolve through the perfection of faith;
second, the generation of the resolve through practice based on understanding; and third, the generation of the resolve through realization.
This indicates that there are three aspects to the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). However, these three types encompass all fifty-one stages;

although they differ in their respective depths and shallows, they are all termed "arousing the mind" because there are different modes of arousal. Specifically, the arousal of the mind through the fulfillment of faith (*śraddhā-sampad-cittotpāda*)—occurring at the culmination of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*) and the first stage of abiding in the arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*)—is the arousal of the initial manifestation. It is also...
Regarding "development" (*fa*): it refers to the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), wherein the three wisdoms (*trividya*) and five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) are developed simultaneously.

Regarding the "arousing of the mind through understanding and practice" (*adhimukti-caryā-prasthāna*): this is the arousal of the mind that initiates practice and progress; its meaning encompasses the stages of practice (*prayoga*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), as one proceeds in accordance with the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) and enters the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Regarding the "arousing of the mind through realization" (*praveśa-prasthāna*): this refers to the Bodhisattvas who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*), having already shattered ignorance (*avidyā*). It is the arousal of the mind [of enlightenment].
The functioning of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the very emergence of that functioning; therefore, it is distinct [from the preceding].

Regarding the "arousing of the mind through the fulfillment of faith": upon what kind of person does this depend, and by practicing what kind of conduct does one achieve the fulfillment of faith and become capable of arousing the mind?
It is said that it depends on sentient beings of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
This heading clarifies the person who has resolved to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Regarding the "indeterminate group" (*aniyata-rāśi*), there are three groups:

the rightly fixed (*samyaktva-niyata*), the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata*), and the indeterminate. Here, the indeterminate group refers to those who have previously developed faith and first resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), yet whose aspiration is not yet firm;
they may advance or retreat. These are called "hair-path ordinary beings" (*vālpa-mārga-prthagjana*), meaning their minds are like hairs suspended in space.
Therefore, it is called the "indeterminate group. This refers to those at the stage of the five grades of practice-and-observation according to Tiantai.

Because they possess the power of cultivated roots of goodness, they believe in karmic retribution, are able to give rise to the ten wholesome actions, feel weary of the suffering of birth and death, and seek unexcelled bodhi.
This explains the causal practice for the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). Regarding "perfuming" (*vāsanā*):

because of the internal perfuming of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) and the external perfuming supported by hearing the teachings that flow from True Suchness (*tathatā*), combined with the causes and conditions of the power of various roots of goodness cultivated in previous lives, one arouses the mind to loathe the suffering of birth and death and desires to seek *nirvāṇa*. However, this alone is only able to...
Believing in the fruits of karma, yet not having yet entered into contemplative practice, one must first believe as described above.
Having encountered various Buddhas and personally received their offerings, one practices this faith for ten thousand kalpas.

Because this faith has been perfected, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct one to resolve upon the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Alternatively, through great compassion, one is able to resolve upon it spontaneously; or else, due to [various] causes...
When the True Dharma is about to perish, one is able to spontaneously resolve [to attain enlightenment] through the causal conditions of protecting the Dharma.

Those who achieve such faith and thus give rise to the resolve enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), never again to regress; they are said to abide within the lineage of the Tathāgata and to be in accord with the true cause.
This clarifies that through the conditions of practice and the completion of the provisions for faith, one dwells in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).

Encountering the various Buddhas is the cause for generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*). A period of ten thousand *kalpas* is the duration of the cultivation. The teachings, commands, and so forth are the external conditions for generating the resolve.
By means of these internal causes and external conditions, one attains the definitive resolve of faith and enters the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Thus...
To give rise to right faith is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood, for from this point on one shall never again fall back or lose it. Below, the indeterminate nature is explained:
if there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight and whose afflictions have been deep-seated for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha...
They may also perform offerings; however, they plant the seeds for rebirth as humans or devas, or plant the seeds for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Even among those who seek the Mahāyāna, their faculties are not fixed, and they may advance or regress.

Some may encounter the Buddhas and make offerings without even ten thousand kalpas having passed, yet within that time, meeting with the right conditions, they too may resolve their minds—namely, by perceiving the physical marks of the Buddha and thereby generating that aspiration—or...
They may resolve their minds because of making offerings to the Sangha; or they may resolve their minds because of being taught by those of the Two Vehicles;

or they may resolve their minds by following the example of others. Such resolutions of the mind are entirely indeterminate; encountering adverse conditions, they may suddenly fall away and descend to the level of the Two Vehicles.
This clarifies those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*). Because their internal and external causes and conditions are weak and inferior, they undergo regression and loss.

Their roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) are meager; this refers to the weakness of the power of internal permeation (*vāsanā*). Their afflictions (*kleśa*) are heavy while their virtues (*guṇa*) are thin; thus, they may mistakenly seek rebirth among humans and devas, or aspire to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Consequently, regarding the Mahāyāna, they remain undecided, advancing and retreating. If they have not yet made offerings to the Buddhas for ten thousand kalpas, then the time has not yet arrived.

[The practice] may be fulfilled, yet if one encounters adverse conditions and cannot prevail, it will lead to decline. This is because, in seeing the Buddha or making offerings to the Sangha, one dwells upon the marks of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*);

or if one encounters an inferior teacher, or if it is not one's original resolve—through such causes and conditions, there is always the risk of falling back. This is because one has not yet entered the stage of faith and has not attained certainty.
Furthermore, regarding the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith: what kind of mind is aroused? Briefly stated, there are three types. What are these three?

First is the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it maintains right mindfulness of the dharma of suchness (*tathatā*). Second is the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because it delights in accumulating all virtuous practices.
Third is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*), because it desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.
The preceding section clarified the causes and conditions for generating the resolve; this section correctly clarifies the mind that is so generated. First, regarding the "straight mind":
it means the mind is as straight as a string, whereby one may enter the Way. This refers to being free from the characteristics of crookedness, bias, or deviance.
Through this, one maintains right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*); this is precisely the *tathatā-samādhi*. One takes True Suchness as the foundation for the two practices.

Because it is endowed with untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*), it serves as the foundation for self-benefit. Because it perceives that the nature of sentient beings is identical [to one's own], it serves as the foundation for benefiting others.
Because it knows that the essence is replete with all virtues, one delights in cultivating all wholesome practices;

since these practices are characterized by "non-cultivation" and each accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*), they constitute the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*). Thus, they serve as the foundation for the practice of self-benefit. This is because of the great [compassion] of identical essence (*samatā-kāya*).
Compassion. It extensively uproots the suffering of sentient beings and causes them to attain bodhi; it is the foundation for practices that benefit others.
Although sublime practices are vast, they are subsumed within these three mentalities. Therefore, it is said that "the three are explained in brief."
Question: It was stated above that the Dharma-realm has a single characteristic and that the essence of the Buddha is non-dual.

For what reason, then, does one not simply contemplate True Suchness (tathatā), but must instead rely on seeking and practicing various wholesome deeds? Answer: It is like a great maṇi jewel whose essential nature is luminous and pure, yet which is defiled by the impurities of ore.
Even if a person contemplates the nature of the jewel, if they do not employ skillful means to polish and refine it in various ways, it will ultimately [not become pure].
There is no attainment of purity. Thus, the *tathatā* (suchness) of sentient beings is empty and pure in its essential nature, yet it is defiled by immeasurable afflictions.
Even if a person contemplates *tathatā*, if they do not cultivate it through various skillful means (*upāya*), there will likewise be no attainment of purity;
for these defilements are immeasurable and pervade all phenomena. Therefore, one must cultivate all wholesome practices as an antidote. If...
A person practices all wholesome dharmas because they naturally accord with and conform to the dharma of *tathatā*.

Question: Since the principle is one while delusions are manifold, it is necessary to cultivate various wholesome deeds. Question: It was stated above that the essence and its characteristics are not different.
"In that case, it would suffice merely to contemplate True Suchness (tathatā); why then rely on manifold virtues? The answer is:
"Because delusions are manifold, manifold virtues are required. By practicing in accordance with principle, one externally purifies delusive defilements and internally accords with True Suchness.
'Expedient means' refers precisely to contemplative practice."
The following clarifies the four kinds of skillful means taught based on the three preceding states of mind.

Briefly stated, there are four kinds of skillful means. What are these four? First is the skillful means of the root of practice, which refers to contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen, thereby departing from false views, not abiding in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and contemplating the causes of all phenomena.

Because the fruits of karma produced through the convergence of conditions are never lost, he gives rise to great compassion. He cultivates all manner of meritorious virtues to gather in and transform sentient beings, yet he does not abide in nirvana, for he accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which is itself non-abiding.

Based on these three superior states of mind, four types of skillful means are established. First, the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*) is explained as the practice of non-abiding by maintaining right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness).
Because one initiates practice based upon *tathatā*, it serves as the root of all practice. This means that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;
by being free from deluded views and relying on great wisdom, one is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, one does not abide in saṃsāra, while contemplating the conditions of phenomena.

The convergence of karma and its fruits is never lost. Relying upon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one cultivates all manner of merit and virtue to gather and transform sentient beings, yet does not abide in nirvāṇa.
This is called "non-abiding" because one does not abide in either emptiness or existence. Since the two benefits are cultivated simultaneously, it is termed the "practice of non-abiding.
Because the nature [of reality] is fundamentally without abiding, one practices in accordance with the *dharmatā*.
The second is the skillful means of cessation, which refers to shame, remorse, and repentance;

it can stop all unwholesome dharmas from increasing, because by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one becomes free from all faults. The third is the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness.
This means diligently making offerings to and prostrating before the Triple Gem, praising and rejoicing in their merits, and entreating all Buddhas.
Because of a heart of pure devotion and reverence for the Triple Gem, one’s faith increases, thereby enabling one to aspire to the unsurpassed path.

Furthermore, because one is protected by the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one can eliminate karmic obstructions and ensure that one’s roots of goodness do not regress. Thus, by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one becomes free from...

Because of the obstruction of delusion, these two rely on the profound mind to cultivate the two beneficial practices of the skillful means of cessation (*śamatha*) and application (*pragraha*). Regarding the skillful means of cessation:
it means that shame and remorse can prevent uncommitted evil from being done, and repentance prevents committed evil from increasing; therefore, it is said:
Feeling shame and remorse for one's transgressions can stop all unwholesome dharmas from increasing.

By practicing conduct that accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā) and remains free from faults, one maintains restraint; this is "stopping and maintaining" (śīla). Third is the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness.
This means causing unperformed wholesome deeds to arise and causing those already performed to increase; diligent offerings and the like are themselves the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
That is to say, by cherishing and revering the Triple Gem (*triratna*) and thereby increasing one's faith, one is able to aspire to the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, through the protective power of the Triple Gem, one is able to eliminate karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), thereby strengthening that faith.

This means that because one’s nature is fundamentally free from hindrances, one practices in accordance with the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) to distance oneself from the hindrance of delusion; through prostration, one distances oneself from the hindrance of pride;

through praise, one distances oneself from the hindrance of slander; and through sympathetic joy, one distances oneself from the hindrance of envy, and so forth. This constitutes the practice of "active maintenance" (*kṛtya-dhāraṇa*).

Fourth is the skillful means of the equality of great vows. This refers to making the vow to continue until the end of the future, transforming and delivering all sentient beings without exception, causing them all to ultimately attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

This is because it accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is uninterrupted; the nature of phenomena is vast, pervading all sentient beings, equal and non-dual, without thoughts of self or other.
Because it is ultimately quiescent.
This refers to the practice of benefiting others through the skillful means of great vows, cultivated based on a compassionate mind.
To vow to deliver all sentient beings until the end of the future is the long-term mind. To ensure that none remain is the vast mind. To cause them all to reach ultimate...

Having attained final nirvāṇa, one accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without interruption. This nature of phenomena is vast, impartial, non-dual, and ultimately quiescent; this is the foremost mind.
Because the Bodhisattva has given rise to this mind, they obtain a partial vision of the Dharmakāya.

By virtue of seeing the Dharmakāya, according to their power of aspiration, they are able to manifest eight ways of benefiting sentient beings, namely: descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, and so forth.

"Dwelling in the womb," "emerging from the womb," "leaving home," "attaining the Way," "turning the wheel of Dharma," and "entering nirvana"—these words describe the benefits of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
Because Bodhisattvas in the ten stages (*bhūmi*) rely on this gate of contemplation, they obtain a partial vision of the Dharmakāya;
thus, there are eight kinds of benefits. A Bodhisattva in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) is then able to manifest the eight phases of enlightenment (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*).
Because he practices this path, he is able to perform these deeds;
