however, this bodhisattva is not yet named the Dharma-body, because of his out-flowing (āsrava) karma accumulated over immeasurable past eons.

They have not yet attained definitive resolution; they experience a slight degree of suffering corresponding to whatever state arises, yet they are not bound by karma, because they possess the sovereign power of their great vows.

This clarifies the distinction from those on the stages (bhūmi), because there is still a subtle fault. That is to say, a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) retains afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten rebirth;
because past karma has not yet been definitively severed, there remains the subtle suffering of both transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and karma-conditioned birth (*vipākaja*).

Therefore, this is not the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Because it is sustained by the power of great vows, [the Bodhisattva] has mastery over the length of life; thus, it is not [the same as the Dharma-body].
They are bound by the same karmic fetters as ordinary worldlings.
As stated in the sūtras, there are those said to fall back and descend into evil realms; however, this is not an actual falling back.
It is merely for the sake of inspiring those beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty and have become indolent, so that they may become courageous.

This refers to the provisional teachings. Question: Since these bodhisattvas have already become detached from the bonds of karma, why does the teaching speak of those who fall back and descend into the evil realms?
Answer: This is not an actual falling back; it is merely intended to warn against the indolence of beginners.
It is not a real regression. In the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Primary Karma), it is stated that those prior to the seventh stage are called...
Regarding the stage of regression: if one does not encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), one may regress from the bodhicitta for as long as one kalpa or even ten kalpas;
encountering the conditions of evil associates, one regresses into the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and falls into the unwholesome realms.
This is merely a provisional means to instill fear in beginners.
Furthermore, once this bodhisattva has awakened the mind of enlightenment, they remain far removed from cowardice and never fear falling into the stages of the two vehicles.

Even upon hearing that nirvāṇa is attained only after enduring diligent practice and difficult austerities for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they do not become disheartened.
This is because, through faith, they know that all phenomena have been in a state of nirvāṇa from the very beginning.
This praises the practice of true realization. Since this bodhisattva has already perceived the Dharma-body, he knows that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind and are ultimately equal.
He knows that throughout kalpas of long duration, there is not a single moment apart from the present thought-instant; he knows that all phenomena are originally in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, he is not timid or weak. This demonstrates that the aforementioned sutra is provisional and not ultimate.
Regarding the "arousing of the mind through practice and understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā-prasthāna*), one should know that it is increasingly superior.

This clarifies the arousal of the mind through practice and understanding. Because the preceding stage of perfected faith constitutes the entry into the stage of fulfilled faith (*śraddhā-paripūri*), whereas this stage involves entering the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*) through the fulfillment of practice, it is said to be "increasingly superior.
Although one previously cultivated the two types of practice, one was still within the stage of contemplative cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā*).

Principle. This refers to emerging from the ultimate truth and entering into conventional reality; therefore, it is increasingly superior. The following explains the reason for this increasing superiority:

because this Bodhisattva, from the time of initial right faith until the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa is about to be completed, has attained a profound understanding that manifests within the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness), and their cultivation is free from signs.

This explains why this stage is superior. That is to say, from the initial stage of right faith until the fulfillment of the tenth stage of Dedication, the Bodhisattva passes through the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, which is superior to the preceding ten thousand kalpas.

This is because practicing the conduct of True Suchness (*tathatā*) that is free from marks (*animitta*) surpasses the practice of the ten wholesome paths, making offerings to Buddhas, and revering the Sangha while remaining attached to marks. This is because one knows all...

Dharma is the very nature of the mind; the body of wisdom is accomplished without depending on the realization of another. Therefore, it is said that one "profoundly understands this supreme characteristic.
Because one profoundly understands the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one practices in accordance with that nature.
Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) in accordance with it.
Because one knows that the dharma-nature is unstained and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) in accordance with it.

Because one knows that the dharma-nature is without suffering and free from anger and affliction, one practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in accordance with it. Because one knows that the dharma-nature is without...
Regarding the characteristics of body and mind: because one is free from indolence, one practices the *vīryapāramitā* in accordance with it;
because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally settled and its essence is without distraction, one practices the *dhyānapāramitā* in accordance with it;
because one knows that the essence of the nature of phenomena is luminous and free from ignorance, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with it.
This clarifies the practice of cultivating the departure from marks (*animitta*). The Sanskrit term *pāramitā* is translated here as "reaching the other shore.
What is called "the other shore" refers to the ultimate reality of the *tathatā* (suchness). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"If one cultivates the six perfections for the sake of human or celestial rebirth, or those practiced by the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), these have all not yet departed from marks; this is because they have not yet realized that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence."
It was previously said that these are merely "dāna" and so forth, but not yet called "pāramitās.
Now, because they are practiced according to the *dharmatā* of *prajñā*, each one is free from conceptual marks; therefore, they can be called "pāramitās," for each reaches the other shore.

This is because, by knowing how to remain free from marks such as stinginess, one practices in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*). Thus, while practicing, there is no mark of practice. Therefore, in the text on dedication:
The "characteristics of suchness" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth correctly manifest the practice that is free from characteristics.
Regarding the "realization of the mind" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*): from the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*) up to the Ultimate Ground of the Bodhisattva, what kind of realm is realized?
It is called suchness (*tathatā*). While it is described as a "realm" based on the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), this realization itself possesses no realm; it is solely...
The wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) is called the *dharmakāya*.

This clarifies the realization of the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). Although it is said that the preceding three stages of the virtuous ones (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*) accord with the nature of reality, they consist only of inferential contemplation;

because ignorance has not yet been destroyed, they have not yet attained direct realization. Now, upon entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the two obstacles of conceptualization (*parikalpita-āvaraṇa*) have already been abandoned, and true [realization]...

Manifesting as it appears, one develops a single mind to serve as the correct realization; therefore, it is called "realized development of the mind" (*pramāṇa-cittotpāda*), because it brings forth the great function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
What is the realm realized? It is precisely True Suchness; this is the characteristic of correct realization.

Regarding the statement that it is called an "object" (*viṣaya*) based on the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*): this reveals that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object;

it is devoid of the characteristics of subject and object. Mind and object are one in suchness. This distinguishes [fundamental wisdom] from the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) of the evolving consciousness, which takes suchness as its object by perceiving emptiness through the transformation of appearances.

Because [the latter] involves the opposition of subject and object, it possesses an "object. Here, true suchness is free from the characteristics of subject and object; thus, wisdom alone remains, and therefore there is no [object].
The realm is the single wisdom of True Suchness (tathatā), which is called the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). In a single moment of thought,
this Bodhisattva can reach all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception, making offerings to all Buddhas and requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma,
solely for the purpose of guiding and benefiting sentient beings, without relying on words and letters.
The following clarifies the supreme functions of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which possesses both provisional and ultimate virtues.

By directly realizing True Suchness, the dharma-realm of the ten directions manifests with equality, as if before one's eyes. The physical forms of self and others are like mirrors reflecting one another’s light;
thus, in a single thought-moment, one can reach the lands of Indra’s net, serve all Buddhas, and request them to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Because he perceives all sentient beings as equal and non-dual, he benefits only all sentient beings.
Since the Dharma he teaches is the single mind of True Suchness (tathatā), it does not rely on words and letters.
This gives rise to the inconceivable activity of True Suchness, wherein the provisional and the ultimate are simultaneously manifested; hence, the text below says, "is able to demonstrate."
Sometimes he manifests the swift attainment of perfect enlightenment by transcending the stages for the sake of sentient beings who are timid;
sometimes he says, "I shall attain the Buddha-way after immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas," for the sake of sentient beings who are indolent.

He can thus manifest such countless skillful means that are inconceivable, yet in reality, the lineage and faculties of the bodhisattvas are equal, and their resolve to attain enlightenment is likewise equal.
That which is realized is also equal; there is no dharma that exceeds it.

Since all Bodhisattvas pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, it is only because the worlds of sentient beings differ—such that what they see, hear, and their faculties, desires, and natures vary—that the practices they exhibit also appear to have distinctions.
This clarifies how, by relying on the qualities and functions of True Suchness (tathatā), the provisional and ultimate practices are manifested. First, the provisional practice is clarified:
for sentient beings who are timid and weak, fearing that the Buddha-way is long and distant, [the Buddha] manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment by transcending the stages [of practice].
Examples include the dragon girl in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Pūrṇamukha in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and Sudhana in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. This is for those who are indolent...
Because sentient beings grow weary and abandon the path midway, [the Buddha] manifests for them the passage of incalculable kalpas;

this is as in the case of Śākyamuni, who fulfilled his practice over three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas. Furthermore, he can manifest countless skillful means to subdue beings according to their faculties, which is inconceivable.
All of these are expedient wisdoms. In reality, when Bodhisattvas rely upon their actual practice, their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is uninterrupted;

therefore, their faculties (*indriya*) and so forth are equal. Because they resolve their minds based on the Truth (*tathatā*), their resolve is equal. Because that which is realized is True Suchness (*tathatā*), their realization is also equal.

Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is impartial, there is fundamentally no dharma that can transcend it. Furthermore, because all have passed through three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), whether time is extended or abbreviated is irrelevant.

At the same time, they are equal in their single limit and possess no marks of distinction; it is only because sentient beings differ in what they see and hear, and because their faculties, desires, and natures vary, that distinctions are shown.
In reality, these true virtues are not different; it is only that they appear differently according to the capacities of those who respond to them.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind, there are three subtle aspects of the mind. What are these three?

First is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), because it is free from discrimination. Second is the mind of skillful means (*upāya-citta*), because it spontaneously and universally acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
Third is the mind of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna-citta*), because its arising and ceasing are subtle.
This clarifies that although there are provisional and ultimate functions on the stages (*bhūmi*), because they are not yet ultimate, they are not the same as those of a Buddha.
Question: If the Bodhisattva possesses such great functions, is this not equivalent to being a Buddha? Answer:

Because of three kinds of subtle mental characteristics that differ [from those of a Buddha], it is not the Buddha. First, the true mind (*tathatā-citta*): because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), it is real.
The first is the mind of wisdom (*jñāna*), which is the wisdom of ultimate reality (*prajñā*). The second is the mind of skillful means (*upāya*), which is the wisdom of expediency (*upāya-jñāna*).

The third is the mind of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), characterized by subtle arising and ceasing. This is because, although this Bodhisattva possesses both the wisdom of expediency and the wisdom of ultimate reality, since their matured retribution (*vipāka*) has not yet been emptied, there still remains subtle arising and ceasing; therefore, this is not the same as that of a Buddha.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva’s merits have reached full completion, he manifests a body of supreme height and magnitude throughout all worlds at the realm of Akaniṣṭha.
By means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, ignorance is suddenly exhausted; this is called the "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).
Spontaneously, there arise inconceivable activities that can manifest throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.

This clarifies the ultimate fruit and virtue. Because the cause has reached its consummation and the fruit is fulfilled, one manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the Heaven of Ultimate Form) to demonstrate the benefits of immediate retribution and to assume the rank of Buddha for the benefit of sentient beings through subsequent retribution.
This is what is meant by the "exhaustion of karmic consciousness": there spontaneously arises inconceivable karmic activity, and thus it is called "accomplishment."
It is the knowledge of all modes. The Akaniṣṭha Heaven is the pinnacle of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

In every instance where a Buddha attains enlightenment, he does so by sitting within a lotus palace in this heaven and manifesting his most sublime and vast body to achieve perfect awakening; this is the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) Buddha.
Question: Because space is infinite, worlds are infinite; because worlds are infinite, sentient beings are infinite;
and because sentient beings are infinite, the distinctions in their mental activities are likewise infinite. Such a realm cannot be delimited; it is difficult to know and difficult to understand.
If ignorance is severed and no mental conceptions remain, how can one be able to comprehend this? It is called "all-encompassing" (sarva).
The Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This question and answer clarify the realm free from conceptual thought and manifest the Knowledge of All Modes.

As for "the Knowledge of All Modes," it refers to the seed of all-knowledge (*sarvajña*), because it is able to know the entirety of the realms of empty space and the mental activities of all sentient beings to their ultimate limit.
To know each and every one of these categories exhaustively is called "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, because the world-systems of empty space are boundless, sentient beings are boundless, and the distinctions in their mental activities are likewise boundless; such realms are difficult to comprehend and difficult to know.
However, since ignorance has been exhausted and mental activity has utterly ceased, how can each [aspect] be known,
such that it is called "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*)? This question is posed because one attempts to fathom the inconceivable realm by means of a conceptualizing mind.
The answer is: All objects of experience are originally one mind, free from conceptualization. Because sentient beings falsely perceive objects, the mind has limitations.
Because they give rise to false conceptualizations that do not accord with the *dharmatā*, they cannot comprehend it.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas are free from the marks of perception; because their minds are truly real, there is nothing they do not pervade. This is the nature of all phenomena.

Its nature is the self-manifestation that illuminates all deluded phenomena. Possessing the function of great wisdom and immeasurable skillful means, it is able to reveal all manner of dharma meanings according to how each sentient being should understand them; therefore, it is named "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This clarifies that the realm free from discursive thought can only be realized through direct correspondence; it cannot be known by the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), and thus it is termed "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñatā*).
It is said that all realms are fundamentally one mind; therefore, when this mind is perfectly realized, sentient beings manifest within that one mind.
Thus, the mental activities of sentient beings are all clearly illuminated within the mind of quiescent extinction.
This is understood. However, sentient beings obstruct themselves with deluded thoughts and thus do not see the mind of the Tathāgata.
Since the minds of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are equal and non-dual with the minds of sentient beings, there is neither subject nor object; they are free from the marks of seeing.
Therefore, there is nowhere they do not pervade. Because the Buddha-mind is true and without delusion, the mind of sentient beings is itself the Buddha-mind.
By means of its own essence, it illuminates all the deluded phenomena of sentient beings within its own mind;

thus, even the most subtle mental thoughts—their arising and ceasing, their frequency, and even their various desires, memories, and discriminations—are all clearly manifest, like images reflected in a mirror.
Therefore, it possesses the function of great wisdom, and by virtue of this, it is able to manifest immeasurable skillful means.
According to the faculties [of beings], he tames them and is able to reveal all manner of dharmic meanings; for this reason, he is named "One of All-Knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is something that can hardly be known through intentional calculation or measurement.

He asked again: "If all Buddhas possess spontaneous karma (*anābhoga-karman*) that can manifest in all places to benefit sentient beings, then all sentient beings—whether they see their bodies, behold their miraculous transformations, or hear their teachings—would none fail to obtain benefit."
Why is it that the world for the most part cannot see [this]? The answer is: The Dharma-body of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is equal and pervasive in all places;
because it is without volitional effort, it is said to be spontaneous (*svayambhū*). It manifests solely in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. As for the minds of sentient beings:
It is just like a mirror: if the mirror is defiled, reflections do not appear. Likewise, if the minds of sentient beings are defiled, the Dharmakāya does not appear.
This question clarifies that the great function of the Dharmakāya is eternally present; it is only because the capacities of sentient beings vary in clarity and obscurity. Question:
If the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is omnipresent and its great function is universally pervasive, why is it that most in the world do not perceive it? Answer:
The great function of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is eternally present and shines universally upon all sentient beings. However, the minds of sentient beings are defiled by the darkness of ignorance.

It is merely obscured; thus it is simply not seen, yet this is not the fault of the Buddha. To illustrate the principle of seeing and not seeing through the metaphor of a mirror, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is like the sunlight shining universally upon the great earth. Those with eyes behold it together, yet those who are born blind alone do not see it.
Nevertheless, even though they do not see it, they still receive its benefit. The intent here values the capacity of the recipient (the *indriya*). Therefore—

It is like a mirror. The preceding section, which analyzed the characteristics of setting out upon the path, clarified the signs of those who have entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by practicing according to the Dharma;
this served to conclude the main body of the treatise with the intent that practice brings about realization.
Having already explained the meaning of the Mahāyāna, the subsequent section on "Cultivating Faith" is specifically intended for those who have not yet entered the stage of right determination.
To reveal and instruct sentient beings in faith, causing them to give rise to correct practice—this clarifies the meaning of "Awakening Faith.
Having already explained the Section on Exposition, I shall now explain the Section on the Practice of Faith.
Regarding the purpose of this section: the preceding part explained the correct meaning to clarify the Mahāyāna. This section on the practice of faith clarifies the arousal of faith;
it is presented for the sake of inspiring right Mahāyāna faith in sentient beings who have not yet entered the state of true concentration.
Therefore, this section follows.
Within this, the practice of faith is taught for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet entered the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This is because those of inferior capacity mentioned previously have not yet resolved their minds definitively and fear falling into the two vehicles;

therefore, the expedient means of practicing faith are specifically taught to cause them to give rise to great faith and advance toward the right determination. This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
"What is faith? How is one to practice? Briefly stated, there are four kinds of faith.

This inquiry initiates the skillful means for faith and practice. The intent is that while the four kinds of skillful means previously explained fully clarify the progression toward cultivation and realization, [the author] now asks again: "What is faith? How is one to practice? That is to say, as for the former...
For those who have already developed right faith, it is sufficient to speak only of the three minds and four practices, because they believe in *tathatā* (suchness) and thus see no divergent paths;
they can immediately advance in their cultivation. However, those of today have inferior capacities and heavy obstructions, and must therefore rely on various skillful means.
Thus, the four faiths and five gates are taught as the method for their training and regulation. It is necessary to employ these gates to attract and guide them; this is not redundant.
It is said: What are the four? First is the root of faith, which refers to delighting in mindfulness of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma.
This indicates the basis of faith; for *tathatā* is the root of the mind of faith and the foundation of the myriad practices. Therefore, one must first...
Regarding "delightful mindfulness": those of superior capacity previously believed in True Suchness (tathatā), so it was simply called "direct mind and right mindfulness.
Now, these of inferior capacity have not yet given rise to right faith; therefore, it is called "delightful mindfulness."

Second is faith in the Buddha. Because he possesses immeasurable merit, one should constantly mindfully approach, make offerings to, and revere him, thereby generating roots of goodness and aspiring for all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Third is faith in the Dharma. Because it provides great benefit, one should constantly mindfully practice the various *pāramitās*.
Fourth is faith in the Saṃgha. Because they are able to practice correctly for their own benefit and the benefit of others, one should always delight in approaching them.

Because the assembly of bodhisattvas seeks to study and practice according to reality, they possess superior internal causes by means of their supreme faith, aspiration, and mindfulness toward *tathatā*. This faith in the Three Jewels constitutes the enhancement of external conditions.

Since both causes and conditions are thus preeminent, they constantly delight in and constantly mindfully recollect [the Dharma], such that from moment to moment it is never forgotten; thus, internally and externally...

Through mutual permeation, it causes the mind of faith to be swiftly accomplished. This is to show that those who previously fell back did so because both their causal conditions and their environment were inferior.
Therefore, in the practice of the Dharma-ending age, if one abandons these causal conditions, there will be no way to give rise to right faith.
There are five gates of practice that can bring this faith to fulfillment. What are these five? First, the gate of giving;
second, the gate of precepts; third, the gate of patience; fourth, the gate of diligence; and fifth, the gate of tranquility and insight.
The four preceding levels of faith are all causes for the arousal [of the mind], while the cultivation of these five gates constitutes the conditions that assist in its accomplishment.
Because the previous "Treasure-Treatment" analogy involved many expedient means, these four faiths and five gates encompass all myriad practices; therefore, they are specifically elucidated here.
Whereas the former was cultivation in accordance with the nature (*xing*), this is exclusive cultivation (*zhuan-xiu*).

How does one practice the gate of generosity? If one sees anyone who comes seeking anything, one gives whatever wealth and goods one possesses according to one's capacity, thereby abandoning one's own stinginess and greed and causing the other to rejoice.

If one sees those in distress, terror, or peril, one bestows fearlessness according to one's ability. If there are sentient beings who come seeking the Dharma, one gives according to what one is able to understand.
He then explained for him: "One should not greedily seek fame, profit, or honor; one should only contemplate benefiting oneself and others, dedicating such merit toward Bodhi.
To benefit sentient beings, a Bodhisattva practices the three kinds of giving (dāna), namely: the gift of material wealth, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma."

How does one practice the gateway of ethical discipline (*śīla*)? It is as follows: refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from double-tongued speech, refraining from harsh speech, refraining from false speech, and refraining from frivolous speech;
and remaining far removed from greed, envy, deceit, guile, crookedness, malice, and wrong views.

If one has gone forth into homelessness, for the sake of subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*), one should likewise remain far removed from bustle and noise, always dwelling in tranquility, and cultivate [this practice].
One should practice fewness of desires, contentment, the dhūta austerities, and so forth; even regarding minor offenses, one should feel dread in the heart, feel shame, and reform with repentance.

One must not treat lightly the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata, but should protect against censure and reproach so as not to cause sentient beings to give rise to false transgressions and faults.
This clarifies the characteristics of the precepts. Now, there are many categories of precepts, which are subsumed within the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*):

namely, the precept of restraining misconduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*). These [precepts], such as the prohibition against killing, sever the evils of the three karmic paths.
Restraint of conduct is the precept of restraining oneself; having few desires and being content is the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas, which subdues afflictions;
fearing even minor transgressions and guarding against reproach so as not to cause sentient beings to commit faults is the precept of gathering sentient beings.
By maintaining the characteristics of one's own restraint, one prevents sentient beings from committing offenses, which is precisely what constitutes gathering sentient beings.
How does one practice the gate of patience? It means that one should endure the afflictions caused by others and harbor no intent for retaliation;
furthermore, one should likewise endure the dharmas of gain and loss, defamation and praise, renown and insignificance, as well as suffering and pleasure.

This is the characteristic of patience (*kṣānti*). Since objects of experience may be either adverse or favorable, one should practice patience toward them all. Enduring the afflictions caused by others is patience toward adversity.
The eight worldly concerns—gain and loss, and so forth—pervade both adversity and favor. Acquiring wealth is called gain; losing wealth is called loss.

Attacking the faults of others is called disparagement; speaking of one’s own virtues is called praise. Praising someone’s virtues to their face is called flattery; speaking of them with piercing words is [called slander].
Evil is called "reproach. To have one's body oppressed is suffering; to have one's mind satisfied is joy. The union of these opposites—favorable and adverse conditions—is termed the "eight winds.
These eight objects can strike the ocean of the sentient being’s mind, giving rise to the waves of afflictions such as greed and anger.

If one can now endure them, then the eight winds will not move one. Furthermore, there are three kinds of patience: patience toward living beings (*sattva-kṣānti*), patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and [patience regarding] the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*).
This is the patience of tranquil extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*); it is the patience of arising.
How does one practice the gateway of progress? It is said that regarding all wholesome deeds, the mind does not slacken or retreat, and one’s resolve is firm and strong.

One should distance oneself from both cowardice and arrogance. One should reflect that since the distant past, one has pointlessly endured all manner of great physical and mental suffering without any benefit.
Therefore, one should diligently cultivate all meritorious virtues to benefit oneself and others, so as to swiftly escape all forms of suffering.

Furthermore, even if a person practices with faith, because they have accumulated many grave sins and karmic obstacles from previous lives, they may be harassed and disturbed by malevolent spirits and ghosts; or they may be entangled by various worldly affairs;
or they may be afflicted by the suffering of illness. Because there are such numerous obstacles as these, one should be courageous...

With fierce diligence, during the six periods of day and night, one should prostrate to all Buddhas, repent with a sincere heart, entreat [the Buddhas to teach], rejoice [in merits], and dedicate [merit] toward Bodhi, never ceasing or abandoning these practices.
By doing so, one shall escape all obstacles and cause one's roots of goodness to increase.

This clarifies the characteristics of diligence (*vīrya*). First, one must ensure that the wholesome mind does not slacken and that one’s resolve is firm and strong; this constitutes the foundation of diligence.
"When one reflects" below [in the text] means to employ contemplation as a spur to progress, so that one cultivates goodness without weariness.

Furthermore, "next" below indicates the skillful means for removing obstacles for those whose afflictions are heavy. As for "paying homage to the Buddha," it means taking refuge in the Most Victorious One and entreating His empowerment.

"Protection. This is the general characteristic of removing obstacles. From "with a sincere heart" onwards, there is the specific removal of four obstacles: first, confession, which removes the obstacle of evil karma;
second, requesting [the Buddhas] to teach, which removes the obstacle of slandering the Dharma; third, sympathetic joy, which removes the obstacle of jealousy toward others;

fourth, dedication toward enlightenment, which removes the obstacle of delighting in the three realms of existence. "Without ceasing or abandoning" summarizes the remedial practices; "to be free from all obstacles" refers to the result.
To summarize that which is to be remedied: by means of these four obstacles, practitioners are prevented from initiating wholesome conduct and from proceeding toward bodhi.
Therefore, when the remedies for these four obstacles are perfected, the roots of goodness increase.

How does one practice the gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight)? That which is called "stopping" (*śamatha*) refers to the cessation of all objective appearances, as it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of *śamatha*.

That which is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the discernment of the characteristics of arising and ceasing produced by causes and conditions, as it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of *vipaśyanā*. How do they accord? By gradually cultivating these two meanings, one does not...
They are mutually exclusive because they manifest as a pair.

This explains the characteristics of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Regarding the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), one should speak of them as the two gates of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); that they are here called *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is [due to the following].
That which exists in the causal stage is called *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; that which exists in the resultant stage is called *samādhi* and *prajñā*.

Now, wishing to cultivate both simultaneously and operate them in tandem—this being precisely the practice of the causal stage—they are combined into a single gate. As for the term *śamatha*, its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

In stating that one cultivates the gate of *śamatha* while "conforming to the meaning of the contemplation of emptiness," the intention is to reveal the contemplation inherent within *śamatha* itself; this is the primary intent.
*Vipaśyanā* (Contemplation) refers to entering contemplation by means of *śamatha* (calm abiding). Tiantai establishes three types of *śamatha* and three types of *vipaśyanā*.

The first is called "Cessation that Embodies Reality" (*tǐzhēn zhǐ*), which corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*kōngguān*). This means embodying and uniting with ultimate emptiness (*zhēnkōng*); all conditions are naturally quiescent, the single mind is luminously radiant, and the myriad dharmas are as they are (*rúrú*).
Therefore, it is contemplation within cessation itself, and thus accords with the meaning of the *śamatha* contemplation of emptiness. This contemplation...
The gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) establishes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). That which is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to discernment and so forth;

it is so called because it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the two skillful means that follow conditions and abide [in stillness]: this corresponds to provisional contemplation (*jia-guan*).

This means that although the mind and its objects are suchness (*tathatā*), it does not preclude observing that all phenomena arising and ceasing exist as illusory manifestations through causes and conditions; though they exist, their nature is eternally [empty].
Because it is empty of self-nature, although one contemplates the causes and conditions of all phenomena, one does not abandon the myriad practices;
thus, there is constant leisure within the single path. Therefore, this is "calm abiding (śamatha) within contemplation. Hence, it is said that this conforms to the provisional meaning of vipaśyanā.

This contemplation pertains to the gate of arising and ceasing, and constitutes the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna). Third is "stopping the discrimination of the two extremes," which corresponds to the contemplation of the Middle Way. That is to say, dwelling in...

While abiding in emptiness, one does not abandon the myriad practices; while traversing the realm of existence, the single path remains pure. Dwelling in neither of the two extremes, principle and phenomena manifest simultaneously.
Within the single mind of the Middle Way, all is clearly reflected like a bright mirror. This is the harmonious integration of emptiness and existence, the wondrous accord with the One Mind.
Thus, through the three types of cessation, the three types of contemplation are achieved; in this way, the three contemplations are the One Mind, fundamentally without distinction.

Now, this [text] clarifies the combined practice of calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā). Although the three contemplations (trivipaśyanā) are not explicitly mentioned, they are in fact fully present in principle;
for by merely understanding the two gates of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the conventional (upāya), the Middle Way naturally manifests within a single mind.

This constitutes the essential gateway for entering the Mahāyāna. Therefore, among these five gates, the first four are merely auxiliary means for accomplishing this goal, which is the intended meaning of the treatise.
Since this treatise focuses exclusively on the single gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it subsequently sets forth the characteristics of cultivation in full detail.

Within the various systems of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* in the Tiantai school’s Great and Small [Treatises], there are many doctrinal approaches; however, the essentials of practice are elucidated solely in this treatise, which is the most concise, essential, direct, and expedient.
May students therefore devote their whole hearts to its study.
The following clarifies the method for cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
If one cultivates *śamatha*, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with a focused mind, neither relying on the inhalation and exhalation of breath nor on physical forms and colors.
Do not rely on emptiness; do not rely on earth, water, fire, or wind; and so on, up to not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.

Eliminate all perceptions as they arise through recollection, and even eliminate the perception of elimination itself. Since all phenomena are fundamentally without perception, they do not arise from moment to moment, nor do they cease from moment to moment.
Furthermore, one should not follow after external objects with the mind and subsequently use the mind to eliminate the mind.
If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately collect it and abide in right mindfulness. Regarding this right mindfulness, one should know that there is only mind and no external objects.
Furthermore, this very mind has no self-characteristic; it cannot be apprehended from moment to moment.

This extensively clarifies the characteristics of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. The method for cultivating the mind and entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is fully demonstrated herein.
"Dwelling in a quiet place" means abandoning external conditions and noisy, bustling environments.

In the *Tiantai Xiao zhiguan*, it is clarified that at the beginning of entering concentration, one first learns to regulate the body, mind, and breath. Herein, "sitting upright" refers to regulating the body; one does not lean forward.

One does not look upward; thus it is called "sitting upright. "Rectifying the intention" means to harmonize the mind. Without sinking or floating, alertness and stillness flow as one; thus it is called "rectifying the intention.
Because one does not rely on the breath, one does not regulate the breath. Not relying on breath or physical form is to be detached from the body.
Not relying on empty space or the four great elements is to be detached from the world. Not relying on seeing or hearing is to be detached from the senses.

Awakening and knowing is the departure from the mind. Therefore, when the ancient masters taught people to practice Zen, they said: "Internally, detach from body and mind; externally, cast off the world.

One need only practice by departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness; one must study by exiting the paths of ordinary beings and sages, and seek by departing from the realm of deluded thoughts.
Therefore, all these are said to be "not relying," which is precisely liberation. The five phrases from "all thoughts" to "moment-to-moment non-extinction" are the very method for applying the mind.
All sentient beings are deluded regarding their original true mind and have consistently relied solely on the functioning of delusive thoughts.
Therefore, in the present practice, the removal of thought is paramount. Thus, the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: "From..."
The aforementioned successive transmission among the sages regarding the single phrase "the naturelessness of delusive thought" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitutes the essential point. Question:
How is this naturelessness of delusive thought eliminated? Answer: All thoughts are eliminated as they arise with mindfulness.
That which is called this "single thought-moment" is precisely the mind of directness, the right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness). At present, when applying the mind, it is solely...
Take this single thought as the master, allowing no second thought. By the power of this single thought’s contemplative illumination, one simply observes wherever delusive thoughts arise;
immediately, that single thought illuminates and shatters them, causing them to vanish on the spot without permitting their continuity.
This is what Yongjia meant by "severing the continuous mind. The essential point of Zen meditation does not exceed this.
"Mindfulness" indicates its essential point. "Also eliminating conceptions" refers to the mindfulness that eliminates conceptions.
Initially, one eliminates conceptions with a single moment of mindfulness; once deluded conceptions have been extinguished, even this single moment of mindfulness has no basis for remaining.
Therefore, it must also be dispelled. Question: Since you speak of "right mindfulness," why must it also be dispelled? Answer:

This single thought is established specifically for the purpose of dispelling conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Since the self-substance of the true mind is fundamentally free from conceptualization, how could there be room for mindfulness?
Because false conceptualization has no inherent nature, it does not exist inherently. Since false conceptualization is not originally present, if [it is absent]...
To establish a single thought in order to await delusive thoughts is itself the very foundation for sustaining delusion.

Therefore, even this thought has nothing that can be established, because the place where it is established is itself the Truth (*tathatā*). When both truth and delusion are extinguished and both subject and object are forgotten, this is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Since not even a single thought is established, every moment of thought is non-arising. If every moment of thought is non-arising, then one is eternally...
The light manifests before one; it is tranquil, illuminating, and radiant, never ceasing from moment to moment. This is the essential point of Zen meditation (*chán*).
As for the statement that one must not follow external thoughts or mental objects, nor subsequently use the mind to eliminate the mind—this demonstrates the illness of improper mental application.
It means that through the power of a single moment of contemplative observation, one should no longer turn along with deluded thoughts.
If, following after deluded thoughts and external objects of perception, one subsequently attempts to eliminate the mind with the mind, this is using delusion to eliminate delusion;
it is merely chasing along the flow of arising and ceasing. To employ the mind in such a manner ultimately does not depart from the deluded thoughts of arising and ceasing;
it is truly an unskillful application of the mind. Therefore, it says below: "If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately..."
To gather [the mind] back and bring it into right mindfulness means that as soon as a deluded thought arises, one immediately illuminates and shatters it.
One does not follow after others; rather, one returns to right mindfulness without waiting for the mind to follow external conditions before gathering it back. Therefore, the conclusion states:

One should know that there is only mind; there are no external objects. Not only are there no external minds or external objects, but even this very mind lacks any intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), because it cannot be apprehended from moment to moment. Thus, both the internal mind and external objects are entirely quiescent.
Thus, through cultivation and refinement in every thought-moment, one naturally becomes embodied in harmony with True Suchness; this is what is called "contemplation within cessation.
When rising from one's seat, whether going or coming, advancing or halting, or performing any other action, at all times one should constantly maintain mindfulness of skillful means.

Observing in accordance [with the teachings], through long-term cultivation and maturation, the mind attains stability. Because the mind abides, it gradually becomes sharp and penetrating, allowing one to enter the Samādhi of True Suchness (Tathatā) in accordance with reality.
Afflictions are deeply subdued, faith increases, and one swiftly achieves the stage of non-retrogression.
Except for those who harbor doubt and uncertainty, lack faith, slander [the teaching], possess the heavy karmic obstacles of evil deeds, are arrogant, or are indolent—
such persons as these are unable to enter.
This demonstrates the practice of "stopping according to conditions" (*suiyuan zhi*). It means that stopping does not consist solely of sitting meditation;

therefore, it shows that one should practice in accordance with circumstances without even momentary interruption. As observation continues for a long time, it gradually becomes pure and matured, and the mind naturally comes to abide in the *samādhi* of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Afflictions are gradually subdued, faith increases, and one can swiftly achieve the stage of non-retrogression.
Regarding this samādhi, there are none who will not attain it, provided they are able to believe and are willing to practice;
only those who lack faith, whose obstacles are heavy, or who are arrogant cannot enter it. This is a case of "revealing by way of exclusion," showing that entry is attained solely through faith.
Thus it is said: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma has faith as its means of entry. This is precisely what that refers to.

Furthermore, by relying on this samādhi, one realizes that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic: namely, that the dharma-body of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings are equal and non-dual.
This is called the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (Samādhi of the Single Practice). One should know that suchness (*tathatā*) is the root of this samādhi;
if a person practices it, they will gradually be able to give rise to immeasurable samādhis.

This section demonstrates the superior benefits of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Regarding the statement, "By relying on samādhi, one knows that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) has a single characteristic":
the dharma-realm refers to the ten dharma-realms, which comprise the differentiated characteristics of the noble and the ordinary, the defiled and the pure. How could these be equal?
Only by relying on the *tathatā-samādhi* (samādhi of suchness) can one contemplate in their entirety that the dharma-bodies of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings are equal and non-dual.

This is called the Samādhi of One Practice. Because the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—is, through the single True Suchness, entirely devoid of any marks of differentiation, it is thus equal.
Since True Suchness is the root of samādhi and possesses inconceivable great functions, if a person practices it, they will gradually be able to attain immeasurable samādhis.
The preceding section concludes the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā; the following section distinguishes the works of Māra.
There may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness, and thus they are deluded and disturbed by various Māras, non-Buddhists, ghosts, and spirits.
If, while sitting, they manifest a terrifying form, or appear in the likeness of handsome men or women, you should contemplate that these are but the mind;
then the objective realm will vanish and they will ultimately not cause you any affliction.
This clarifies how demonic activities (*māra-karman*) destroy the concentrated mind, briefly indicating their characteristics so that one may know the remedies.

The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* explains demonic activities in detail; they manifest while the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within meditative concentration have not yet been destroyed, numbering fifty types of varying depth.
It further states: "Or there may be celestial Māras, various evil ghosts and spirits, *piśācas*, *rākṣasas*, and *kumbhāṇḍas*, all coming forth..."
It vexes you; or it may be that your own *skandha-māra* or *citta-māra* has produced this affliction. I have explained each of these in detail, yet here I have merely provided a general outline.

This refers to various *māras*, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and spirits who, while practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) during their causal stage, fell into this state due to evil habits and false views. Therefore, the residual influence of their meditative concentration manifests and issues forth.

It merely manifests forms to cause distress. As for the statement that [distress] will cease if one contemplates that objects are "mind-only," this means that although external māras may cause interference, it is actually due to one's own evil habitual tendencies being stimulated by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Consequently, within one’s own consciousness, those external substances are relied upon as bases, and their reflected images transform into harm.
Therefore, it is said to be "mind-only" and that there are no external objects. If one contemplates mind-only, then [the affliction] will cease of itself.
They vanish.
Sometimes they manifest in the form of devas or bodhisattvas, and also in the form of Tathāgatas, complete with all the marks and signs of perfection.
They may preach dhāraṇīs, or speak of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; or they may speak of the equality of emptiness.
Signless and wishless; without enmity and without kinship; without cause and without effect; ultimately empty and quiescent—this is true nirvana.
Or it may cause one to know past events from former lives, as well as future events, and attain the knowledge of others' minds.
Possessing unimpeded eloquence, they cause sentient beings to become greedily attached to worldly fame and profit;

this is the demon of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-māra*). This demon arises because practitioners have long been intimately familiar with the Buddha-dharma yet have not forgotten their attachment to signs (*nimitta*), or because they practice the view of emptiness as the ultimate goal and crave the insights of past lives; therefore, it now manifests due to these causes.

It is manifested through the power of meditative cultivation within samādhi; thus, this phenomenon appears. Because the original cause was not upright, it causes one to become greedily attached to worldly fame and profit.
This is precisely the manifestation of the transformation of the Mind-only.

Furthermore, it causes those one employs to be frequently angry and frequently joyful; their nature lacks constancy. They may become excessively compassionate, or suffer from excessive sleep and illness;
their minds become indolent, or they suddenly exert diligence only to later abandon it. They give rise to lack of faith, becoming full of doubt and deliberation;
or they may forsake their original superior practices to cultivate miscellaneous activities, or even become attached to the various entanglements of the world. It can also...
If one causes others to attain various samādhis that are only partially similar [to the true state], these are all what is attained by non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and are not true samādhi;
this is the demon of affliction (kleśamāra). This demon arises because, having previously practiced the samādhis of non-Buddhists, one has not yet severed the afflictions.

Although they now practice according to the Buddha-dharma, because they have not yet entered right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they manifest these events as the arousal of past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Alternatively, it may cause a person to abide in concentration for one day, two days, three days, or even up to seven days.
In the midst [of this], one obtains naturally fragrant and delicious food and drink; body and mind are at ease and joyful, free from hunger and thirst, causing others to feel attachment.
Or it causes people to eat without moderation—sometimes much, sometimes little—and their physical appearance changes.
For these reasons, the practitioner should constantly observe with wisdom, ensuring that this mind does not fall into the net of error. One should diligently maintain right mindfulness and not...
If one takes [the objects of desire] without attachment, one can remain far removed from these karmic obstructions.

This is the demon of desire (*kāmadeva*). Because sentient beings dwell amidst the five desires and take food as their life-sustenance, they grasp at the "food of desire" (*kāmāhāra*), giving rise to much craving and attachment;
their habitual tendencies are so deep that they have never, even for a single thought-moment, relinquished this food of desire.
Therefore, although one is currently in a state of meditative concentration, the habitual tendencies of desire are incited because the body and mind experience pleasure; thus, deep attachment arises.
For this reason, it is taught that one should constantly employ wise observation and diligently maintain right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging, so as to become detached.
One should know that all the samādhis of the non-Buddhists do not depart from the mind of views, craving, and self-conceit, for they are greedily attached to worldly fame, profit, renown, and honor.
As for the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā), it does not abide in the mark of seeing, nor does it abide in the mark of attainment;
even upon emerging from meditative concentration, there is no indolence or pride. All afflictions gradually become thin and subtle. If ordinary people [do not...]
It is impossible for one who practices these dharmas of samādhi to enter the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

This is because, by cultivating worldly dhyānas and samādhis, they frequently give rise to attachment through savoring them; relying on the view of self, they remain bound to the three realms and share commonality with non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, if they are not protected by a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will give rise to the views of non-Buddhists.

This distinguishes the heterodox from the orthodox to demonstrate true cultivation. Because non-Buddhists cultivate based on the habitual tendencies of self-clinging, craving, views, and pride, their practice entirely constitutes demonic activity;
thus, they are internally attached to heterodox views and externally attached to heterodox desires, which is what is meant by "erroneous and confused cultivation.
By means of the samādhi of True Suchness, one abides in profound stillness with a single mind, forgetting subject and object, and extinguishing all mental images.
Free from indolence and pride, and having extinguished the afflictions, there is no practitioner who has not entered the lineage of the Tathāgata by means of this samādhi.
All other worldly dhyānas and samādhis are attached to the view of self and are shared with non-Buddhists;
if one is not protected and guided by a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one will fall into the evil views of non-Buddhists. Thus, the Laṅkāvatāra [Sūtra]...
One must strictly admonish oneself to distance from non-Buddhist paths and should instead draw near to the most excellent spiritual friends.
Furthermore, those who diligently and single-mindedly practice and study this samādhi shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in the present life.
What are the ten? First, one is constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Because one perfectly accords with the Buddha-mind through the samādhi of true thusness (tathatā), one is thus protected and remembered.
Second, they cannot be terrified by various māras or evil spirits; third, they cannot be deluded or disturbed by the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist heretics, ghosts, or spirits.
Because they have abandoned evil habits and false views, they are free from the delusions of celestial Māras and non-Buddhist paths.
Fourth, by remaining far removed from slandering the profound Dharma, their heavy karmic obstacles gradually diminish.
Fifth, they extinguish all doubts and all evil discursive thoughts.
Because one has deep faith in one's own mind, one is free from slander; because habitual tendencies are gradually eliminated, karmic obstructions become thin and slight;
and because of a straightforward mind and right mindfulness, doubt is extinguished and correct contemplation arises.
Sixth, one gains increasing faith in the realm of all Tathāgatas. Seventh, one remains free from sorrow and regret;
amidst birth and death, one is courageous and undaunted. Eighth, one’s mind becomes gentle and supple; having abandoned arrogance, one is not troubled by others.
Ninth, although one has not yet attained meditative concentration, at all times and in all objective spheres, one is able to diminish [afflictions].
9. One diminishes afflictions and takes no pleasure in the world. 10. If one attains samādhi, one is not startled or disturbed by any external sounds or conditions.
6–7. Because one has attained resolute faith, one believes in the Buddha’s realm; thus, free from sorrow, one is undaunted. 8. One is free from the notion of self.
1. By forgetting people, one is not troubled by others. 2. Because the nine afflictions have diminished, one does not delight in the world. 3.

Because one is tranquil and has forgotten external conditions, one is not moved by the outside. Regarding the six sense objects, specifically sounds: this is because at the time of entering meditative concentration, [the mind is withdrawn from them].
The five sense organs are all closed, yet the faculty of hearing alone remains open and unobstructed; therefore, sounds easily stir the mind.
That it now remains unmoved is what is meant by "entering the stream and losing the object."
Having completed the cultivation of *śamatha* above, one now cultivates *vipaśyanā* below.
Furthermore, if a person cultivates only *śamatha*, the mind will become sunken, or laziness will arise, and they will take no delight in various wholesome qualities.
They are far removed from great compassion; therefore, one practices contemplation.
For those whose minds sink into despondency, because they are directed toward *tathatā* (suchness) and are single-mindedly intent on entering quiescence, their minds easily become submerged.
Thus, there are two faults: first, through indolence and failure to practice, one loses self-benefit. Therefore, the contemplation of lower phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is used to remedy this.
Cultivate it through the contemplation of diligence to bring it to completion. If one is far removed from great compassion, one will fail to benefit others;
therefore, apply the contemplation of great compassion to remedy this, and cultivate it through the contemplation of great vows to bring it to completion.
One who practices contemplation should observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world cannot endure for long, but undergo transformation and decay in an instant.

There are four types of contemplative practice: first, the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); second, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); third, the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*); and fourth, diligence (*vīrya*). First, the characteristics of phenomena:
The middle four [meditations] begin with this contemplation of impermanence (*anityatā*).
All mental formations (*saṃskāra*) arise and perish from moment to moment; for this reason, they are suffering (*duḥkha*).
This is the contemplation of suffering.
One should contemplate all phenomena thought of in the past as being as insubstantial as a dream. One should contemplate all phenomena thought of in the present as being like a flash of lightning.
One should contemplate all phenomena thought of in the future as being like clouds suddenly arising.
This is the contemplation of non-self. The past has no substance and is difficult to pursue; the present does not abide for even a single moment;
and the future is originally without accumulation. It exists only as a sudden emergence through the gathering of conditions; it does not come from the ten directions.

One should contemplate that all embodied beings in the world are entirely impure, defiled by various kinds of filth, and not a single one is worth delighting in; this is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

It should be understood that the four preceding contemplations eliminate the four inversions (*viparyāsa*). This concludes the contemplation of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*).

In this way, one should reflect upon all sentient beings: from time immemorial, because they have been perfumed by ignorance, their minds undergo arising and ceasing, causing them to endure all manner of great suffering of body and mind. Even now, they are beset by immeasurable oppression;
the suffering they will face in the future is likewise boundless. Yet, finding it difficult to relinquish and difficult to part with, they remain unaware of it—such are sentient beings.
This is indeed deeply pitiable.
This is the contemplation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because they do not know suffering, they lack the mind that finds weariness in suffering; thus, their suffering is likewise limitless.
This is what is pitiable. Were it not for profound compassion, there would be no salvation.
Having reflected thus, one should immediately establish a great vow with vigor: "May my mind be free from conceptual discrimination;

therefore, throughout the ten directions, may I practice all virtuous merits until the end of the future, employing immeasurable skillful means to rescue and deliver all suffering beings, enabling them to attain the ultimate bliss of Nirvāṇa."

This is the contemplation of the great vow. Because one contemplates [all beings] as being of the same essence (*samatā*), one vows to rescue and deliver them. To be free from conceptual discrimination is "sameness of essence.
To extend until the end of the future is the "long-term mind. To rescue and deliver all beings is the "vast mind. To attain *nirvāṇa* is the "supreme mind."
Because they have generated such aspirations, at all times and in all places, they practice and study all manner of wholesome qualities to the best of their ability,
never abandoning them, and their minds remain free from indolence.
This is the contemplation of diligence.
Except for the time when one is seated and focuses exclusively on *śamatha* (calm abiding), in all other circumstances, one should always observe what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Whether walking, standing, lying down, or rising, one should always practice both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (insight) together. That is to say, although one is mindful of all [phenomena]...

The intrinsic nature of phenomena is unarisen; yet, one further contemplates that through the harmony of causes and conditions, the karmic actions of good and evil and their retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed.
Although one contemplates these causes and conditions and the retributions of good and evil karma, one simultaneously contemplates that their intrinsic nature is unattainable.
This teaching involves the simultaneous practice of both tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) throughout the four modes of conduct.

Although one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen—this is tranquility—one simultaneously observes that the causal conditions of good and evil and the resulting karmic fruits are indestructible; therefore, one extensively cultivates all forms of goodness to gather and transform sentient beings.

This is the cessation (śamatha) within contemplation (vipaśyanā). Although one contemplates causes, conditions, karma, and retribution, this is contemplation; yet, because the nature of thought is ungraspable, this is the cessation within contemplation.
Therefore, one dwells in emptiness without abandoning the myriad practices, and engages with existence while the single nature remains serene.
This is called the dual cultivation of cessation and contemplation.

If one cultivates *śamatha*, it serves as the antidote to the ordinary person’s attachment to the mundane world and enables the relinquishing of the timid views of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

If one cultivates *vipaśyanā*, it serves as the antidote to the fault of the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their narrow-mindedness, and it brings about the distancing from the ordinary person’s failure to cultivate roots of goodness.
For this reason, these gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* mutually assist and perfect one another, never being separated.
If śamatha and vipaśyanā are not complete, one will be unable to enter the path to bodhi.

This explains śamatha and vipaśyanā in terms of their respective remedies: because ordinary beings are greedily attached to the world and the followers of the two vehicles fear birth and death, [the Buddha] demonstrates śamatha that is identical with vipaśyanā, so that ordinary beings may know the world is impermanent and thus cease their attachment.
The world [is thus understood]. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles know that the fundamental nature is true and eternal, they do not fear birth and death;
therefore, it is said that this serves as an antidote to ordinary beings who dwell with attachment to the world, and enables them to abandon the timid views of the Two Vehicles.

This is the "calming" (śamatha) within contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which remedies these two faults. If one cultivates "contemplation" within calming, it remedies the narrow and inferior mind of the Two Vehicles, causing the Great [Vehicle] to arise.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) also cures the ordinary person’s mind of detachment from craving and leads them to know that the world is impermanent, thereby diligently cultivating all manner of goodness.

Therefore, it is said that [compassion] serves as the antidote to the two faults: the failure of the followers of the Two Vehicles to give rise to great compassion, and the ordinary person’s distancing themselves from the cultivation of roots of goodness. These are the two errors.

From "By this" onwards, it concludes that śamatha and vipaśyanā proceed together, mutually supporting one another. Because ordinary beings are able to weary of the world, they diligently cultivate various virtues;
because those of the Two Vehicles do not fear birth and death, they are able to give rise to great compassion.

Through this mutual assistance of śamatha and vipaśyanā, they are able to dwell neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, and are thus able to proceed directly toward bodhi. This is their simultaneous practice.
This is its benefit.
Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds are timid and weak.

Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they fear that they will not always be able to encounter the Buddhas to personally receive their teachings and make offerings; thus, they dread that their faith might falter.
It is difficult to achieve. For those whose minds wish to retreat, you should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to protect and sustain their faith;

namely, through the causal conditions of single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, they shall, according to their vows, be born in the buddha-fields of other directions and constantly behold the Buddha.

They shall forever be free from the evil realms. As stated in the Sūtra: "If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward the vow to be born in that world, they will immediately attain rebirth there.
Because they constantly behold the Buddha, they shall never again fall back. If one contemplates the Tathatā-Dharmakāya of that Buddha and practices this diligently and constantly, until—"
They ultimately attain birth because they abide in right concentration;
this refers to those of inferior capacity, for whom the skillful means for preventing regression are demonstrated. That is to say, for beginner sentient beings who have not yet attained right faith.
Since their inner minds are weak and they lack superior external conditions, they fear falling back and losing their progress;

therefore, the Tathāgata establishes supreme skillful means to gather in and protect their minds, namely, by directing their thoughts single-mindedly toward the Buddha and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, thereby relying on the Buddha’s protection.
For example, by recollecting Amitābha Buddha, one attains birth in the Western Land and dwells on the stage of non-retrogression; this is its practice.
However, regarding non-retrogression in the Pure Land, there are three stages. First, it is like a lotus flower that has not yet opened, where the practice of faith is not yet perfected;
this is called "non-retrogression" only in the sense that, due to the location, there are no conditions for falling back. Second, the flower opens and one beholds the Buddha. When...
When the stage of faith is fulfilled, one partially perceives the Dharma-body and dwells in the assembly of those fixed in rightness; this is true non-retrogression.
Third, when the three stages of the virtuous ones are fulfilled, one enters the first ground (*bhūmi*), realizes the all-pervading Dharma-body, and is born in boundless Buddha-lands;
this corresponds to the subsequent stage.
The section on the Practice of Cultivating Faith is concluded. Next is the section on the Benefits of Encouraging Practice.
Having already explained the section on the Practice of Cultivating Faith, I shall now explain the section on the Benefits of Encouraging Practice.
Thus, I have already given a general exposition of this Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas.

This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one. As has already been fully explained above, this treatise comprehensively subsumes the vast and profound teachings of the Tathāgata;
therefore, it is called a "general exposition.
If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to right faith regarding the extremely profound realm of the Tathāgata and remain free from slander, [they should study this].
Entering the Path of the Mahāyāna, one should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it; thus, one will ultimately attain the unsurpassed path.

From here below, the text clarifies the benefits and harms of faith and slander in order to encourage practice. "If there be... and so forth, generally reveals the benefits of the three types of wisdom:

"upholding" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); "contemplating" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and "practicing" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). These three constitute the means of entry, as follows:
The "one mind and two gates" explained above are the profound realm realized by all Buddhas; because they are that which must be entered, one must practice them.

If, upon hearing this Dharma, a person does not give rise to cowardice or weakness, it should be known that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and will surely become [a Buddha].
This is the prediction bestowed by all Buddhas;

it specifically reveals the benefits of the wisdom derived from hearing. Since the True Suchness of the single mind elucidated in this treatise is the very foundation for attaining Buddhahood, those who accept it with faith and without cowardice will surely perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas.
Suppose there were someone who could transform all sentient beings filling the three-thousandfold world system and cause them to practice the ten wholesome paths of action;
this would not equal a person who, for the duration of a single meal, correctly contemplates this Dharma. The merit of the latter exceeds that of the former beyond comparison.

This specifically clarifies the benefit of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). While the ten wholesome [paths of action] are with outflows (*sāsrava*), this dharma—a single moment of faith—immediately becomes the seed of Buddhahood;
therefore, it cannot be compared [to them].
Furthermore, if a person upholds this treatise and observes its practice for even a single day and night, the merit they acquire is immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be fully described.

Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to praise that merit for immeasurable, boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they could not exhaust it. Why is this? It is because of the nature of the Dharma.
Because the qualities of the nature (*dharmatā*) are inexhaustible, the merit of this person is likewise thus, without limit.

This specifically reveals the benefit of cultivating wisdom through meditation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). That is to say, by relying on this treatise for cultivation, because it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), even in a single day and night, one's merit is boundless;
since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inexhaustible, it cannot be fully extolled. Therefore...
Even if one were to praise its merits, they could not be fully exhausted.
Should there be sentient beings who slander and do not believe this treatise, the retribution for their sins will last for immeasurable kalpas.
They will experience great suffering and distress. Therefore, sentient beings should simply rely on faith;
they should not slander it, for doing so deeply harms themselves and harms others, severing the seeds of the Triple Gem.
This is because all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying upon this Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas enter the wisdom of the Buddha by practicing according to it.

This passage cites the sin of slandering [the teaching] as a solemn admonition to encourage its cultivation. The phrase "Those who... and so forth cites the sin of lack of faith as a warning to encourage its cultivation;
it means that what this treatise elucidates is the very life-force of the Buddhas' wisdom, the seed-nature of the Triple Gem, and the Dharma-body of sentient beings.
Therefore, if one slanders and does not believe it, one cuts off the lineage of the Buddhas, severs the Triple Gem, and harms sentient beings.
This is the Dharma-body. Therefore, to harm it is to harm oneself and others; the retribution for such a sin is immeasurable.
It is that upon which all Tathāgatas rely to realize nirvāṇa, and by means of which Bodhisattvas attain Buddhahood. One must certainly believe in it and not slander it.
One should know that bodhisattvas of the past have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma;
bodhisattvas of the present are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma; and bodhisattvas of the future shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma.
Therefore, sentient beings should diligently practice and study it.

"Know that... and so forth concludes with the exhortation to believe and practice. This means that since all Buddhas have attained Buddhahood by means of this Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time rely upon it to cultivate the causes [of enlightenment], one must therefore certainly believe in and practice it.
The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now explain in accordance with the *dhāraṇī*.
May this merit, in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), Universally benefit the entire realm of sentient beings.
This is the concluding dedication. The first line concludes the meaning; the second line concludes the text; the final two lines constitute the dedication.

To say it is "profound, vast, and great" refers to the meaning of the three greatnesses—essence, characteristic, and function—which constitute the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Now, by condensing this into over eleven thousand words without omission, it is called a "general exposition";
that is to say, a concise text that encompasses manifold meanings. Nevertheless, the primary purpose of composing this treatise is to enable sentient beings to eliminate their doubts.
Having relinquished attachment, one now dedicates [the merit] so that all sentient beings may universally receive benefit.

This is intended to cause all sentient beings to give rise to true faith in *tathatā* (suchness), to rely upon it for practice, and thereby attain *samādhi*, proceeding toward the fruit of the unsurpassed path of Bodhi.
This is what is called dedication to the three locations. Regarding the term "dharma-nature," it refers to *tathatā-bodhi* (suchness-enlightenment). Universally...
Benefiting all; it is merely for the sake of sentient beings.
